items.body_text:
Libération de millions de barils de pétrole brut et de gazole par le G7 : quels effets attendre sur les prix des carburants ?
ENTRETIEN - Emmanuel Macron a annoncé vendredi que les pays du G7 avaient accepté de libérer une partie du stock stratégique. Le Figaro a interrogé l’économiste Patrice Geoffron pour évaluer les conséquences de cette décision.
Passer la publicité
Patrice Geoffron est professeur d’économie à l’université Paris-Dauphine et directeur du Centre de Géopolitique de l’Énergie et des Matières Premières (CGEMP). Il livre son analyse sur les annonces du G7 concernant la libération de «jusqu’à 100 millions de barils de pétrole brut et de gazole», censée permettre une baisse des prix du carburant.
Le Figaro - Depuis mars dernier, l’Agence internationale de l’énergie (AIE) a déjà procédé à la libération de 300 millions de barils. En comparaison, 100 millions de barils semblent bien peu. À quels effets peut-on s’attendre en Europe et aux États-Unis ?
Patrice Geoffron - En mars, on a surtout mis du brut sur le marché. Or aujourd’hui le problème n’est pas le brut, c’est le raffinage, avec les frappes ukrainiennes sur les raffineries russes, les arrêts au Moyen-Orient et la Chine qui garde ses carburants pour elle. Libérer directement du gazole, c’est mieux viser le goulot d’étranglement. Mais je reste dubitatif sur la portée de l’effet. 50 millions…

Désormais retenu par les autorités émiraties, Hammam Al-Hammami semble s’être radicalisé progressivement, notamment après un passage par la Syrie.
Cet homme de 29 ans, né aux Émirats arabes unis d’un père omanais et d’une mère syrienne, avait rejoint la compagnie Flydubai il y a huit mois, et avait démontré une ferveur religieuse hors du commun. L’un de ses collègues, dont le témoignage est relayé par le Times of Israël, a raconté qu’il «priait excessivement tout au long de la journée et refusait de serrer la main des femmes». L'enquête sur le vol Flydubai dérouté vers Tel-Aviv avance. Selon le procureur général des Émirats, le copilote planifiait un «acte terroriste». Les chaînes Al-Arabiyah, CNN et ABC ainsi que le Wall Street Journal affirment qu’il était interdit de vol par les autorités de son pays, qui le soupçonnaient de radicalisation. Selon Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, les investigations concernant l’incident du vol flydubai FZ1073 ont révélé que «le copilote avait commencé à mettre à exécution un acte terroriste», qu’il avait «agressé le commandant de bord dans le cockpit à l’aide de la hache de secours» et tenté «de prendre les commandes de l’avion». Il a précisé que l’enquête se poursuivait «afin d’établir toutes les circonstances de l’incident et ses motivations».
Hammam Al-Hammami, dont le père est omanais et la mère syrienne, aurait été influencé par des groupes islamistes radicaux lors d’un séjour en Syrie. Selon les mêmes médias, le futur agresseur avait rejoint Flydubai après avoir quitté son employeur Oman Air et postulé sans succès à un poste chez la compagnie Emirates.
Passer la publicité
L’incident a eu lieu le 30 septembre à bord d’un avion reliant Dubaï à Tel-Aviv, en Israël. Le copilote a poignardé en plein vol le commandant de bord indien, lequel a tout de même réussi à ouvrir la porte du cockpit, permettant à des passagers et membres d’équipage de maîtriser l’agresseur. L’avion, qui avait vertigineusement chuté pendant l’échauffourée, a pu se poser en urgence en Arabie saoudite. Les circonstances exactes de cette attaque et les motivations, encore floues, de l’agresseur, font l’objet d’une enquête aux Émirats arabes unis, où les deux pilotes ont été transférés.

items.title: "Madame Merzouk n'a jamais été interpellée": l'avocat de la mère de Nahel dément l'information selon laquelle elle aurait été arrêtée en marge des mobilisations lycéennes
items.summary: Des médias et des publications sur les réseaux sociaux relaient l’information selon laquelle la mère de l'adolescent a été interpellée en marge d'une manifestation lycéenne. Son avocat dénonce une attaque "malveillante" alors que la justice rendra sa décision sur la qualification retenue à l'encontre du policier qui a tué Nahel Merzouk le 24 novembre prochain.
items.body_text:
"Madame Merzouk n'a jamais été interpellée": l'avocat de la mère de Nahel dément l'information selon laquelle elle aurait été arrêtée en marge des mobilisations lycéennes
Son avocat réfute l'information. Mounia Merzouk, mère de l'adolescent tué par un policier en 2023 lors d'un contrôle routier, est accusée d'avoir été interpellée par les forces de l'ordre en marge d'une mobilisation lycéenne. Dans un communiqué de presse transmis à BFMTV, Me Franck Berton dément.
"Depuis le 2 octobre, plusieurs médias et publications sur les réseaux sociaux relaient de manière malveillante une information manifestement erronée selon laquelle madame Mounia Merzouk, mère de Nahel, aurait été interpellée en marge de mouvements de blocus lycéens. Nous démentons formellement ces affirmations: madame Merzouk n’a jamais été interpellée, entendue, ni visée par la moindre mesure policière ou judiciaire", écrit ainsi l'avocat.
"Le calendrier judiciaire entre dans une phase cruciale pour obtenir justice pour son fils"
Il estime également que "la diffusion de ce mensonge porte gravement atteinte à sa dignité et intervient alors que le calendrier judiciaire entre dans une phase cruciale pour obtenir justice pour son fils". En effet, la justice a examiné ce mardi les circonstances de la mort de Nahel Merzouk en 2023 à Nanterre et rendra le 24 novembre sa décision sur la qualification retenue à l'encontre du policier qui l'a tué, a indiqué la cour d'appel de Versailles.
"Nous refusons que la douleur d’une mère soit instrumentalisée pour tenter de discréditer son combat et pour servir les agendas politiques de certains", poursuit Me Franck Berton.

items.body_text:
INFO BFMTV. Femme visée par un spray transformé en lance-flammes à Marseille: un mineur de 15 ans interpellé et placé en garde à vue
Un mineur de 15 ans a été interpellé et placé en garde à vue ce vendredi 2 octobre dans l'après-midi, dans le cadre de l'enquête sur une femme visée par un spray transformé en lance-flammes artisanal lors des manifestations de lycéens à Marseille, a appris BFMTV.
Jeudi après-midi, aux abords de la place du 4 septembre dans le 7e arrondissement de Marseille, une femme s'opposait aux dégradations en cours - de manière pacifique - quand un individu tout de noir vêtu et capuche sur la tête a utilisé un spray avec un briquet pour en faire un lance-flammes. La victime a été touchée au visage.
Pas de séquelles apparentes
La victime avait déposé plainte ce vendredi matin. Selon nos informations, son visage n'a pas été brûlé de manière apparente. Elle ne souffre pas non plus de séquelles apparentes.

items.body_text:
Ce que l'on sait de l'agression d'un policier à Belfort après l'interpellation d'un adolescent dans une rivière, en marge de la mobilisation lycéenne
Un commandant de police a été violemment frappé par plusieurs personnes à Belfort vendredi matin. Des vidéos ayant circulé sur les réseaux sociaux le montrent en train d'interpeller un jeune un peu plus tôt dans un cours d'eau.
Dans un contexte de mobilisation des lycéens dans plusieurs villes de France, les images d'un policier haut gradé passé à tabac par des jeunes à Belfort (Territoire de Belfort), vendredi 2 octobre, ont suscité l'indignation jusqu'au plus haut niveau de l'Etat. Le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, a promis que "tout sera mis en œuvre pour identifier les auteurs de cet acte abject".
Des images très violentes montrant le tabassage d'un policier ont été largement relayées dès la fin de matinée vendredi, sur les réseaux sociaux, notamment par des syndicats de policiers. Un gradé en civil, commandant du renseignement territorial, apparaît poursuivi par "une horde d'individus particulièrement agressifs vraiment à son encontre", a décrit Paul-Edouard Lallois, procureur de la République de Belfort, lors d'un point-presse. L'un des protagonistes le fait chuter en arrière. Le policier est alors roué de coups. Un individu lui assène plusieurs coups de poing à la tête, un autre lui frappe le crâne à coups de pied.
La seule personne interpellée est sortie libre
Des renforts de police "sont rapidement intervenus pour disperser le groupe d'agresseurs" et porter secours au policier, a fait savoir le procureur. Il précise que la scène s'est déroulée à 9h15, aux abords du lycée Gustave-Courbet de Belfort. Le commandant en civil venait d'interpeller un jeune homme "suspecté d'avoir débuté un incendie sur la zone herbeuse qui entoure la zone proche du lycée".
Dans un post sur X, publié vendredi après-midi, quelques heures après les faits, le ministre de l'Intérieur Laurent Nuñez annonce qu'une enquête pour tentative d'homicide volontaire a été ouverte par le parquet de Belfort. Il souligne que le commandant de police "volontairement ciblé" a été "hospitalisé après avoir perdu connaissance" mais que "son état n'inspire plus d'inquiétude majeure". "Les premiers examens sont rassurants", a appris France Télévisions samedi matin de source policière, rapportant que le commandant de police souffre "de traumas superficiels".
Une seule interpellation liée à ce passage à tabac a, pour l'heure, eu lieu, celle d'un adolescent de 17 ans, scolarisé au lycée Gustave-Courbet, et n'ayant pas d'antécédents judiciaires. Le lycéen a été arrêté juste après l'agression du policier, a fait savoir le procureur de la République de Belfort. Sa garde à vue a pris fin samedi matin, a-t-il déclaré à France Télévisions, précisant qu'il est sorti libre, sans poursuites, puisqu'"aucun élément n'indique qu'il a pris part au lynchage", même s'il a reconnu avoir été présent sur les lieux.
Le magistrat assure que les investigations "avancent bien" et que plusieurs individus ayant participé au passage à tabac "ont été formellement identifiés" mais pas encore interpellés. Des parents "se sont manifestés par civisme et ont fourni des vidéos aux autorités de police", relaie également Paul-Edouard Lallois.
De nouvelles images sèment l'émoi
Vendredi après-midi, de nouvelles images diffusées après cette agression ont cependant été partagées et largement commentées sur les réseaux sociaux. Elles ont été filmées juste avant le lynchage du policier, a confirmé Paul-Edouard Lallois à France 3 Bourgogne Franche-Comté, qui les a authentifiées.
Dans une vidéo floue d'une trentaine de secondes, le commandant de police apparaît debout, les pieds dans une rivière, en train d'interpeller un jeune agenouillé dans l'eau. Le visage de l'individu semble entrer en contact avec la rivière et, alors qu'il paraît résister à l'interpellation, le policier le retient et tente de le menotter.

Le copilote du vol FlyDubai FZ1073, qui a poignardé le pilote du vol qui reliait Dubaï (Emirats arabes unis) à Tel-Aviv (Israël) avec 174 personnes à bord mercredi 30 septembre, a tenté de commettre un "acte terroriste", a confirmé le procureur général des Emirats arabes unis cité par l'agence d'Etat WAM, samedi 3 octobre. L'assaillant a utilisé une hache de secours du cockpit pour prendre le contrôle de l'appareil, selon la même source. Sans attendre les conclusions de l'enquête, le Premier ministre israélien, Benyamin Nétanyahou, a dénoncé une "tentative d'attentat terroriste jihadiste". S'il n'a pas écarté la possibilité d'un acte lié à des problèmes psychiatriques, Benyamin Nétanyahou a assuré que le copilote, de nationalité omanaise, "avait subi un endoctrinement islamiste radical".

items.title: "Nous sommes en premières lignes des dangers des pesticides" : une cinquantaine d'organisations appelle à une mobilisation dans l'Eure
items.summary: Des milliers de manifestants sont attendus samedi près de l'usine de pesticides du groupe Syngenta à Saint-Pierre-la-Garenne.
items.body_text:
"Nous sommes en premières lignes des dangers des pesticides" : une cinquantaine d'organisations appelle à une mobilisation dans l'Eure
Des milliers de manifestants sont attendus samedi près de l'usine de pesticides du groupe Syngenta à Saint-Pierre-la-Garenne.
Les mobilisations se multiplient après l'été caniculaire qu'a subi la France. Samedi 3 octobre, des "milliers de manifestants" sont attendus à Saint-Pierre-la-Garenne, dans l'Eure, près de l'usine du groupe Syngenta, géant des pesticides, pour protester contre leur utilisation. La Confédération paysanne, Les Soulèvements de la Terre, Cancer Colère et le Collectif de soutien aux victimes des pesticides de l'Ouest (CSVPO) sont à l'origine de cet appel, soutenu par une cinquantaine d'organisations réunies derrière le slogan "Stop pesticides".
Le parcours de la manifestation, proposé par les organisateurs, a été autorisé par la préfecture de l'Eure, a fait savoir Thomas Gibert, porte-parole de la Confédération paysanne. Il prévoit un cortège d'au moins 25 tracteurs. Dans l'Eure, "il y aura une présence en nombre de personnes malades et donc fragiles. On ne cherchera pas à rentrer sur le site, classé Seveso, et on ne souhaite pas qu'il y ait de confrontation avec les forces de l'ordre", ajoute le porte-parole.
"Cette manifestation est le fruit d'une alliance essentielle entre paysan.nes, victimes des pesticides, habitantes de territoires impactés par leurs usages et travailleurs.euses du secteur chimique", décrivent Les Soulèvements de la Terre dans un communiqué. Les participants souhaitent dénoncer les effets des produits phytosanitaires sur l'environnement et sur la santé, documentés par de multiples études. "Nous sommes en premières lignes des dangers des pesticides que nous produisons, les travailleurs agricoles aussi", lance le syndicat SUD Chimie-Solidaires.
Un site historique de Syngenta
Face à ces effets, les manifestants déplorent l'inaction des pouvoirs publics. "Tous les recours démocratiques ont été épuisés ou alors sont complètement niés par le gouvernement et le législateur", accuse Fleur Breteau, fondatrice de Cancer Colère et figure médiatique de la pétition de 2025 contre la loi Duplomb, qui souhaitait réintégrer l'acétamipride.
"Des bus et des convois de tracteurs s'organisent, des délégations internationales se préparent" donc pour se rendre à Saint-Pierre-la-Garenne. Syngenta, fabricant d'origine suisse, désormais chinois et "leader mondial", d'après son site, y est présent depuis plus de 20 ans.
"Les pesticides produits par les multinationales de l'agrochimie comme Syngenta valent-ils mieux que nos vies et celles de la biodiversité ainsi que notre santé ?"
Monique Savatier, du Collectif de soutien aux victimes des pesticides de l'Ouest
lors d'une conférence de presse
S'il assure respecter "pleinement le droit de se rassembler et de manifester", un porte-parole de Syngenta dénonce le "mal fondé" du choix du site pour le rassemblement : "70% de la production actuelle du site est utilisable en agriculture biologique", défend-il. items.title: Michigan won the game on a Hail Mary and got dropped out of the AP Top 25 anyway. Why?
items.summary: Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood (19) talks with Chris Bracy (7) after an NCAA college football game against the Western Michigan Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026, in Ann Arbor, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)2026-09-09T11:10:06Z Michigan won the game against Western Michigan but lost most of its support in The Associated Press Top 25 college football poll.Just like many viewers Saturday night, Top 25 voters were confused when one second was put back on the clock after it appeared time had run out at Mi
items.body_text:
Michigan won the game on a Hail Mary and got dropped out of the AP Top 25 anyway. Why?
Michigan won the game against Western Michigan but lost most of its support in The Associated Press Top 25 college football poll.
Just like many viewers Saturday night, Top 25 voters were confused when one second was put back on the clock after it appeared time had run out at Michigan Stadium. And they were dazed when JJ Buchanan came down with Bryce Underwood’s second Hail Mary pass to turn the four-touchdown-underdog Broncos’ 12-7 upset into a 13-12 loss.
The Mid-American Conference submitted appeals to the NCAA and the College Football Playoff administration asking for the result to be overturned to let the record show the Broncos actually won the game for purposes of rankings, evaluations and selection deliberations. The NCAA said its rules don’t allow a move like that and the CFP won’t release its first rankings until November.
Top 25 voters have weighed in, though.
The Wolverines dropped from No. 16 in the preseason poll to out of the Top 25 altogether in the first regular-season poll. It was the biggest fall from ranked to unranked after a win since at least 2008.
Michigan had appeared on all 69 preseason ballots and was listed as high as No. 10 on one. The Wolverines were on just 22 ballots Tuesday.
Bob Asmussen of the Champaign (Illinois) News-Gazette, in his 16th year as a voter, put Michigan No. 12 on his preseason ballot and said he knew that was a mistake as he watched Michigan’s offense sputter after scoring on its first possession. Voters sometimes hesitate to penalize a team that wins, but Michigan was going to drop off Asmussen’s ballot regardless. Forty-six other voters agreed with him.
“I saw them lose in my mind, but they didn’t technically lose,” Asmussen said. “It was so easy to drop them because of how horrible they were.”
Kirk Bohls of the Houston Chronicle, in his fourth decade as a voter, had Michigan No. 20 on his preseason ballot but said the Wolverines looked nothing like a Top 25 team. Bohls said he was disturbed by the way the end of the game played out, and the Big Ten’s statement about why 1 second was put on the clock after it showed zeroes didn’t convince him.

items.body_text:
In North Carolina, a race is on to restore critical peatland before it dries up or is destroyed
Scientists and investors are restoring a 23-square-mile (60-square-kilometer) tract of peatland in North Carolina to help curb climate-warming emissions and restore native habitat. (AP Video: Joshua A. Bickel)
BELHAVEN, N.C. (AP) — The birds are up with the sunrise — warblers, flycatchers, sparrows and towhees calling across the treetops. Deer browse on tender buds emerging from dense shrubs. Black bears scrounge for roots, insects and other edibles.
It’s an idyllic setting in North Carolina’s Inner Banks, where fields of cotton, soybeans and corn stretch for miles, country roads wend through stands of pines and thousands of bird watchers converge to witness the spring migration.
But it’s what’s underground that has drawn scientists and investors to this 23-square-mile (60-square-kilometer) tract: spongy, dense peat up to 15 feet (5 meters) deep.
They’re here to save it.
Fifty miles (80 kilometers) of ditches dug decades ago for an abandoned farming venture drained much of the water from thousands of years of accumulated peat, leaving the site vulnerable to drought and wildfires, altering its native habitats — and allowing it to emit 130,000 tons of climate-warming carbon dioxide a year.
“Our goal is for perpetuity to conserve these lands so they can’t become oil and gas fields, so they’re not mined for phosphorus or turned into parking lots and shopping centers,” said Tripp Wall, CEO of Colorado-based company Pantheon Regeneration. “They’re just these incredible systems that I feel are underappreciated here in the U.S. (that) for 10,000 to 15,000 years have been climatologically resilient until we screwed them up.”
Peatlands are a climate paradox. Though they account for just 3% of global land surface, they store one-third of the Earth’s carbon dioxide, more than all forests combined. But when degraded — primarily when farmers lower the water table to grow crops — destroyed or burned, they become part of the problem, releasing huge volumes of greenhouse gases, now about 6% of the annual global total from all sources.
And the type of peatlands found in North Carolina, and for hundreds of miles along the Eastern Seaboard, are among the most threatened in the world.
Pantheon plans to reverse the damage by blocking off ditches to control the water table and significantly reduce carbon dioxide emissions. Then it will cull invasive species and replant native grasses, flowers and other plants.
The restoration is modeled after other projects by nonprofits and government agencies, including at the adjacent 175-square-mile (453-square-kilometer) Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge — one of the largest peatland restoration projects in the U.S. — which provides habitat for threatened and endangered species such as red wolves, yellow pitcher plants and Atlantic white cedar, and has become an important stopover for migrating birds such as Tundra swans.
But what sets apart Pantheon’s project is a plan to sell carbon credits to tech companies and other corporations that want to compensate for their own greenhouse gas emissions, then use the money to restore and preserve a million acres (1,562 square miles, or 4,047 square kilometers) of peatland from Virginia to northern Florida over the next decade.
Each property will be permanently conserved and rewilded — “big corridors, big birding habitats, big biodiversity hotspots that have an outsized impact on climate,” said Wall.
Ancient ecosystems under threat
Neal Flanagan pushes a metal tube through roots and around buried logs until it sinks about a meter (3 feet). When he pulls it out, it’s packed with black soil.
Near the surface, it’s dry and full of dead fibers from plants like wood fern, blueberry and Lyonia. The middle is crumbly, moist and odorless, with bits of charcoal from long-ago fires. But the saturated bottom, 50% carbon, is the consistency of axle grease.

Flavio Bolsonaro: In the name of the father, sons, and holy ideology
The first round of Brazil’s presidential election on Sunday pits two well-known names in the political ring: Lula vs. Bolsonaro. But it’s not former president Jair Bolsonaro facing off against the incumbent head of state – it’s his eldest son, Flavio Bolsonaro. He’s less charismatic than his father but just as ideologically radical as the family patriarch.
Will “Son No. 1” become the second president from the Bolsonaro family? Flavio, the eldest of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro’s five children, is neck-and-neck in the polls with incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva as the country heads to the polls Sunday in the first round of the presidential election.
Jair Bolsonaro is likely following his 45-year-old son’s campaign closely. For the patriarch, this is not just a matter of family pride. Sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison after his convicting for plotting a coup following his 2022 election defeat, the former president is surely rooting for his son. “Bolsonaro Junior”, the Liberal Party’s candidate, has promised to grant his dad a pardon as soon as he assumes Brazil’s highest office.
But first, the eldest son must defeat incumbent President Lula. That is not a foregone conclusion.
Brand Bolsonaro
Flavio Bolsonaro is widely considered a shadow of his father. He is not a “charismatic and popular leader", said Andreza Aruska, director of the Brazil Institute at King’s College London. “He’s not a great orator either and he can come across as lacking in self-confidence,” added Corneel Weyers, a Brazil specialist at the Paris-based Center for International Studies (CERI) at Sciences Po.
While he is running under the Bolsonaro banner, the son has also had to maintain some distance from his convicted and jailed father on the campaign trail. “Jair Bolsonaro is no longer as popular, and slightly more than half the population believes he should serve his full sentence,” noted Georg Walter Wink, a Latin America specialist at the University of Copenhagen who has studied the foundations of Brazil’s far right.
But it’s still the power of the family name that has managed to catapult Flavio Bolsonaro into a statistical dead heat with Lula in the opinion polls.
At the official launch of his campaign in July, an AI-generated video of his jailed father endorsing the son was screened on stage. The video sparked a storm, with Brazil’s Supreme Court demanding an explanation about the appearance of the AI clone of Jair Bolsonaro, who is barred from making public statements while serving his sentence. The former president had to deny authorising the use of his image and voice for the deepfake video.
Read moreBrazil's Jair Bolsonaro denies authorizing deepfake for election message
Opting for a legally risky video screening in a country where the use of deep fakes is as widespread as it is strictly regulated does not exactly signal a break with Bolsonaro senior.
Watch moreFocus: What's real and what's fake? How AI is impacting Brazil's election race
But Flavio Bolsonaro is no stranger to public scrutiny. Last month, it emerged that Candidate Bolsonaro was under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering linked to the upcoming film “Dark Horse”. He is accused of seeking funding for the biopic glorifying his father, played by Jim Caviezel, a US actor linked to far-right circles. The film was originally scheduled for a September 11 release, but it was postponed indefinitely.
Political schizophrenia
Flavio Bolsonaro actually has little choice but to campaign on the strength of his family name. “He has almost nothing else to legitimise his candidacy,” noted Aruska.

items.title: Markets digest bank earnings after recent turmoil

Stocks slid Friday after a slate of earnings beats from big banks fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its next two meetings.
    
            Still, the major indices gained for the week. The Dow rose 400 points, or 1.2%. The S&P 500 gained 0.8% and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 0.3%.
    
            JPMorgan Chase on Friday reported first-quarter profit and revenue that crushed expectations, boosted by the Fed’s interest rate hiking campaign. Citigroup, Wells Fargo and PNC Financial also reported strong results.
    
            CEO Jamie Dimon warned investors in the company’s post-earnings conference call that they should prepare for interest rates to be higher for longer than expected.
    
            Wall Street seems to have taken note. Analysts increased their bets on a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed’s meeting in May and another in June.
    
            Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Friday that the central bank needs to continue tightening monetary policy, further weighing down markets.
    
            Austan Goolsbee, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said that it’s “definitely” possible the United States enters a mild recession after the tumult in banking last month.
    
            Meanwhile, retail sales data declined more than expected, suggesting that Americans’ spending power and the US economy are weakening.
    
            Consumer sentiment held fairly steady in April, even as concerns about a recession linger, according to the University of Michigan’s latest monthly survey.
    
            “There was too much news to digest this morning, but the key takeaway is that the Fed has room to do more harm,” Edward Moya, senior market analyst at OANDA, said in a note.
    
            The Dow slipped 144 points, or 0.4%.
    
            The S&P 500 tumbled 0.2%.
    
            The Nasdaq Composite sank 0.4%.
    
            As stocks settle after the trading day, levels might still change slightly.

items.title: Still haven't filed your taxes? Here's what you need to know
items.summary: So far this tax season, the IRS has received more than 90 million income tax returns for 2022.
items.body_text:
So far this tax season, the IRS has received more than 100 million income tax returns for 2022.
That means tens of millions of households have yet to file their returns. If yours is among them, here are some last-minute tax-filing tips to keep in mind as the Tuesday, April 18 deadline approaches.
Not everyone has to file on April 18: If you live in a federally declared disaster area, have a business there — or have relevant tax documents stored by businesses in that area — it’s likely the IRS has already extended the filing and payment deadlines for you. Here is where you can find the specific extension dates for each disaster area.
Thanks to many rounds of extreme weather in recent months, for instance, tax filers in most of California — which accounts for 10% to 15% of all federal filers — have already been granted an extension until Oct. 16 to file and to pay, according to an IRS spokesperson.
If you’re in the armed forces and are currently or were recently stationed in a combat zone, the filing and payment deadlines for your 2022 taxes are most likely extended by 180 days. But your specific extended filing and payment deadlines will depend on the day you leave (or left) the combat zone. This IRS publication offers more detail.
Lastly, if you made little to no money last year (typically less than $12,950 for single filers and $25,900 for married couples), you may not be required to file a return. But you may want to anyway if you think you are eligible for a refund thanks to, for instance, refundable tax credits such as the Earned Income Tax Credit. (Use this IRS tool to gauge whether you are required to file this year.) You also are likely eligible to use IRS Free File (intended for those with adjusted gross income of $73,000 or less) so it won’t cost you to submit a return.
Your paycheck may not be your only source of income: If you had one full-time job you may think that is the only income you made and have to report. But that’s not necessarily so.
Other potentially taxable and reportable income sources include:
- Interest on your savings
- Investment income (e.g., dividends and capital gains)
- Pay for part-time or seasonal work, or a side hustle
- Unemployment income
- Social Security benefits or distribution from a retirement account
- Tips
- Gambling winnings
- Income from a rental property you own
Organize your tax documents: By now you should have received every tax document that third parties are required to send you (your employer, bank, brokerage, etc.).
If you don’t recall receiving a hard copy of a tax form in the mail, check your email and your online accounts — a document may have been sent to you electronically.
Here are some of the tax forms you may have received:
- W-2 from your wage or salaried jobs
- 1099-B for capital gains and losses on your investments
- 1099-DIV from your brokerage or company where you own stock for dividends or other distributions from their investments
- 1099-INT for interest over $10 on your savings at a financial institution
- 1099-NEC from your clients, if you worked as a contractor
- 1099-K for payments for goods and services through third-party platforms like Venmo, CashApp or Etsy. The 1099-K is required if you made more than $20,000 in over 200 transactions during the year. (Next year the reporting threshold drops to $600.) But even if you didn’t get a 1099-K you still must report all the income that you made over third-party platforms in 2022.
- 1099-Rs for distributions over $10 that you received for a pension, annuity, retirement account, profit-sharing plan or insurance contract
- SSA-1099 or SSA-1042S for Social Security benefits received.

items.title: Retail spending fell in March as consumers pull back
items.summary: Spending at US retailers fell in March as consumers pulled back amid recessionary fears fueled by the banking crisis.
items.body_text:
Spending at US retailers fell in March as consumers pulled back after the banking crisis fueled recession fears.
Retail sales, which are adjusted for seasonality but not for inflation, fell by 1% in March from the prior month, the Commerce Department reported on Friday. That was steeper than an expected 0.4% decline, according to Refinitiv, and above the revised 0.2% decline in the prior month.
Investors chalk up some of the weakness to a lack of tax returns and concerns about a slowing labor market. The IRS issued $84 billion in tax refunds this March, about $25 billion less than they issued in March of 2022, according to BofA analysts.
That led consumers to pull back in spending at department stores and on durable goods, such as appliances and furniture. Spending at general merchandise stores fell 3% in March from the prior month and spending at gas stations declined 5.5% during the same period. Excluding gas station sales, retail spending retreated 0.6% in March from February.
However, retail spending rose 2.9% year-over-year.
The effect of smaller tax returns
Smaller tax returns likely played a role in last month’s decline in retail sales, along with the expiration of enhanced food assistance benefits, economists say.
“March is a really important month for refunds. Some folks might have been expecting something similar to last year,” Aditya Bhave, senior US economist at BofA Global Research, told CNN.
Credit and debit card spending per household tracked by Bank of America researchers moderated in March to its slowest pace in more than two years, which was likely the result of smaller returns and expired benefits, coupled with slowing wage growth.
Enhanced pandemic-era benefits provided through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program expired in February, which might have also held back spending in March, according to a Bank of America Institute report.
A slowing labor market
Average hourly earnings grew 4.2% in March from a year earlier, down from the prior month’s annualized 4.6% increase and the smallest annual rise since June 2021, according to figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The Employment Cost Index, a more comprehensive measure of wages, has also shown that worker pay gains have moderated this past year. ECI data for the first quarter of this year will be released later this month.
Still, the US labor market remains solid, even though it has lost momentum recently. That could hold up consumer spending in the coming months, said Michelle Meyer, North America chief economist at Mastercard Economics Institute.
“The big picture is still favorable for the consumer when you think about their income growth, their balance sheet and the health of the labor market,” Meyer said.
Employers added 236,000 jobs in March, a robust gain by historical standards but smaller than the average monthly pace of job growth in the prior six months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The latest monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, or JOLTS report, showed that the number of available jobs remained elevated in February — but was down more than 17% from its peak of 12 million in March 2022, and revised data showed that weekly claims for US unemployment benefits were higher than previously reported.
The job market could cool further in the coming months. Economists at the Federal Reserve expect the US economy to head into a recession later in the year as the lagged effects of higher interest rates take a deeper hold. Fed economists had forecast subdued growth, with risks of a recession, prior to the collapses of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.
For consumers, the effects of last month’s turbulence in the banking industry have been limited so far. Consumer sentiment tracked by the University of Michigan worsened slightly in March during the bank failures, but it had already shown signs of deteriorating before then.

items.body_text:
The FlyDubai co-pilot accused of attacking a captain on a Tel Aviv-bound flight earlier this week allegedly used the cockpit's "crash axe" in the attack and has been identified as a 29-year-old Omani national.
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, a Middle Eastern source told Fox News, adding that he was barred from flying with Oman Air — his country's airline — in 2024 due to concerns about extremist views.
The source also said authorities believe the co-pilot moved to Dubai later that year.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation into the attack on FlyDubai Flight 1073, said the co-pilot attacked Capt. Smit Machchhar with the cockpit's crash axe, incapacitating him and causing the aircraft to plummet before passengers on board seized control of the plane.
FLYDUBAI PASSENGER SAYS CO-PILOT STABBED CAPTAIN BEFORE TERRIFYING PLUNGE, EMERGENCY LANDING
The source said al-Hammami spent a significant part of his life outside Oman, including time living with his mother, who is from Syria.
According to the source, FlyDubai did not check with Oman Air about al-Hammami before hiring him.
A Gulf diplomat told The Associated Press that investigators are working to determine whether al-Hammami acted as a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups."
The AP separately reported that Oman had barred al-Hammami from flying over concerns that he had adopted extremist views.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday described the incident as an act of terrorism, saying the attacker had undergone "Islamic radicalization."

items.body_text:

FLYDUBAI PILOT SHOWED WORLD 'THE HIGHEST FORM OF COURAGE,' INDIA'S PM SAYS
The new details come as The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter, that the Omani national had previously been banned from flying over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views before later being hired by FlyDubai. The newspaper reported it was unclear whether Omani officials shared those concerns with other countries or airlines.
Fox News has not independently verified the reason the co-pilot was grounded by Oman Air.
The alleged attack unfolded Wednesday aboard FlyDubai Flight 1073 as the aircraft traveled from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
According to passengers and officials, the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain inside the cockpit, sending the aircraft into a steep dive that nearly tore it apart before two reserve pilots aboard the flight regained control and safely diverted the aircraft to Saudi Arabia. Passengers and crew members then helped overpower the suspect, according to accounts of the incident.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday described the incident as terrorism, saying the attacker had undergone "Islamic radicalization."

The United Arab Emirates is leading the investigation into the incident. A UAE spokesperson declined to comment to the Journal on the suspect's background, saying officials did not want to prejudice the outcome of the investigation or interfere with its course.
The incident has prompted renewed scrutiny of airline pilot vetting procedures and aviation security on flights serving Israel. Aviation security analysts told the Journal the episode represented a significant security failure and raised questions about how warning signs may have gone undetected before the co-pilot entered the cockpit.
FlyDubai has suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv following the attack.

items.title: UK man accused of planning terrorism acts against Nigel Farage also charged in murder of another politician
items.summary: British prosecutors charged Ann Widdecombe murder suspect Joshua Kerry with preparing terrorist acts allegedly targeting Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
items.body_text:
British prosecutors announced terrorism charges Friday against a 28-year-old man already in custody for the alleged murder of a conservative politician.
The Crown Prosecution Service charged Joshua Kerry of South Yorkshire with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, accusing him of "engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism, including against [Reform UK leader] Nigel Farage MP."
Kerry has been in the custody of His Majesty's government since late July, after he was arrested and accused of murdering former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe.
Prosecutors say Widdecombe was eating lunch in her Devon home July 8, when Kerry allegedly walked through the front door, beat her 21 times in the head with a hammer, took her wallet and was gone in an attack that lasted only two minutes.
IRAN PROBED IN ALLEGED TERRORISM PLOT AT UK BASE
Authorities say the latest charges against Kerry are related to events between May 31 and July 8.
In a statement, Senior National Coordinator for Counterterrorism Policing, Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, said, "The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the Counterterrorism Policing network. This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of inquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge."
U.K. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, posting on X, called the new charges against Kerry "extremely concerning" and sent her "profound sympathies" to the Farage family. She added that "an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all. This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life."
The Jo Cox Foundation, set up in honor of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016, said in a statement, "No one in public life should have to fear for their safety. Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endangered individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life. We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics."
Kerry is due back at Westminster Magistrates’ Court Wednesday.
Separately on Friday, Counterterrorism Policing announced charges against two Iranian men accused of plotting "to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area."
The Crown Prosecution Service charged 36-year-old Salam Ahmadyan and 34-year-old Rahman Salehi with "engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts, contrary to Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006," alleging that two men were "in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot."
SUSPECT CHARGED IN MURDER OF UK POLITICIAN ANNE WIDDECOMBE
Evans called the charges "extremely serious" while reiterating that "we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Evans noted the alleged plot comes during the High Holy Day period and "coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing antisemitic incidents across the U.K."
Ahmadyan and Salehi have been remanded and are scheduled to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court Saturday.
Fox News’ Thomas Ferraro and Stephanie Bennett and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

items.title: Brazil's big political rematch: What to know
items.summary: Four years after President Lula narrowly defeated Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil is back at the ballot box. This time, Lula faces Bolsonaro's son, Flávio, in a high-stakes rematch.
items.body_text:
Brazil's big political rematch: What to know
RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazil's presidential election is a rematch of the country's bitter 2022 contest — but with a twist. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is facing Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the man he narrowly defeated four years ago, Jair Bolsonaro.
Flávio, a 45-year-old senator, is carrying his father's political movement into Sunday's election. Jair Bolsonaro is now serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to overturn that loss. His son has promised to pardon him if elected.
The younger Bolsonaro says he is "a more moderate Bolsonaro," but has voiced few policy differences from his father. He pledges to pardon his father over the coup conviction, has cast doubt on humans' responsibility for climate change, and supports making it easier for Brazilians to buy guns.
Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth presidential term. The result will determine whether Brazil stays with Lula's left-leaning government or returns the Bolsonaro movement to the presidency.
The stakes extend well beyond the two families.
The next president is expected to nominate four of 11 Supreme Court justices, giving the winner a significant influence over the court for years to come.
The next president will also shape Brazil's economy and environmental policy, its relationship with the United States, and the future of its young democracy.
Here's what you need to know about Brazil's Oct. 4 election.
The election could stretch into late October
Polls suggest a tight race between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro among a field of presidential candidates. Federal and state legislative seats and state governorships are also up for grabs. If no candidate for president or governor receives more than 50% of the valid votes Sunday, the two candidates with the most votes will continue to a runoff on Oct. 25.
Brazil uses electronic voting machines and typically counts the results within hours. By Sunday night, it will likely be clear who is headed to a runoff — and how strongly each candidate performed in the first round.
The Bolsonaro name is carrying a lot of baggage
Jair Bolsonaro lost the 2022 election to Lula by a narrow margin and then became the central figure in an effort to reject the result. He is now serving a sentence for plotting a coup to overturn that loss, a scheme that included a plan to assassinate Lula, according to police.
The younger Bolsonaro has made clear that he intends to stand by his father. His pledge to pardon Jair if elected has turned the former president's legal fate into a campaign issue — and raised broader questions about the consequences of a Bolsonaro return to power for Brazil's democratic institutions.
Lula was jailed on corruption and money laundering charges in 2018, but the Supreme Court annulled his convictions in 2021 on procedural grounds. The episode remains a point of contention in Brazilian politics. His supporters point to other parts of his record, including reductions in poverty and efforts to protect the Amazon rainforest.
Both political camps inspire intensely loyal supporters — and fierce opposition. Polarization has remained high since the political and economic crisis of the mid-2010s, after which, said Federal University of Paraná political scientist Fábio Vasconcellos, "it became very difficult for any president to reach the higher approval ratings of previous decades."
Domestic issues could shape the vote
For all the attention on the Bolsonaro family and the battle over Brazil's political direction, voters are also focused on problems much closer to home.
Insecurity is a top issue for voters. items.title: How Brazil's two leading presidential candidates are talking about crime
items.summary: Crime is at the top of voters' concerns in Brazil ahead of Sunday's national elections. Many are calling for tougher measures — part of a broader rightward shift across Latin America.
items.body_text:
How Brazil's two leading presidential candidates are talking about crime
Crime is at the top of voters' concerns in Brazil ahead of Sunday's national elections. Many are calling for tougher measures — part of a broader rightward shift across Latin America.
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:
Brazilians want tougher measures to combat crime. Polls show that's their top issue going into this Sunday's elections, and that's not good news for Brazil's leftist president. He's perceived to be soft on criminals, and he's locked in a tight campaign against the conservative son of the country's former far-right president. NPR's Carrie Kahn reports.
(SOUNDBITE OF TURN SIGNAL CLICKING)
CARRIE KAHN, BYLINE: Robson Florencio hits the turn signal as he heads on to a busy boulevard in Belem, his working-class neighborhood on Sao Paulo's eastern side.
ROBSON FLORENCIO: (Non-English language spoken).
KAHN: "You're about to see all the people living on the streets, taking and selling drugs anywhere you see a shuttered shop," he says. "We don't go out at night anymore," adds the 38-year-old father of two small kids.
FLORENCIO: (Non-English language spoken).
KAHN: We head into one of Sao Paulo's more chic, or affluent, areas. He points to a tree-lined median. About two months ago, an assailant ran up to his car, smashed the window and snatched the cell phone right out of the hand of his client sitting in the backseat. It doesn't matter where you are, he says.
FLORENCIO: (Non-English language spoken).
KAHN: "Violence hits even where the rich people live," he adds. While public security data shows a drop in Brazil's homicide rate and in violent robberies, street crime remains high in many cities. Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro are infamous for snatch-and-grab cell phone theft.
Crime dominates conservative presidential hopeful Flavio Bolsonaro's regular stump speech. He's considered more moderate than his bombastic father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, now jailed for attempting a coup. However, the younger Bolsonaro has taken to waving a huge plastic machete at recent rallies.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
FLAVIO BOLSONARO: (Non-English language spoken).
(CHEERING)
KAHN: "Attention all rapists, abuser of women and children - chemical castration is coming for you," he says. Crime and insecurity used to be key issues in only local races since Brazil's states run most public safety forces. But Roberto Simone, a Brazilian risk analyst, says this year is different. It's become key in the top ticket races and presidential contest.
ROBERTO SIMON: It is definitely mobilizing voters. And generally speaking, that's bad news for the left. It is a topic that traditionally favors more conservative candidates.
KAHN: On the campaign trail, incumbent leftist president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva talks more about moving people out of poverty and improving opportunities as a way to fight crime, along with better coordination to take down crime bosses.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
PRESIDENT LUIZ INACIO LULA DA SILVA: (Non-English language spoken).
KAHN: "Working together, I guarantee the Brazilian people will win," he recently told the hosts of a popular global network news show. Such long-anoterm reform messages don't excite Latin Americans as much as the iron fist or Mano Dura approach to fighting crime. Right-wing candidates have chalked up big wins in the region with tough-on-crime campaigns, says Ben Gedan of the Washington-based Stimson Center.
BEN GEDAN: In the short term, voters want to see more police on the streets and more criminals in jail or in the morgue.
KAHN: The last seven presidential contests in Latin America all went to conservatives and far-right candidates.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Non-English language spoken).
KAHN: At a Bolsonaro rally overlooking Copacabana's beach, 63-year-old Marli Alves says she voted for Lula four years ago. But with what she says is out-of-control crime, she's switching to Bolsonaro.
MARLI ALVES: (Non-English language spoken).
KAHN

items.title: The G7 will release 100 million reserve barrels of diesel fuel over the next 4 months
items.summary: After increased pressure from Washington, the G7 held an emergency meeting on energy. The world's wealthiest nations say they will release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel fuel in their reserves.
items.body_text:
The G7 will release 100 million reserve barrels of diesel fuel over the next 4 months
After increased pressure from Washington, the G7 held an emergency meeting on energy. The world's wealthiest nations say they will release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel fuel in their reserves.
JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:
It seems President Trump has prevailed on the world's wealthiest nations to release diesel from their stockpiles. That decision came earlier today at an emergency G7 meeting. Trump had been threatening to stop all exports of U.S. diesel fuel if Europeans didn't release their own diesel. A U.S. ban would have pushed already high global diesel prices even higher. And those steep prices, which have risen substantially since the U.S. went to war with Iran, are already squeezing everyone, from farmers to small business owners. NPR's Eleanor Beardsley joins us now from Paris. Hi there.
ELEANOR BEARDSLEY, BYLINE: Good afternoon, Juana.
SUMMERS: Eleanor, tell us more about what the G7 decided today.
BEARDSLEY: Well, in this emergency meeting, they decided to release 100 million barrels over the next four months, beginning immediately, and they'll begin by releasing barrels of diesel fuel in the first 20 days. France chairs the G7, and President Emmanuel Macron convened the meeting by video conference, which included the head of the International Energy Agency, which is based in Paris.
Macron said the release would be coordinated by the IEA. Macron said G7 members would also coordinate to increase production and bring down transport costs like the insurance for tankers, he said, and push to get more tankers flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.
SUMMERS: And, Eleanor, President Trump's earlier threat to cut off diesel fuel experts - did it work?
BEARDSLEY: Well, I would say, yes, that pressure did work, even though no one outright said so. You know, Europe is extremely dependent on imports of oil and diesel from the Middle East and the U.S., and its dependence has increased since Russia's war on Ukraine - because Russia no longer is a supplier - and since the Iran war and the choking of the Strait of Hormuz. Macron has called a possible U.S. diesel export ban, quote, "catastrophic." Just take France. It consumes about 600,000 barrels of diesel a day and imports half of that.
Macron convened today's meeting after calling President Trump. Macron wants a coordinated approach between partners to the energy crisis, and the French president spoke to the media just after the G7 put out its statement, and he said this. Let's listen.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
PRESIDENT EMMANUEL MACRON: (Speaking French).
BEARDSLEY: "We have also agreed there will be no export bans or limitations between partners in any category," he said. "There were rumors in the market about that, and that's what made prices rise," said Macron. "So what we've done sends a signal of unity, and this should also help bring world prices down." You know, the G7 statement includes in writing that commitment of no export restrictions on energy products between G7 partners. That's a win for the Europeans who import a lot of oil and diesel from the U.S.
SUMMERS: What are the domestic political considerations for EU leaders?
BEARDSLEY: Well, they're huge. You know, while Europeans are not involved in the Iran War and did not support it, skyrocketing energy prices are hurting consumers and businesses on the continent and putting so much pressure on governments that are already not very popular. Europe's diesel prices have more than doubled since the start of the U.S.-Iran war in late February.
In France, Juana, diesel is $10 a gallon. Farmers, fishermen, truckers - all these categories of workers use diesel. They're also known to protest and shut down cities and highways, so leaders are really worried about social unrest. You know, we've seen some student protests turn violent here in France in the last week. It wasn't directly related to fuel costs, but anything could happen.

items.title: ‘Digger’ Gives Tom Cruise A Belief System Even Crazier Than Scientology
items.summary: Part of Tom Cruise’s contemporary appeal has been, in old-school movie-star fashion, his distance from the dirge of hot topics trending in the news. items.body_text:
Part of Tom Cruise’s contemporary appeal has been, in old-school movie-star fashion, his distance from the dirge of hot topics trending in the news. In catastrophe or calm, we could rely on him to blow up terrorist bunkers, hang off airplanes, and save civilization without lecturing us about it. “Top Gun: Maverick” flew closer to politics, but even that was patriotic escapist fantasy. Cruise’s latest role, as the eccentric oil tycoon at the center of Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s “Digger,” brings these worlds into head-on collision.
“Digger” is an environmentalist screed dressed as a pastiche of Stanley Kubrick’s “Dr. Strangelove,” the great Cold War satire of nuclear brinkmanship and mutually assured destruction. Cruise plays Digger Rockwell, a larger-than-life Texas oil baron who trots around his stately home in silk pajamas and cowboy boots, obsesses over his gaunt and withering cat, and bellows questions at subordinates who stutter back like stunned imbeciles. His Southern twang is so heavy that Daniel Craig in “Knives Out” begins to sound understated.
When one of Rockwell’s Greenland drilling sites, following a spate of ignored warnings, destabilizes a colossal ice shelf that breaks free and heads toward Europe, the film erupts into environmental apocalypse on the scale of an Al Gore fever dream. Riz Ahmed is excellent as Ganesh, Digger’s tree-hugging scientist, whose vintage-inspired suits and nervous mannerisms make him feel transported from a Wes Anderson set. But this is Cruise’s show. If you enjoyed his gloriously repellent Les Grossman in “Tropic Thunder,” there is considerable pleasure in watching him commit to the bit.
For its first act, “Digger” works surprisingly well. The performances are spirited, the pacing taut, and Emmanuel Lubezki’s camera — often peering upward from bizarrely low angles — gives the absurdity a wonderfully warped grandeur. Then the film begins accumulating ideas, detours, and stylistic conceits faster than Iñárritu can organize them. What begins as a briskly staged catastrophe comedy gradually drifts into something more ponderous and self-conscious, and much of the comic momentum simply evaporates.
The overarching failure of “Digger” is that Iñárritu takes his subject too seriously for the satire to land. He is far too talented a filmmaker to misunderstand “Strangelove,” but his political obsessions keep narrowing the joke. Kubrick subjected everyone to ridicule: generals, Soviets, scientists, Red Scare hysterics, and the strategic minds who had rationalized mankind to the brink of annihilation. “Digger” only knows whom it wants you to despise. It is like making Luigi Mangione the protagonist of a movie about health insurance and expecting the satire to remain even-handed.
A genuinely Strangelovian climate comedy might have turned the hysteria itself into part of the target: some rogue eco-billionaire blocks out the sun with geoengineering, world leaders retreat to a crisis bunker, and everyone accidentally triggers a permafrost doomsday loop while arguing over carbon offsets. Iñárritu instead gives us villainous capitalists, buffoonish Republican-coded politicians, and environmental prophets whose warnings are vindicated almost wholesale.
There is another important difference. “Dr. Strangelove” confronted the spectre of nuclear annihilation without becoming hopeless. Its cynicism was rooted in the absurdity of mankind possessing the means to destroy itself and then entrusting those means to vain generals and bureaucrats. Beneath the black comedy was still an appeal to sanity. “Digger’s” environmental apocalypse feels foreordained (“that ship has sailed,” Ganesh tells us, before disappearing into a bottle of whisky to drown the portent). Its warnings have already been ignored, and its calamities are irreversible. It is a remarkably joyless worldview for a supposed comedy.

Congratulations, gals; we did it! We beat the Final Boss on the way to complete liberation from the bounds of the patriarchy and the confines of our own sex, and found that the grand prize is womanhood’s propensity to toxify our own freedom.
For what brings about this celebration? Motherhood, of course. Not just any old run-of-the-mill mom. Mother of the Year! She goes by “Erika,” and she, her daughter, and her (apparently total deadbeat) husband attended the September 25 San Francisco Giants game versus the Minnesota Twins.
What was a normally innocuous family outing turned into the Rorschach test of our deranged, post-sex society. Erika was caught on camera returning from concessions to her seat, juggling a tower of food in both hands with her toddler strapped to her in a carrier. The on-air broadcast team proceeded to narrate an imaginary scenario in which Erika was doing all the things — juggling the kid, food, and navigating safely to her seat — while her husband flippantly greeted her and chowed down on the grub, leaving his wife to act as the holder of child and dinner. How rude!
Mom of the year https://t.co/nUTgAhr0nr
— Barstool Sports (@barstoolsports) September 24, 2026
Naturally, the ultrafeminists swooped in, circling the family as they writhed under the white-hot glare of the social media spotlight.
What Erika had to explain to the TikTok toxic feminist crowd and conspiratorial online busybodies (after she had to prove to a handful of weirdos that she was an actual person, not some AI manifestation) is that her husband was carrying the weight of the death of a beloved and longtime friend. Wives might know him as “that guy” — your husband’s friend who he’s had since before you were even dating, the guy who has the childhood/grade school/college stories that may or may not end with someone in jail, the guy who you felt like you had to ask for your husband’s hand in marriage, and who, after marriage, felt like an adopted part of the family. That kind of friend. And Erika was doing her part to lighten some of that weight.
This pile-on is an indictment of the online mob that thinks so highly of itself and its worldly wisdom that it can judge an entire marriage and family dynamic from a one-minute clip narrated by two dudes in a broadcast booth. But in our TikTok age, where social contagion and relentless judgment join forces from behind the unblinking eye of a cellphone, this is the price of admission.
To me, an actual run-of-the-mill mom, this is another day that ends in Y. Not because I’m a slave to my husband or broken under the weight of my three young children or there’s some nefarious network of men conspiring to keep women under the heels of the patriarchy. This is a case of a mom working at maximum efficiency. It’s what we do best. And if the harpy crowd of permanently insufferable suffragettes had any sense of the world, that’s what they’d see, too.
It’s been 106 years since American women gained the right to vote through the 19th Amendment. Since then, women have been welcomed into the workforce, athletic playing fields, politics, entertainment, the arts, organized religion, civic organizations, the military, and media. Heck, even the Boy Scouts, which by its very name seems pretty cut-and-dry about who it accepts, made space for us. But it just isn’t enough, is it? There must be some explanation about why women are more unhappy than ever, why we just can’t shake off the chains of oppression that must exist despite us having surpassed all of these benchmarks of equality and freedom. After all, we can even have babies and kill them for any reason or no reason! and men will just shrug.
We can strut all the slut walks we want and demand not to be treated like sexual objects. We can dress provocatively and then screech about toxic masculinity when the male gaze is offered in our direction. We can climb to the top of corporate ladders and complain about work-life balance. We can insist that women are strong, indep

* * *

Busy raising a brood under the age of six, Kate assures me, “I guess I normally look like I’m about to get thrown up on.” No matter what, she’s ready for anything.
After a few minutes, I feel like I’ve known forever. She has the empathy of a best friend. It makes sense, considering how she found her true calling in empowering others to take charge of their health.
She spent her early career working in a life-saving trauma hospital in Washington, D.C., providing care for everything from “gunshot wounds to catastrophic heart attacks.” But she recalls, “I started to see really young people having these end-stage organ failures and massive cardiovascular events, strokes, heart attacks, or complications from years and years of hypertension.”
That’s when she left her bedside gig, hoping to incentivize preventative care at Blue Cross Blue Shield. But she was still working against the clock, just “checking boxes and making sure that people are taking their medications … Nobody gets healthy in the doctor’s office.”
“I thought working inside of the health care system would be how I would have an influence on people’s health and wellness,” she says. Like it did for so many people, the lockdown reshaped her vision of health. “I started to realize … if you want to impact real health, you have to be able to talk to them where they live. And that’s really my heart and mission.” She’s bringing her family along for the ride.

She cooks up healthy family meals with her kids as sous chefs, and you’ll see them on Instagram climbing into her lap or hanging over her shoulders during home gym workouts or confessionals in the car.
Kate could probably nurse anyone back to health, but I laugh when she cites the Pew Research Center for this fun tidbit: “The number one thing that vexes women in their forties in their marriages is their husband’s lack of health.” (Don’t freak out — she thinks it works both ways in the best partnerships.) “I want you to find me attractive, I want to be healthy for you, I don’t want to become a burden for you because of the choices I’ve made,” she advises. “There are so many things that are out of our control when it comes to health. But the things that I can take control of, I want to do that.”

If you’ve ever heard Kate’s advice about moving your body, it should come as no surprise that she gets moving as soon as she can. She wakes up around 5:30 a.m. while the house is still quiet to grab a black coffee and tidy up.

items.body_text:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito said he considered retiring this year but decided to stay because he believed he could still contribute to the court, according to a CBS News interview clip released Friday.
Alito, 76, was nominated by President George W. Bush and joined the Supreme Court in 2006. He told CBS News chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford that he expects to revisit the decision each term. He did not give a departure date, leaving open whether President Donald Trump will get another opportunity to nominate a justice.
Crawford asked why Alito remained on the bench despite pressure for him to retire.
“I thought about it,” Alito said.
Asked to confirm that he had considered leaving, Alito explained that retirement had become a question he needed to weigh regularly.
“Well, it’s something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term,” he said. “But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place. So that was basically it.”
Crawford then asked whether he would reconsider each year.
“Yeah, I think I have to,” Alito replied.
Crawford also asked whether waiting could put his work on the court at risk. Alito said neither his personal circumstances nor the politics surrounding a future vacancy could be predicted with certainty.
“I think it’s too hard to predict,” he said. “It’s too hard to predict how for anybody, and particularly when you reach a certain age, what your situation will be a year from now, two years from now and so forth.”
“And it’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be and what any president might do with respect to a replacement,” he added.
A vacancy during Trump’s presidency would give him a chance to select a fourth Supreme Court justice. During his first term, Trump nominated Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. All three won Senate confirmation.
In an exclusive interview with Breitbart News in July, Trump said he was “certainly prepared” to fill a possible Supreme Court vacancy. He praised Alito as “one of the greatest of all time” and said he would like to appoint a younger version of him. Trump did not name a potential replacement.
“Well I think, you know, if you listen to people, there are three potential vacancies for various reasons, so I’m certainly prepared,” Trump told Breitbart News. “There are a lot of great people out there who would like to have that position.”

items.title: Republicans Pull The Plug On 2 Swing States As GOP’s Midterm Prospects Become Increasingly Grim
items.summary: Republicans Pull The Plug On 2 Swing States As GOP’s Midterm Prospects Become Increasingly Grim
items.body_text:
Republican political action committees (PACs) and the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) scaled back their time and resources in North Carolina and Georgia while pouring large sums of money into keeping red seats just weeks before the midterm elections.
Republican committees and PACs spent unprecedented amounts of money in red states and districts while polling results shifted against Republican candidates. These PACs pulled support away from North Carolina and Georgia, where Republican Georgia Rep. Mike Collins and Republican North Carolina Senate nominee Michael Whatley face tight races, according to Punchbowl News.
Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff led Collins by an average of eight points, and former Democratic North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper led by nine points, according to RealClearPolling.
The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), the main GOP super PAC, paused its ad spending in North Carolina Friday after spending $30 million on the Senate race, Semafor first reported. The super PAC was launching a seven-figure ad campaign in Kansas, a traditionally red state where Republican Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall faces tough competition against Democratic Kansas Senate nominee Adam Hamilton. (RELATED: Republicans Pouring Unprecedented Amounts Of Money Into Midterms To Save GOP Candidates In Red States)
Kansas has not had a Democratic senator since 1939. Marshall became embroiled in controversy after he sued 700 patients for debts, leading to 81 arrests, according to The New York Times.
“SLF’s job is to maintain the majority and this move reflects the most effective and efficient use of resources to do exactly that,” a spokesperson said.
A spokesperson for Whatley’s campaign remained confident the campaign had the resources to defeat Cooper. The campaign did not clarify if any other group or PAC would pick up the slack to help Whatley win.
“Roy Cooper recently said about federal elections in North Carolina, ‘Democrats are often ahead until they are not,’” spokesperson DJ Griffin told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “Undecided Voters who break late decide the election in North Carolina and the majority of those Late-Breakers typically go Republican. We feel confident we have the resources to highlight Career Politician Roy Cooper’s 40 Years of Failures and win in November.”
Republican North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis announced he would not seek reelection in June 2025 after President Donald Trump threatened to back a primary challenger over the senator’s vote against the One Big Beautiful Bill. Trump endorsed Whatley early in the cycle after he chaired the Republican National Committee alongside his daughter-in-law, former co-chair Lara Trump, during Trump’s winning 2024 presidential campaign.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer appeared optimistic about the SLF’s pause.
“The fact that the biggest Republican Senate Super PAC took its money out of North Carolina today and put it into Kansas says all you need to know about which direction the Senate Majority is headed,” Schumer said.

items.title: AOC, Bernie Sanders Introduce Bill To Ban Feds From Using Flock Cameras
items.summary: ‘Cannot allow America to become a surveillance state’
items.body_text:
Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democratic Oregon Sen. Jeff Merkley and independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced legislation Friday to effectively end the federal use of automated license plate readers (ALPRs).
The Ban Flock Act would prohibit the federal government from purchasing, using or possessing an ALPR, accessing its data or using federal funds to purchase ALPRs, but it does not outright ban the cameras, according to the bill’s text. It would block certain federal grant funding for state and local governments that use ALPRs or contract with ALPR companies, such as Flock Safety, although it does not outright prohibit local agencies from purchasing the technologies with local tax dollars.

No lawmakers have introduced bills to ban the cameras altogether. Republican Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna said in July she planned to introduce a bill to ban the cameras, although she has yet to introduce the bill.

items.summary: This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. items.body_text:
This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
During the Sand Creek Fire, which has burned since the start of August in southwestern Montana, difficult terrain and fire-weakened trees posed hazards to crews searching for areas still smoldering on steep slopes after the blaze passed. So instead of relying only on firefighters to find hidden embers, fire managers used unmanned aircraft to seek out heat sources.
The operation is part of a broader technological shift underway in wildfire response. The US Forest Service is evaluating firefighting robots on the ground, and researchers are exploring how artificial intelligence could help predict where wildfires will ignite and how quickly fires will spread. Federal agencies already use drones to map fires, detect hotspots and ignite prescribed burns, and are testing their capability to drop firefighting foam and water on blazes.
“Drones are now a critical tool in federal wildfire response, providing real-time infrared imagery to map fire perimeters, detect hotspots, and monitor dangerous or inaccessible terrain, which helps firefighters make safer, faster tactical decisions,” said Meredith Hollowell, a Forest Service press officer, in a statement to Inside Climate News.
The Federal Aviation Administration said drones provide real-time situational awareness by detecting hotspots, mapping fire perimeters and aiding firefighter efforts in dangerous environments.
But drones are no longer being used just to watch fires from above.
During aerial ignition operations in which fire managers intentionally burn vegetation to expand control lines or remove fuels before the main fire reaches them, unmanned aircraft can reduce the exposure of pilots or firefighters to some high-risk conditions, Hollowell said.
The technology has become established enough that federal agencies now have specific positions for UAS pilots, managers, module leaders and data specialists, as well as procedures for ordering drone resources for wildfire incidents.
The Forest Service is also testing autonomous ground vehicles that could carry equipment and supplies into areas where conventional vehicles or manual transport may be difficult or unsafe. In June, the agency and its partners tested robotic vehicles on rough terrain in Georgia that was designed to replicate conditions encountered during wildfire operations.
The vehicles were expected to carry payloads of up to 800 pounds, including firehose packs, heavy hand tools, water containers, and medical supplies. Evaluators tested their ability to navigate rocky roads, uneven ground, and slopes while carrying operational loads.
While the technology is not yet ready for routine wildfire operations, Charlie Gray, a Forest Service district fire management officer, said it shows promise for reducing firefighters’ exposure to risk while getting equipment and supplies to the fireline.
Hollowell said the Forest Service expects advances in AI-enabled unmanned aerial systems, combined with improved fire-behavior models and data from satellites, cameras and weather models to revolutionize wildfire detection and tracking, suppression efficiency and firefighter safety.
Researchers are already examining the potential advantages of combining drones with artificial intelligence.
Phinehas Lampman, a researcher at the University of Idaho, developed a system using thermal-infrared images collected by drones and machine-learning models to analyze fire behavior and predict a fire’s rate of spread. Lampman spent seven years working on engine and hotshot crews for the Clearwater-Potlatch Timber Protective Association and the Forest Service before turning to research, according to his University of Idaho bio.
