items.body_text:
Delegations from the government and the opposition began a second round of talks on Saturday afternoon to discuss various issues, including the PTI’s planned Oct 4 march to Islamabad.
The meeting, chaired by National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq, is aimed at defusing the country’s ongoing political crisis. It comes ahead of the PTI’s planned Oct 4 protest march demanding the release of party founder Imran Khan, which has emerged as the latest point of contention between the party and the federal government.
As the huddle began, the NA speaker expressed his hope that the talks would proceed in the same “cordial atmosphere” as Friday’s, according to a post on the NA’s X account.
The government side includes minister for frontier regions Amir Muqam, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, PM’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah.
Senator Sherry Rehman and MNAs Syed Naveed Qamar and Ejaz Hussain Jakhrani are representing the PPP.
The opposition delegation comprises Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, PTI interim chairman MNA Gohar Ali Khan, Opposition Chief Whip Amir Dogar, MNA Asad Qaiser, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja and PTI Sindh President Haleem Adil Sheikh.
KP CM adamant on long march
Earlier in the day, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi voiced his determination to hold the long march on Oct 4 and vowed to prevent a repeat of the events of May 9, 2023.
In response, Chaudhry said the KP CM’s statements could affect the ongoing negotiation process and urged PTI leaders not to engage in such discourse.
In his post, CM Afridi said PTI was the largest and most popular political party in Pakistan. “Pakistan is a democratic country whose Constitution grants us the right to peaceful protest.”
Detailing his long march plan, Afridi said an “ocean of people” would begin its journey from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat at 1pm on Oct 4.
The party would continue its struggle until the supremacy of the Constitution and the law was ensured in Pakistan and an independent judiciary was restored, the PTI leader added.
“All demands of the PTI are in accordance with the constitution and the law.”
In his post, he stressed that the party would “neither allow May 9 to happen again nor allow anyone else to repeat it”.
Reacting to the KP CM’s remarks, Chaudhry said Afridi’s statements could affect the ongoing negotiation process even though the government wanted them to be “meaningful and fruitful”.
He urged PTI leaders to refrain from making such statements until the final stage of the negotiations, so that the dialogue process was not “harmed”.
“The language that Sohail Afridi is using against his opponents and our leadership does not seem like that of a chief minister; his statements are extremely indecent and reprehensible,” Chaudhry said.
Speaking to reporters ahead of the meeting, PPP’s Rehman stressed that her party was making efforts to solve issues in a democratic manner.
Asked about KP CM being adamant on the PTI march, the PPP leader said it was up to the PTI, but added that she would refrain from making comments before the talks conclude.
While acknowledging that each party had its positions, she noted that the objective of holding negotiations was to “discuss those positions”.
Opposition decides SOPs
Earlier in the day, the opposition held a meeting in which standard operating procedures (SOPs) for the talks were finalised.
It was decided that it would be proposed during the meeting that no one from either side would speak to the media during the talks and that a joint statement would be issued afterwards to avoid any misunderstanding.

items.body_text:
Pakistan summoned the Indian chargé d’affaires to lodge a strong protest over the killing of two Pakistani civilians by Indian Border Security Force (BSF) personnel in the Bedian sector along the international border, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Saturday.
Two unarmed Pakistani civilians were martyred and another was injured in firing by India’s BSF near the border in Kasur on Friday.
“The BSF personnel resorted to unprovoked and lethal force against unarmed civilians. Such use of force was wholly unjustified and grossly disproportionate, resulting in the tragic loss of two precious lives,” the FO said.
Pakistan categorically rejects any attempt to mischaracterise the deceased as “infiltrators”, it added.
The FO said the incident constituted a serious violation of fundamental human rights, including the right to life, and raised concerns over the protection of civilian life under international law.
It called on the Indian side to “conduct an immediate, transparent and credible investigation”, take appropriate disciplinary and legal action against those responsible, and formally communicate the findings and action taken to the government of Pakistan.
India was further urged to “respect fundamental human rights and international law, strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements and established border procedures, exercise maximum restraint in such situations, and take effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future”, the FO said.
The three civilians were residents of Ladhar village and had moved a few steps ahead of a border pillar when the BSF opened fire on them without warning. All three were unarmed.
The deceased were identified as Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jutt, both residents of Jattan Wali Haveli, Ladhar. The injured civilian was taken for medical treatment.
According to security sources, none of the three men had attempted to cross the border fence, with the incident described as a violation of the border agreement and standard operating procedures governing the international border.
The development comes a day after Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry lampooned India’s claims of “neutralising” a “terrorist” allegedly linked to the Pakistani military, presenting the individual during a press conference.
Asked whether the recent allegations could trigger another armed conflict between the neighbours during the press briefing, he affirmed that Pakistan’s armed forces were always ready for any such move and warned of “very harsh” retribution.

items.body_text:
Hasan Nawaz’s fighting 96 went in vain as Pakistan fell 19 runs short of India’s 212-run target to settle for silver in the Asian Games men’s cricket final at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin, Japan on Saturday.
Hasan struck five fours and seven sixes in his 51-ball innings before being caught behind off Shivam Dube from the final ball of the match, with Pakistan finishing on 192 for six.
Needing 33 from the last over after reaching 179 for five, Pakistan kept their hopes alive when Hasan hit Dube for a boundary and then a six. But a yorker from the India all-rounder followed by two dot balls left Hasan needing four for his century from the final delivery.
He attempted to clear the infield but was caught by wicket-keeper Sanju Samson, ending an innings that had briefly brought Pakistan back into contention.
Hasan’s dismissal completed a remarkable recovery after Pakistan had been 39 for three after six overs. He and Saim Ayub put on 87 for the fourth wicket before Saim was dismissed for 29 off 22 balls in the 15th over.
Hasan had reached his half-century from 28 balls and continued to attack India’s spinners, particularly Ravi Bishnoi, who conceded 44 from his three overs.
Pakistan were 126 for three after 14 overs, requiring 86 from the last 36 balls, but Dube removed Saim and Abdul Samad in successive stages of the closing overs to keep India ahead.
Saim was caught by Washington Sundar at square leg for 29 after attempting to use Dube’s pace, while Samad made nine before being caught by Tilak Varma off Washington in the 18th over.
Despite those setbacks, Hasan continued the assault. He reached 68 from 36 balls after hitting Axar Patel for a six in the 16th over and then struck two fours in Dube’s next over, one of them coming through an edge after he flashed at a short, wide delivery.
Pakistan reached 160 for four after 17 overs, needing 52 from the final 18 balls.
Saad Masood kept the chase alive with two sixes in his unbeaten 12 off five balls, but Bumrah’s fourth over yielded only 11 runs, leaving Pakistan 33 short with six balls remaining.
Dube was given the final over and conceded a boundary and a six to Hasan, but his yorkers at the crucial moment denied Pakistan the chance to complete the chase.
India’s bowlers had earlier kept Pakistan under pressure after the batters had posted 211 for six.
Pakistan’s chase had begun brightly enough but lost momentum after Sahibzada Farhan and Usman Khan departed in successive overs.
Farhan made 10 off 11 balls before attempting a slog-sweep against Sundar and finding Patel at deep midwicket. Usman followed for three off six, slogging a fuller delivery from Patel to Dube at midwicket.
Maaz Sadaqat, who made 23 off 18 balls with three fours, was then caught by Sundar off Patel at the start of the seventh over to leave Pakistan 39 for three.
Hasan and Saim rebuilt the innings, taking Pakistan to 76 for three at the halfway stage. Hasan was then 26 off 18 and Ayub 12 off nine.
The pair accelerated through the middle overs, with Hasan reaching his half-century from 28 balls. Their 87-run partnership gave Pakistan a realistic chance of chasing India’s imposing total, but Dube’s dismissal of Saim at 126 proved a significant turning point.
Varma stars
India had earlier been propelled to 211 for six by Varma and Dube, who added 62 from 31 balls for the sixth wicket.
Varma remained unbeaten on 51 off 22 balls, striking three fours and four sixes, while Dube made 27 off 15 with two fours and two sixes.
India had lost three wickets between the eighth and 15th overs after making an explosive start, but the late partnership lifted them beyond 200.
Abhishek Sharma provided the initial impetus with 61 off 28 balls, hitting three fours and seven sixes. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi made 15 off nine before being caught by Usman off Saim, while Sanju Samson was dismissed for two by Ahmed Daniyal.

Lewis Hamilton’s romance with Kim Kardashian is heating up—but apparently, not everyone in his inner circle is celebrating.
The seven-time F1 champion has faced fresh scrutiny after his Spanish Grand Prix ended early because of brake trouble, followed by a whirlwind getaway with Kardashian that took them from Lake Como to Paris, London and even a casual ride on Lime Bikes.
While fans have enjoyed seeing the couple together, some of Hamilton’s friends are reportedly worried the Ferrari driver is becoming too distracted by his relationship.
“Lewis has Kim on his mind 24/7, even when they aren’t together,” an insider told Heat magazine. “He’s totally consumed by this relationship and, as far as his friends are concerned, it’s already starting to change him.”
The couple, who went Instagram official in June, have also faced plenty of online teasing, with critics mocking Hamilton for appearing on Kardashian’s film set with lunch and later poking fun at their London bike ride.
But Hamilton reportedly isn’t buying the idea that Kardashian is affecting his performance.
“Lewis doesn’t want to dial anything back with Kim – if anything, he wants her around more,” the source said.
“It’s very upsetting to him that people are trying to put his loss on her shoulders; he hates that she’s in this position.”
The insider added that Hamilton’s friends want him focused on the championship rather than constant jet-setting.
“No one is saying he should stop seeing Kim but they do feel like all the jet-setting needs to stop until the end of the season.”
For now, Hamilton appears determined to keep both his racing career and romance moving at full speed—despite the internet having plenty to say about both.

items.title: Ladson children's deaths: coroner identifies victims as affidavits reveal new details
items.summary: Ladson children's deaths: coroner identifies victims as affidavits reveal new detailsA Ladson woman charged in the deaths of two young children found in a Pinewood Drive home had been visited repeatedly by law enforcement and other agencies before the tragic incident.<p...
items.body_text:
Published October 03, 2026
A Ladson woman charged in the deaths of two young children found in a Pinewood Drive home had been visited repeatedly by law enforcement and other agencies before the tragic incident.
The details emerging from the affidavit reportedly add context to May’s arrest and two charges of homicide by child neglect.
According to the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, which released the identities of the victims, said, “During a welfare check at the residence on September 29, deputies found the bodies of a 2-year-old girl and a 15-month-old girl.
The coroner’s office later ruled both deaths homicides and determined the children died from starvation and dehydration due to neglect.
Justine May, 31, was arrested on September 30 and charged with two counts of homicide by child neglect.
May reportedly told law enforcement officials that she “did not remember” the last time she fed her two daughters, who were discovered dead in the Ladson home.
The Charleston County Sheriff’s Office in its statement issued on Thursday, October 1, said the officers visited the home 13 times since August 10.
The agency said it last visited the home before the children were found on September 20 and involved May alone.
Nine days later, the deputies and the family’s Department of Social Security (DSS) caseworker responded to another request for a welfare check at May’s home.
They encountered May when she exited the residence. Investigators said deputies and the DSS caseworker then stepped into the home and discovered the bodies of two children.
The affidavits read, “The defendant unequivocally demonstrated an extreme indifference for human life in that she failed to provide both of her own children, according to her, with the basic sustenance to maintain life.”
May was held at Sheriff Al Cannon Detention Centre and declined a scheduled bond hearing.
With no further charges announced, the investigation remains ongoing.

items.title: Govt-PTI second round of talks begins amid deadlock over Oct 4 Islamabad march
items.summary: National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq is chairing the second round of meeting between the of government and the opposition team at the Parliament House in Islamabad on October 3, 2026. — Geo News Second meeting important "round of negotiations": PTI chief.PTI members back...
items.body_text:
Published October 03, 2026
- Second meeting important "round of negotiations": PTI chief.
- PTI members back continuation of talks with govt: sources.
- Members suggest quitting assemblies in case of emergency: sources.
After multiple delays, the second round of negotiations between the federal government and the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has finally begun, with both sides remaining at odds over the Imran Khan-founded party’s planned long march towards Islamabad on October 4.
National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq is chairing the government-opposition talks between the government and opposition to ease the ongoing political tensions in the country.
The government’s delegation includes Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Kashmir Affairs Minister Amir Muqam, State Minister for Interior Talal Chaudhry, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, PPP leaders Naveed Qamar, Sherry Rehman and Ejaz Jakhrani.
The opposition team comprises Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, Asad Qaiser, Salman Akram Raja, Aamir Dogar and Haleem Adil.
Talking to the media moments before the second round, the PTI chief said efforts were being made to stop his party’s long march, adding that talk of taking extreme steps had also been heard from the treasury benches.
Without naming anyone, he expressed disappointment over statements made by some ministers. “Negotiations would be fruitful,” he said, expressing hope for a positive outcome.
The first round of the talks was held on Friday at the National Assembly speaker's chamber, with no agreement reached between the government and the PTI.
The six-member opposition delegation included PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas and PTI leaders Asad Qaiser, Salman Akram Raja, Amir Dogar and Haleem Adil Sheikh.
The former ruling party had reconstituted its delegation for the meeting after Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Ayin-e-Pakistan (TTAP) chief Mahmood Khan Achakzai refused to attend the meeting at the NA speaker's chamber, saying he would attend the talks if they were held at a neutral location.
Following the talks, the PTI chairman said the meeting lasted around an hour, with both sides presenting their respective positions.
The PTI chief had said on Friday that the second round of talks would be held at 2pm today. He later announced that the meeting would take place at 3pm. However, the second round of talks between the government and opposition is yet to begin in the federal capital.
"Today at 3pm in the afternoon, the second and important round of negotiations will take place between the government and opposition delegations in the office of the speaker of the National Assembly," Barrister Gohar wrote in a post on X.
Separately, sources said that members of the PTI's political and core committees have suggested that the long march could be postponed rather than called off if the government made positive progress in the talks.
Barrister Gohar briefed members on the negotiations during the meeting, while members also discussed the party's future strategy, sources said.
According to sources, a majority of members expressed the view that the negotiations should be expanded.
The PTI secretary general told the meeting that there appeared to be a plan to impose an emergency, sources said, adding that some members suggested quitting national and provincial assemblies if the federal government imposed an emergency in KP.
The meeting also agreed that statements should not be issued to the media during the negotiations, while members criticised statements made by PM's aide Rana Sanaullah and PPP leader Sherry Rehman.
Some members suggested that some PTI leaders attend a meeting with the party's founder at the Adiala jail.
Members were of the view that a meeting of Achakzai and Abbas with the PTI founder could help find a way forward.

items.title: PTI holds firm on Oct 4 long march as govt-opposition talks underway
items.body_text:
PTI holds firm on Oct 4 long march as govt-opposition talks underway
- By Web Desk -
- Oct 03, 2026
PESHAWAR: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) on Saturday reaffirmed its decision to proceed with its October 4 long march to Islamabad as the second round of talks between the PTI-led opposition and the ruling coalition commenced at Parliament House.
Speaking to the media at Parliament House, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan said he had spoken to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Muhammad Sohail Afridi regarding the long march.
“The decision to hold the long march remains unchanged,” Gohar said.
Second round of talks delayed
The second round of talks between the government and PTI has commenced amid reservations expressed by the PTI negotiating team over statements made by members of the government’s negotiating team.
According to sources, PTI expressed strong reservations over media statements by Tariq Fazal Chaudhry and Talal Chaudhry.
The PTI negotiating team reportedly called for “serious” people to be included in the negotiations.
Sohail Afridi vows to proceed with march
Meanwhile, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Muhammad Sohail Afridi reaffirmed that the long march would begin from Lakki Marwat on October 4.
In a statement on X, Afridi said the march would begin from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat and continue until, according to him, the supremacy of the Constitution and law and the restoration of an independent judiciary were ensured.
Khawaja Asif alleges PTI-TTP collaboration to create ‘May 9-like’ violence
He said PTI was the country’s largest and most popular political party and maintained that the Constitution guaranteed the right to peaceful protest.
Afridi said PTI’s demands were in accordance with the Constitution and law.
He also levelled a series of allegations against the federal government and other political actors, accusing them of pursuing policies that he said had harmed the country and contributed to instability.
Afridi said the terrorism was primarily affecting the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Pakistan and should not be treated merely as a “narrative war”.
He said PTI founder Imran Khan had consistently opposed military operations against the country’s own population and the displacement of civilians, arguing that such measures were not a lasting solution.
Afridi claimed that peace could be restored in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa within 100 days through a change in policy, saying the existing approach had not produced the desired results.
He also said PTI would neither allow a repeat of the May 9, 2023 events nor allow anyone else to do so.
Pakistan Army vows decisive action against any attempt to create 9 May-like situation

items.title: Azeri woman case: Suspects in custody confess assaulting Diana
items.body_text:
Azeri woman case: Suspects in custody confess assaulting Diana
- By Babar Khan -
- Oct 03, 2026
LAHORE: Three suspects arrested in connection with the gang rape of an Azerbaijani national have confessed to their crime during police interrogation, ARY News reported.
The Deputy Inspector General (DIG) of Investigation informed that one remaining suspect is still at large and will be arrested soon.
The DIG Investigation stated that police traced and apprehended the three suspects through human intelligence and modern technological assistance.
Detailing the heinous crime, the DIG said that a gang-rape case was registered at the Defence C Police Station against unidentified perpetrators. The culprits allegedly raped the foreign national after taking her to a flat in a private housing society.
After committing the crime, they drove around with her in a vehicle along the Ring Road before dropping her off near the Defence Phase 8 Interchange. The perpetrators also fled with the victim’s mobile phone and purse.
The DIG noted that police swung into action following a complaint lodged by a passerby on the 15 emergency helpline, after which special police teams were formed to arrest the culprits.
The DIG Investigation added that he personally supervised the investigation and confirmed that a medical examination of the victim was conducted, which corroborated the rape.
He further stated that medical swabs from both the victim and the suspects have been sent to the forensic laboratory. Expressing firm resolve, the DIG vowed that the case would be brought to its logical conclusion.
Meanwhile, sources revealed that the Azerbaijani woman, Diana, was boarded onto a flight back to her home country, Azerbaijan, but she refused to leave Pakistan.
Sources added that although airline staff and relevant authorities attempted to persuade her to board the flight, she remained firm on her decision to stay in Pakistan.
Consequently, she was offloaded from the plane and shifted to the international briefing hall at Lahore Airport.”I do not want to leave Pakistan of my own free will,” she stated.

Deadly shooting claims five lives in Larkana district
- By Web Desk -
- Oct 03, 2026
LARKANA: Five persons were killed in a firing incident at Ratodero Jacobabad road here, police sources said on Saturday.
Officials said that an old enmity between two rival groups of Ghanghro clan resulted the deadly shooting incident, which claimed lives of a father, his two sons, a relative and a passerby.
The deceased identified as Rajab Ali, his two sons Qurban and Riaz, a relative Rajab Ghanghro and a passerby Abdullah Brohi.
The gunmen after the shooting incident, fled from the crime scene.
Police shifted five dead bodies to hospital.
Sindh Police chief Javed Alam Odho has summoned a detailed report of the deadly incident from the DIG Larkana Police.
IG Sindh has also ordered the police to use all available resources for arrest of culprits without any delay.

items.body_text:
Construction begins on first phase of Iraq’s Madinat Al Ward
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – ORA Iraq awarded CRC Dorra the building contract for the first phase of Madinat Al Ward, paving the way for large-scale development in Iraq.
The deal was signed in the presence of Naguib Sawiris, Chairman of ORA, and Mohamed Dorra, Vice Chairman of Dorra Group, as the project progressed from ground preparation to primary construction.
CRC Dorra will begin construction after POWERCHINA has completed the earthworks and ground preparation for Phase One, according to ORA Iraq.
The deal adds another important regional contractor to the development.
CRC Dorra is the contracting arm of Dorra Group, an engineering and construction business founded in 1943 that operates in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Iraq.
Its work includes residential, commercial, office, and hotel developments, as well as design-build projects.
ORA said that the selection was based on CRC Dorra’s construction expertise and capacity to perform large-scale projects.
The commencement of construction marks a key milestone for Madinat Al Ward as ORA expands its investment and development efforts in the Iraqi market.
The company said that it continues to be dedicated to building the project as an integrated community, with the new contract advancing Phase One from site preparation to physical construction.

items.body_text:
US Treasury approves waiver for Iranian flights to Iraq
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Minister of Foreign Affairs Fuad Hussein announced on Friday, October 2, 2026, that U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent has agreed to exempt religious pilgrimage flights to holy sites in Iraq from secondary sanctions imposed on Iranian aviation, following intensive bilateral talks held in Washington.
The decision resolves mounting diplomatic friction surrounding the status of Najaf International Airport, granting legal clarity for passenger arrivals while shielding Iraqi aviation infrastructure from punitive measures.
In a statement shared on X (formerly Twitter) and reported by the 964 Network, Hussein outlined that discussions with Bessent encompassed the overarching trajectory of U.S.-Iraqi economic and security ties, regional fiscal stability, and the spillover impacts of American sanctions enforcement on the domestic Iraqi economy.
Hussein specifically raised the operational paralysis facing Najaf International Airport—a vital national transport hub serving millions of international religious pilgrims annually—emphasizing that economic restrictions should not impede lawful civilian travel or religious observances. Secretary Bessent acknowledged Iraq’s sovereign concerns, formally approving a targeted waiver for flights directed toward the holy shrines.
During the diplomatic session, Hussein reaffirmed Baghdad’s appreciation for past U.S. and International Coalition support in the campaign to defeat Daesh (ISIS), while reiterating the federal government’s constitutional roadmap under Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi to monopolize arms under the state and maintain sole authority over war and peace.
Commending Washington’s accommodation, Hussein noted that recognizing the importance of religious freedom and facilitating pilgrim transit reflects shared values of mutual respect and tolerance, reinforcing a stable, long-term bilateral partnership between Iraq and the United States.

items.body_text:
ITEX 2026: Iraqi AI and tech startups expand
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi, regional, and international technology enterprises showcased cutting-edge solutions in artificial intelligence, network synchronization, and enterprise digital transformation during their participation in the Iraq International Information and Communications Technology Exhibition in Baghdad.
The participating companies expressed strong ambition to expand operations and capture growing commercial opportunities in Iraq’s rapidly developing technological sector.
Hassan Abdul-Baqi Khalaf, founder of domestic startup Al-Burhan for AI Image and Video Recognition, told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that the venture originated from registered patents specializing in automated media verification and tamper protection against digital forgery and deepfakes.
Khalaf—a computer science student at the American University of Iraq – Baghdad (AUIB) collaborating with a doctoral partner in mathematics and physics—highlighted that their platform processes requests for more than 3,000 daily active users across private corporate clients and the public.
Delivering up to 95 percent accuracy in identifying manipulated content, the company is leveraging its inaugural exhibition presence to pursue operational partnerships with federal entities, specifically the Ministry of Interior, to detect fabricated media and enhance sovereign cyber verification tools.
International infrastructure providers also underscored their entry into the domestic market. Engineer Ahmed Mustafa of Canada’s Al-Mamas, an IT and network engineering specialist, revealed that the firm is seeking to establish an operational foothold in Iraq following successful deployments in the UAE, Qatar, and Egypt.
Al-Mamas holds exclusive distribution rights across the Middle East and North Africa for precision German-manufactured timing and synchronization hardware, which is critical for maintaining ultra-low-latency architectures across telecommunications networks, industrial automation, data center facilities, and distributed artificial intelligence systems.
Highlighting regional corporate expansion, Samer Al-Yasin, sales director for Qatar-headquartered conglomerate Mannai Corporation, affirmed that Iraq represents a fertile and attractive destination for long-term tech investment.
Marking its second exhibition appearance in Baghdad, Mannai—which employs over 15,000 personnel across the Gulf—formally established its Baghdad branch three months ago and is actively preparing to launch regional offices in Erbil and Basra.
Al-Yasin emphasized that the group is deploying enterprise digital transformation, cloud integration, and systems architecture tailored for federal ministries, banking institutions, and healthcare providers, aiming to transfer its regional technical expertise to drive national modernization and support sovereign institutional revenues.

items.body_text:
As October draws to a close, interest has risen regarding date of the clock change in Egypt for 2026—specifically, when Daylight Saving Time ends and Winter Time begins.
Winter Time 2026
Daylight Savings Time began on Friday, April 24 pursuant to the provisions of Law No. 24 of 2023 regarding the Daylight Saving Time system.
When are clocks set back by 60 minutes?
In Egypt, the transition from Daylight Saving Time to winter time is scheduled—in accordance with the law—for the end of the last Thursday in October.
Upon the switch to winter time, clocks are set back by 60 minutes, reverting to standard time from the daylight saving time observed previously, during which clocks had been advanced by one hour.
For mobile phones, the clock can be set automatically by accessing the settings, selecting “Date & Time,” and enabling the automatic date and time setting feature.
If the clock does not update automatically, the user can check the time zone settings, ensure that automatic updates are enabled, and adjust the clock following the switch to winter time.

items.body_text:
Unconfirmed report asserts official detention order issued for Matsda2sh team amid security leaks, media accusations          
A report that emerged on Friday night has claimed that the Supreme State Security Prosecution issued a formal detention order on Thursday for the six journalists from the Matsda2sh editorial team who were arrested earlier in the week.
The Al-Masry Al-Youm report described the issuance as ordering the journalists’ detention for 15 days.

Security forces arrested and forcibly disappeared the six members of the Matsda2sh editorial team in the span of 24 hours in a campaign that was launched Monday night. No official statement on the arrest was published until Thursday.
None of the journalists have been presented formally before prosecuting authorities, EIPR lawyers told Mada Masr, and neither their families nor the Journalists Syndicate have been informed of their place of detention, the syndicate source confirmed.
The Al-Masry Al-Youm report was back-dated to October 1, but was not available to readers until late on October 2. The report stated that a 15-day detention order had been issued for the six journalists following the Interior Ministry’s Thursday announcement of their arrest. The newspaper’s report had not been shared on the privately owned newspaper’s social media channels at the time of writing.
It cited unnamed “security sources” to describe ongoing investigations into the independent fact-checking platform.
Islam Salama, a lawyer for the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, which is legally representing the journalists, said that there is no case number indicated in the news. Commenting on its publication to Mada Masr, Salama added that the charges for which the six journalists are being investigated are not described in the privately owned newspaper, which instead echoed claims that the fact-checking platform’s founder is a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.
Salama added that what is described in the report goes no further than reproducing claims that were already circulating on social media in the preceding days.
A Journalists Syndicate source, meanwhile, said that the way the news is written suggests it to have been a “backdoor leak” amid security agencies’ efforts to escalate against the detained newsroom.
Salama and Nasser Amin, the director of the Arab Center for Independence of the Judiciary and the Legal Profession, said it that a prosecution decision of the kind described in the news report could give authorization to investigating authorities under the counterterrorism law to detain the journalists for up to 30 days in order to continue inquiries without needing to present them before the prosecution.
Claims against the journalists have escalated in the domestic media over recent days, which has since Friday sustained an accusatory tone linking them to the Muslim Brotherhood.
Mohamed al-Baz, the editor in chief of Al-Dostour newspaper, which belongs to the United Media Services conglomerate, sought on Friday to incriminate Matsda2sh, describing it as a “Brotherhood cell” and its journalistic work as “skeptical content that contributes to the spread of rumors.”

Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing opposition, reshuffled hope for Idris’s govt, tribal violence engulfs South Darfur, military opens road to West Kordofan, China on Sudan’s coast          
Sudan’s government is taking a long hard look in the mirror, and they don’t like what they see, sources close to Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the Transitional Sovereignty Council told Mada Masr this week.
Ushered in on a promise of hope a year ago, Idris’s government has faced significant issues. Some of those come down to war-time trials, but infighting and attempts to delimit the remit of a civilian government backed by a powerful and intrusive military council have been persistent issues.
Now the government is considering a reshuffle of ministerial and gubernatorial appointments to address executive imbalances and shortfalls, particularly on economic and service-related issues, according to a source in Idris’s office.
While Idris and the TSC may see an administrative reshuffle as a way to address war-time woes, the armed movements that signed the 2020 Juba peace agreement insist that any bureaucratic rearrangement must not change the power-sharing agreement inked in the South Sudanese capital.
For now, the reshuffle is all just talk. But the movements do not view it in isolation from the larger reshaping of the political landscape of recent months, a leader in one of the Juba armed movements told Mada Masr, particularly as the planned national dialogue will have to address their relationship with the government.
Outside military-controlled areas, the Rapid Support Forces have also been dealing with internal discord over the last two weeks, though the dispute they are presiding over has a decidedly less understanding and diplomatic tenor.
Throughout September, deadly inter-tribal clashes have engulfed South Darfur. With heavy weapons in hand and grappling with a faltering rainy season, tribes in Gereida, about 90 km south of Nyala, and in southern parts of Nyala itself, have become embroiled in violent confrontations.
The RSF has tried to step in to calm the situation, deploying troops to prevent it from continuing to spiral out of control. As residents look on to see how effective these immediate tamping down measures will be, civil society and RSF sources agree that the much more difficult problem will be halting the spread of heavy weapons into residential communities, which allows competition over water, pasture and farmland during droughts to become increasingly militarized.
On Sudan’s battlefields this week, the military cleared the last major RSF defensive positions in North Kordofan, effectively opening the West Kordofan front. These losses have triggered yet another defection from the paramilitary group, as Al-Tayeb “Waheedo” Mohamed Ahmed arrived to Omdurman, saying he left after witnessing “tragedies” and “collapse” within the RSF’s ranks.
But while frontline battles remain consequential, drone warfare continues to figure in Sudan’s conflict. RSF drones struck targets in Gezira and North Kordofan over the week, reaching fuel infrastructure east of Wad Madani and multiple sites in Obeid, where at least six civilians were killed.
This week also saw a series of tense diplomatic exchanges. The first came at the UN General Assembly’s debate on Monday, with the United Arab Emirates and Sudanese delegations engaging in tug-of-war over the narrative on Sudan’s conflict. A former official said the spat does not necessarily signal another diplomatic rupture.
But the second tense diplomatic moment could prove more consequential. Ethiopia, recently plunged into another civil war, accused Sudan of abetting opposition fighters then took the more drastic diplomatic step of expelling Eritrean and Egyptian diplomats.
While wars and their fallout dominate the headlines this week, Sudan is taking steps toward a post-war future. And as with previous attempts to attract foreign powers to Khartoum, this future projection involves lucrative real est

items.body_text:
Prisoner protests, lack of readiness delay enactment of new Criminal Procedures Law          
The Criminal Procedures Code’s deferred enactment, approved by Parliament yesterday, was attributed by MPs and the government to a lack of preparedness. However, parliamentary and legal sources told Mada Masr the impact of the law’s enactment on the hundreds of detainees being held in remand could be among the reasons that led to the last-minute postponement.
The bill to postpone the law’s enactment, brought forth by the Nation’s Future Party, which is close to state authorities, proposed an amendment to the 2025 bill to delay enforcement until October 2027, replacing an article in the original text that had set October 1 as the operative date.
According to Parliament, the decision to enforce the new bill next year was taken primarily out of concern for the readiness of the digital system, which the law stipulates be used for judicial notifications and remote court proceedings.
During yesterday’s Legislative Committee meeting ahead of the plenary session vote on the postponement draft, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Hany Hanna said the ministry backed the bill in order to allow for greater preparedness ahead of implementation, noting that “some courts have been prepared, while others, such as felony appeal courts, still need preparation.”
But the Justice Ministry had issued several decisions in August which indicated its readiness to implement the digital system. On August 30, the ministry announced that the required courtroom and training facility adjustments to implement the new system were completed in coordination with the courts of appeal and the Lawyers Syndicate.
Later, on September 9, the ministry announced that criminal court judges, clerks and lawyers within different jurisdictions were fully trained to use the digital system.
It seems the bill’s postponement had causes beyond the system’s readiness. Speaking on condition of anonymity, a source in the General Secretariat of the House of Representatives said the postponement was based on security reports and recommendations from the National Security Agency. According to these reports, there are certain clauses within the law whose implementation needed more time, such as Article 363, which puts some limitations on the duration of remand detention, in accordance with Article 124.
Article 124 of the law sets the maximum total limit for remand detention at four months for misdemeanors, 12 months for felonies and 18 months if the maximum punishment for the crime is life imprisonment or the death penalty.
According to the source, these limits could have immediate effects on current prisoners, requiring judicial and investigative authorities to release hundreds of individuals who are being held in remand in excess of these time limits.
Nabih al-Genady, human rights lawyer and founder of the Tbian for Rights and Freedoms, pointed to mass protests by remand detainees in terrorism cases that took place in the Badr Court last week as the reason behind the decision to postpone the bill. Despite calling the government and Parliament’s stated reasons for the postponement “genuine and positive,” he said they are not the primary cause.
Genady recounted what he personally witnessed in Badr Court at the Badr Prison Complex during a series of terrorism trial sessions last week. Over three consecutive sessions, defendants protested in court against the repeated renewal of their remand terms. Confined to their dock, defendants banged on the glass at the end of the first session, chanting “freedom,” as Judge Wagdy Abdel Moneim left the courtroom. On the second day, they smashed the cameras inside the glass dock, still chanting “freedom.” On the third day, they also banged on the glass as Abdel Moneim took the bench.

items.title: ‘Red Flag’ offers distinctive experience as I seek variety: Ahmed Hatem
items.summary: Egyptian actor Ahmed Hatem continues to establish a distinctive presence in the Egyptian film industry with his latest feature, Red Flag, which opened in cinemas on 9 September across Egypt, Saudi Arabia and several other Arab markets. items.body_text:
Egyptian actor Ahmed Hatem continues to establish a distinctive presence in the Egyptian film industry with his latest feature, Red Flag, which opened in cinemas on 9 September across Egypt, Saudi Arabia and several other Arab markets.
Blending social comedy with an exploration of the complexities of romantic and marital relationships, the film takes its title from the now widely recognised concept of “red flags” — behaviours, patterns and warning signs that can undermine trust and ultimately reshape the dynamics of a relationship.
The film marks Hatem’s second collaboration with actress Gamila Awad, following their successful pairing in “Arousty,” and also brings him together with veteran actor Sherif Mounir. Beyond the screen, “Red Flag” has generated considerable attention through an inventive promotional campaign, particularly a series of tongue-in-cheek videos inspired by the contradictions and everyday tensions of married life, most notably the “Go Back to Your Father’s House” clips.
In an exclusive conversation, Ahmed Hatem reflects on the making of Red Flag, the appeal of playing a character unlike those he has previously portrayed, his creative rapport with Gamila Awad and Sherif Mounir, his recent association with comedy, and the projects he is currently preparing.
How would you describe your experience with Red Flag now that audiences have had the opportunity to see it?
Red Flag represents a genuinely different experience for me, whether in terms of its narrative, subject matter or the character I portray. The film examines the warning signs that can emerge within romantic and marital relationships, but approaches them through social comedy. That distinctiveness was one of the main reasons I was drawn to the project in the first place.
What, in particular, drew you to the film’s central concept, especially as the expression “red flag” has become such a familiar part of everyday language?
The premise is inherently relatable because every relationship can involve behaviours that make you pause and question whether what you are experiencing is healthy or acceptable.
The film explores behaviours that may constitute genuine red flags — dishonesty, selfishness, infidelity, neglect, or any repeated behaviour that causes emotional harm to the other person.
At the same time, I don’t believe every disagreement or difficulty within a relationship should automatically be labelled a red flag. It becomes more serious when someone deliberately does something that hurts you, knows the impact it has on you, and nevertheless chooses to repeat it.
You play a pilot, while Gamila Awad plays the manager of an advertising company. What made this particular character appealing to you?
The character represents unfamiliar territory for me in many respects, and that was precisely what excited me about taking it on. The story follows a married couple whose relationship is placed under considerable strain by doubt, a breakdown of trust and jealousy, with those tensions gradually surfacing through a succession of comic situations.
Reuniting with Gamila Awad for the second time, following Arousseti, was equally rewarding. There is a genuine creative understanding between us, and I feel very comfortable whenever we share a project. I would certainly welcome another opportunity to work together.
The film’s promotional campaign has attracted considerable attention, particularly the “Go Back to Your Father’s House” videos. How did that concept originate?
The idea came from Khaled Gohar, who was overseeing the promotional campaign. He suggested that I create a series of humorous videos built around satirical observations and tongue-in-cheek advice about relationships and married life.
I immediately liked the concept and we began developing it, but I honestly never anticipated that it would gain the level of traction it eventually achieved. The audience responded remarkably well, particularly women. Approximately 81% of the followers were women, which

items.summary: Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for intensified regional and international efforts to de-escalate tensions related to the crisis with Iran and prevent the conflict from widening, while stressing the need to preserve freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab Al-Mandab and reject the use of maritime chokepoints as instruments of pressure. Abdelatty […]
items.body_text:
Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for intensified regional and international efforts to de-escalate tensions related to the crisis with Iran and prevent the conflict from widening, while stressing the need to preserve freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab Al-Mandab and reject the use of maritime chokepoints as instruments of pressure.
Abdelatty made the remarks during separate phone calls with Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, and Massad Boulos, senior adviser to the US president for Arab and African affairs.
Egypt’s Foreign Ministry said Abdelatty and his Qatari counterpart discussed the crisis involving Iran and the latest regional escalation, as well as developments in Yemen and the Red Sea. Abdelatty called for strengthening political and diplomatic channels to prevent a broader confrontation.
He also stressed that navigation through the Red Sea and Bab Al-Mandab should remain secure and unrestricted, rejecting the use of strategic waterways as leverage in regional disputes.
In a separate call with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan, the two sides discussed developments in Yemen, Iran and the Red Sea and agreed on the need to protect freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab Al-Mandab.
Abdelatty said Egypt fully supports Saudi Arabia’s security and stability and rejects attacks on its territory or sovereignty, while backing measures taken by Riyadh to protect its security.
The Egyptian minister also spoke with UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed about bilateral relations and regional developments. The two sides called for intensified efforts to reduce tensions and support political and diplomatic settlements.
During his call with Boulos, Abdelatty discussed strategic relations between Cairo and Washington, as well as developments in Sudan. He reiterated Egypt’s position in support of Sudan’s unity, sovereignty and national institutions, a stance Cairo has also conveyed in earlier talks with the US adviser.
The calls came as part of Egypt’s continuing diplomatic efforts to coordinate with Washington and Gulf states on regional crises, with a focus on containing escalation and safeguarding freedom of navigation along key maritime routes.

items.title: FATF Experts in Damascus: What Does Syria Need to Exit the Grey List?
items.summary: The FATF experts' arrival in the Syrian capital coincides with an announcement by the Central Authority for Control and Inspection of a major financial measure in a separate case concerning oil sector contracts. The post FATF Experts in Damascus: What Does Syria Need to Exit the Grey List? first appeared on The Syrian Observer.
items.body_text:
Experts from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) have begun a field visit to Syria to review the implementation of its action plan on combating money laundering and terrorist financing. It is the first inspection of its kind since the country was placed on the “grey list” in 2010, at a time when the Syrian government is trying to prove it is making the necessary efforts to have its name removed from the list.
The FATF is an intergovernmental body founded in 1989 to set international standards for combating money laundering and terrorist financing and protecting the global financial system. It places on the “grey list” countries with strategic deficiencies in their financial and regulatory systems that have committed to an action plan to address these gaps under the group’s monitoring.
For years, the FATF has said that Syria completed the agreed action plan at the technical level, but the security situation prevented an on-site visit to verify that the required reforms had actually begun to be implemented and could be sustained.
But what does the arrival of FATF experts in Damascus mean? What will they look for inside Syrian institutions? And could exiting the grey list be another step on Syria’s road back to the global financial system?
A File Pending Since 2014
Syria’s relationship with the grey list dates to February 2010, when the Assad regime’s government made a high-level political commitment to work with the FATF and the Middle East and North Africa Financial Action Task Force (MENAFATF) to address strategic deficiencies in its anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing system.
In June 2014, the FATF concluded that Syria had substantially addressed its action plan at the technical level, including criminalizing terrorist financing and establishing procedures for freezing terrorist assets. But the closing of the file stalled at a key stage, as the group was unable to carry out an on-site visit to verify that the reforms had actually begun and were sustainable.
The FATF’s latest statement on jurisdictions under increased monitoring, in June 2026, repeats the same position, stating that Syria has completed the agreed action plan and that the group will conduct the on-site visit as soon as possible.
The FATF explains that a country seeking to exit monitoring must have addressed all or most of the items in its action plan, before an on-site visit is organized to confirm that the required legal, regulatory and operational reforms are being implemented and that there is political commitment and institutional capacity to sustain them.
Under its internal rules, if the visit’s outcome is positive, the group may decide to remove the country from public monitoring at one of its subsequent plenary meetings.
Two Tracks Before Syria
The FATF experts’ visit comes as the country prepares for a broader milestone: a new round of “mutual evaluation” of its financial system. On July 23, a high-level MENAFATF delegation visited Damascus, headed by the group’s president Hamed Saif al-Zaabi and including its executive secretary Suleiman al-Jebreen and the two co-chairs of the mutual evaluation working group.
The delegation met the governor of the Central Bank of Syria, Safwat Raslan, and the ministers of interior, justice, economy and industry, finance, endowments, social affairs and labor, local administration and communications, as well as representatives of the financial intelligence unit, the judiciary, law enforcement agencies and supervisory authorities.
MENAFATF said the visit aimed to support Syria’s readiness for the mutual evaluation process and to strengthen the effectiveness of its national system for combating money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing.
Syria thus has two connected but distinct tracks before it. The first concerns its old FATF file and exiting the grey list. The second is the new mutual evaluation, which will subject the Syrian financial system to a broader review under the curr

items.title: Syrian Officials and Hezbollah Held Secret Talks in Turkey to Contain Security Tensions, Reuters Reports
items.summary: The Syrian Ministry of Information denied that such a meeting took place. The post Syrian Officials and Hezbollah Held Secret Talks in Turkey to Contain Security Tensions, Reuters Reports first appeared on The Syrian Observer.
items.body_text:
Officials from the transitional Syrian government and representatives of the Lebanese Hezbollah militia held secret talks in Turkey last September aimed at containing security tensions, according to Reuters on Thursday, October 1. The agency cited six informed sources, including Syrian and American officials and a Lebanese security source close to the party. The Syrian Ministry of Information denied that such a meeting took place.
Syrian intelligence and Foreign Ministry officials took part in the meeting, along with Hezbollah representatives, at the invitation of Turkish security agencies seeking to bring the two sides closer. The meeting followed a deterioration in relations between Damascus and the party, which sent fighters to Syria for years in support of the Assad government. The new authorities have since accused it of smuggling weapons through Syrian territory, while the United States has encouraged the Syrian army to send forces into Lebanon to fight the party. The sources did not disclose the location or duration of the meeting.
Security Understandings Without a Final Agreement
The talks focused on resolving security disputes. A Syrian official described them as positive, saying the two sides agreed there was no mutual hostility and that Damascus pledged not to intervene militarily in Lebanon to disarm Hezbollah. In return, the Syrian officials asked the party to help stop arms smuggling across the border and to dismantle its cells, especially in southern Syria. Hezbollah pledged not to interfere in Syrian affairs, without responding directly to the demands.
The demands came after the Syrian authorities announced on Tuesday the arrest of a cell affiliated with Hezbollah that was preparing to launch rockets in the south of the country. The party denied this the next day, affirming that it has no security or military activity inside Syria.
The report quoted a Lebanese security source as saying that the two sides made progress on security files, noting that Hezbollah is seeking to protect its borders and positions in Lebanon from any potential Syrian attack. Even so, they did not reach a final agreement and did not plan to announce the meeting, according to the sources.
Turkey Leads the Mediation, Iran Outside the Talks
The meeting came on a Turkish initiative, as part of efforts by Ankara, a key ally of Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa, to address regional tensions and strengthen stability in Syria. It was preceded by Syrian Foreign Minister Assaad al-Shibani’s announcement in July that Damascus was open to meeting Hezbollah, while the party’s Secretary-General Naim Qassem said in a televised speech in August that the party does not object to meeting the Syrian leadership. According to three sources, Turkey pushed for the meeting, and contacts began through its mediation about two months ago.
Iran was absent from the talks, even though it knew about them in advance and approved the party’s participation, according to the Lebanese security source. The source pointed to Tehran’s displeasure at being excluded, especially after Sharaa’s refusal to establish direct relations with it for now.
The talks come as part of the new Syrian government’s efforts to reorder its regional relations, amid differences over Iran’s role and tensions with Hezbollah. The Syrian, Turkish and American foreign ministries, and the Turkish defense ministry, did not respond to Reuters’ inquiries, while Hezbollah’s media office declined to comment.
The talks reflect the complexities of how the transitional Syrian authorities manage their regional relations, given the fallout from earlier military interventions, the overlap between Syrian and Lebanese security files, and the competition for influence. This makes border and security understandings one of Damascus’s main challenges.
This article was translated and edited by The Syrian Observer. The Syrian Observer has not verified the content of this story. Responsibility for the information and views

items.title: Five drones enter Moldovan airspace, leaving wreckage and damage – photos
items.summary: Five drones crossed Moldova’s airspace during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine, with wreckage found in several locations and property damaged.
items.body_text:
Five drones enter Moldovan airspace, leaving wreckage and damage – photos
On the morning of 3 October, Moldova's national airspace monitoring system detected several drones flying over the country.
Source: Newsmaker, citing Moldova's Defence Ministry and General Police Inspectorate, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The drones were spotted near the settlements of Anenii Noi, Ștefan Vodă, Hîncești, Tudora and Căușeni.
The National Army's Air Operations Service said that five drones crossed Moldova's airspace between 07:45 and 08:00.
The Defence Ministry noted that the incident occurred amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. According to monitoring data, explosions were heard near the settlements of Crocmaz, Ștefan Vodă, Delacău, Puheceni, Anenii Noi, Bozieni and Hîncești, as well as near Dubovca, Constantinovca and Căușeni.
Police and National Army teams were dispatched to investigate the incidents.
Police added that residents of the Căușeni, Ștefan Vodă, Anenii Noi and Hîncești districts had begun reporting sounds of explosions in the morning. Officers found smoking drone wreckage on the outskirts of Căușeni.
Drone wreckage was also found near Dubovca in Hîncești District and between the villages of Delacău and Puheceni.
In Crocmaz, a drone crashed in a vineyard, setting dry vegetation on fire and shattering windows in a nearby house.
Police said no one had been injured in the incidents. Law enforcement agencies are documenting all the cases and working to establish the circumstances.
Background:
- On the morning of 30 September, a drone flew through Moldovan airspace before crashing outside the village of Hîrbovăț in Anenii Noi District and exploding.
- According to the General Police Inspectorate, the drone exploded at an altitude of 40 metres after colliding with a communications line pole.
- Another drone flew over Moldova later that day, prompting the authorities to close the airspace over the northern and central parts of the country.
- Moldovan Defence Minister Anatolie Nosatîi said the drone was jet-powered.

items.title: IAEA reports damage to transformers near Zaporizhzhia NPP, seeks truce for repairs
items.summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has reported a series of drone attacks in recent weeks that have further heightened the threat to nuclear safety and security at the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP).
items.body_text:
IAEA reports damage to transformers near Zaporizhzhia NPP, seeks truce for repairs
The IAEA reported this on X, according to Ukrinform.
The agency said the reported attacks included strikes on September 19, 20 and 27 on the nearby Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant (ZTPP), damaging transformers that are of vital importance for supplying off-site power to the ZNPP, which has experienced frequent external power outages during the war.
The agency said that to enable necessary repairs at the ZTPP, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi is negotiating a new localized ceasefire with both sides with the aim for it to take effect very soon. It would be the eighth such IAEA-brokered ceasefire to help secure off-site power for the ZNPP.
In addition, an attack on September 22 reportedly disabled an off-site radiation monitoring station, reducing the capability to monitor radiation levels near the ZNPP.
Grossi said that attacks endangering nuclear safety and security remain completely unacceptable and must cease immediately. In order to prevent the risk of a nuclear accident during the conflict, all sides must exercise maximum military restraint near such facilities and their power infrastructure installations, he added.
On September 7, Ukrainian energy workers restored operation of the Ferosplavna-1 power line, which supplies external power to the Zaporizhzhia NPP.
Photo: Kostiantyn Liberov

items.title: Lubinets urges Kazakhstan to prevent extradition of Ukrainian citizen to Russia
items.summary: The Ukrainian Parliament's Human Rights Commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, has urged Kazakhstan's Ombudsman Artur Lastayev to prevent the extradition to Russia of a Ukrainian woman who was lured to Astana by Russian special services and her grandson's new family.
items.body_text:
Lubinets urges Kazakhstan to prevent extradition of Ukrainian citizen to Russia
According to Ukrinform, Lubinets said this in a Facebook post.
"I received an appeal from Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska, who was detained in Kazakhstan at the request of the Russian Federation. Liubov arrived in Kazakhstan for humanitarian reasons – to take her minor grandson and return him to Ukraine. Instead, she herself ended up in custody over a criminal case that Russia opened back in 2023," the ombudsman said.
Lubinets said Rozhanska was effectively lured to Kazakhstan through deception. The child's so-called "new" relatives in Russia, working with the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB), contacted the woman and tried to lure her out of Ukraine so that she would come and pick up the child herself. The woman believed them and traveled to Astana, unaware that preparations for her detention were already underway in Russia.
"Handing a Ukrainian woman over to Russian law enforcement agencies would pose a direct and serious threat to her personal safety, health and respect for her fundamental rights. We know all too well what happens to Ukrainians who fall into the hands of the Russian system," Lubinets said.
"Therefore, I immediately appealed to Kazakhstan's Ombudsman Artur Lastayev, urging him to prevent any extradition, handover or forcible transfer of Liubov Rozhanska to Russia. I also held a separate phone call with him," Lubinets said.
He is insisting on an examination of the conditions of Rozhanska's detention and the legal grounds for depriving her of her liberty, as well as ensuring full access to her by Ukrainian diplomatic and consular representatives and her lawyer.
Lubinets noted that the case has another extremely troubling aspect – it concerns a Ukrainian child.
According to available information, the boy's mother took him to Russia back in 2021. In 2022, she obtained Russian citizenship for herself and her child. At the same time, in March 2025, the Supreme Court of Ukraine determined Odesa as the child's place of residence.
The ombudsman clarified that the grandmother traveled to retrieve the Ukrainian child and bring him home, and it was then that she herself was detained in connection with a case initiated by Russia.
"This once again shows how dangerous it is to try to retrieve children who are in Russia on your own," Lubinets said.
He also urged people whose children are in Russia or in temporarily occupied territories not to try to resolve the matter on their own, but to contact official Ukrainian state institutions.
In particular, the Ombudsman's Office facilitates the return of Ukrainian children who have been deported or forcibly transferred, including from foreign countries, in cases where documents are missing or various legal issues are involved. The hotline number is 1678.
Traveling to Russia independently or attempting to retrieve a child through third countries may create serious risks and jeopardize the child's subsequent return, Lubinets said.
The ombudsman also published a video purportedly showing the boy boarding a plane to Kazakhstan. He noted that the video had been deliberately staged to lure the woman out.
Ukrinform reported earlier that Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska was detained at Astana airport in Kazakhstan at Russia's request after traveling there to retrieve her grandson and take him to his father in Odesa.

items.title: SOS - Ukraine’s Looming Dark Winter Demands Decisive Action
items.summary: As Russia steps up attacks on Ukraine’s power grid and transport links, Western partners must move beyond sympathy to the decisive action Kyiv needs. This means Washington removing. restrictions on ATACMS strikes and funding Ukrainian defense production. Europe, meanwhile, should transfer air-defense systems, finance mobile anti-drone teams, protect and decentralize Ukraine’s energy grid, and release frozen Russian assets to pay for weapons and repairs.
items.body_text:
Russia’s winter playbook is running again, and its logic is evident. Missile and drone attacks have spread from regional power centers to the core of Kyiv’s infrastructure – high-voltage substations and main bridges over the Dnipro River.
Moscow is not trying to hide what it’s doing. The aim is to paralyze the capital, make life there impossible, and choke the supply lines for troops and equipment to the east.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Western sympathy won’t intercept the missiles over the Dnipro, and it certainly won’t turn on heat in a hospital when the power goes out. If Ukraine’s partners really want to help the country survive this winter, then they need to stop offering sympathy and concern and start changing policy.
That starts in Washington. For months, the US administration has operated in a strange operational double standard: Ukraine will defend itself against incoming missiles, but it shouldn’t attack the airfields and bases inside Russia from where those attacks are being launched, nor the energy-generating sites that sustain the Kremlim’s war effort.
For air defense crews to hunt cruise missiles seconds before they collide – rather than blowing up bombers on the tarmac or storming missile depots in Kursk and Belgorod – is a losing strategy. The US must drop all target restrictions on ATACMS soon.
At the same time, Washington should stop tying military aid to slow domestic procurement schedules and instead fund Ukrainian defense factories directly. Kyiv is developing long-range drone missiles and tactical ballistic systems that are cheaper, faster to deploy, and free from foreign political restrictions. Europe, meanwhile, must take greater responsibility for security in its own neighborhood rather than waiting to see what the US Congress does next.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Site, Crossing, Belgorod Hubs
The first fix is air defense. Firing two-million-dollar interceptors at fifty-thousand-dollar Shahed drones is a quick way to run out of ammunition. European partners that own Patriot, NASAMS, and IRIS-T systems need to hand batteries over directly to help cover cities and transit points like the bridges of Kyiv.
To counter daily drone swarms, European funding should go toward building Ukraine’s mobile fire teams. That’s the only way to clear the lower skies without burning through high-end missile stocks amid ballistic threats. Small teams with thermal scopes, pickup trucks, searchlights, and jammers are the only way to get out of there.
The second solution is the grid. Trying to fix up massive, centralized power plants when bombs are still falling is a waste of time and money. European aid needs to stop making those long-term post-attack repairs and focus on physical armor and decentralization.
Electrical transformers, the hardest components to replace, should be housed in reinforced concrete shelters that can take direct shrapnel hits. Aid should target mobile gas turbines, industrial generators, and battery storage units in the cities on the generation side. If a city can run its water pumps and district heating on local micro-grids and the main power plant is destroyed, it loses most of the terror value.
Europe must stop holding back money. Around $200 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets is in European accounts, most of it at Euroclear in Belgium. For years, lawyers have been debating whether to touch this money while Ukrainian cities get flattened. European leaders need to take these assets and not just skim the annual interest but use them directly for Ukrainian weapons buying and grid repairs.
Making the aggressor pay for the damage isn’t just a nice idea; it’s basic common sense. None of these choices require complex diplomacy or grand ideological speeches. They are practical decisions: let Ukrainians hit back at the sites bombing them, give them the hardware they need to keep the power on, and use Russian money to pay for it.

items.title: Russia Hits Major Pharma Warehouse Near Kyiv
items.summary: A Russian air strike hit a major distribution warehouse belonging to pharmaceutical distributor Venta near Kyiv on Friday, Oct. 2, setting fire to inventories containing medicines from Bayer, Pfizer, and domestic producers. While the Ministry of Health confirmed no systemic national drug shortages, the attack highlights escalating strikes on logistics following drone hits on schools and warehouses across the capital.
items.body_text:
A major pharmaceutical storage warehouse belonging to Venta, one of Ukraine’s largest drug distributors, caught fire near Kyiv following a Russian air strike on Friday, Oct. 2, news agency UNIAN reported.
The facility housed substantial inventories of pharmaceutical products manufactured by prominent domestic and multinational pharmaceutical corporations, including Bayer, Sanofi, Pfizer, Teva, Darnytsia, and Farmak.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Emergency response teams and municipal firefighters deployed to the site to contain the blaze, while company representatives and regional authorities continue to assess structural destruction and quantify losses to commercial pharmaceutical reserves.
While the full extent of the inventory damage remains under evaluation, Ukraine’s Ministry of Health stated that the incident has not triggered a nationwide systemic deficit of critical medications, although localized distribution disruptions were documented.
The ministry noted that pharmaceutical distributors have reorganized logistical networks under wartime regulatory reforms that permit companies to disperse pharmaceutical inventories across multiple regional storage facilities rather than concentrating stock in single vulnerable hubs.
Civilian infrastructure targeting
The strike on the pharmaceutical facility forms part of an escalating Russian aerial campaign targeting commercial infrastructure, logistics hubs, and residential districts across the Ukrainian capital and surrounding province.
Russia May Be Using Mesh Relays in Kyiv to Steer Drones, Adviser Says
On Thursday, Oct. 1, a Russian Geran-4 jet-powered strike drone struck a four-story secondary school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while more than 100 students and 60 teachers were sheltering inside during a morning air raid alert.
Kyiv police and emergency services reported that the drone’s 50-kilogram warhead punched through a stairwell between the second and third floors without detonating, allowing bomb disposal specialists to extract the unexploded ordnance.
President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the attack, characterizing strikes on schools and kindergartens as a deliberate Russian tactic designed to target ordinary civilian life.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that the Thursday assault also caused damage to warehouse facilities in the Solomianskyi district and sparked fires in commercial buildings.
The strikes follow a coordinated Russian assault on Wednesday, Sept. 30, when ballistic missiles and jet-powered loitering munitions struck multiple capital districts, killing three civilians and injuring seven others.
In the Obolonskyi district, a jet drone clipped the roof of a nine-story residential apartment block before crashing near a children’s playground without detonating.

items.title: Russian Strike Hits Liberian Ship in Odesa Port, Killing 1
items.summary: Russian forces attacked a civilian Liberian-flagged cargo ship docked in an Odesa region port, killing one crew member and injuring three others as 13 sailors were evacuated. The strike marks the latest in Moscow’s escalating campaign targeting Black Sea commercial shipping and port infrastructure.
items.body_text:
Russian forces launched a strike against a civilian cargo vessel sailing under the flag of Liberia in an Odesa region port, killing one crew member and injuring three others, the Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority (USPA) reported on Saturday, Oct. 3.
According to an official dispatch published by the USPA, 13 crew members were successfully evacuated to a safe location following the bombardment.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The strike killed a motorman sailor aboard the commercial vessel, while three other crew members sustained varying injuries and were provided emergency medical assistance.
“Russia has once again attacked a civilian vessel,” the port authority stated, noting that emergency crews and port security personnel responded immediately to secure the vessel and assess the destruction.
Targeting of Black Sea commercial vessels
The attack on the Liberian-flagged freighter follows a pattern of Russian strikes directed against foreign commercial shipping operating in and around Odesa’s maritime hubs.
On Sept. 10, a Russian strike hit the foreign-flagged tugboat Tedy – which operated under the flag of Somalia – in the Odesa region, killing two Azerbaijani crew members and wounding eight others.
Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the fatalities, identifying the deceased as Azerbaijani citizens Aslan Aliyev and Asim Gasimov, while two wounded sailors were hospitalized in the nearby port city of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Reconstruction, Infrastructure and Transport condemned that engagement as part of an institutionalized Russian campaign targeting civilian maritime logistics, while Baku cautioned its citizens against transiting active conflict zones.
Russia May Be Using Mesh Relays in Kyiv to Steer Drones, Adviser Says
A similar deadly incident occurred in June, when a Russian strike on a commercial vessel killed five Azerbaijani sailors. Recent months have also seen strikes on commercial ships in Black Sea transit lanes cause the deaths of at least five Indian seafarers, prompting diplomatic demarches from New Delhi to both Moscow and Kyiv.
Kremlin maritime blockade
The strikes reflect Moscow’s declared intention to disrupt maritime transit to Ukrainian ports following the collapse of the UN-brokered Black Sea Grain Initiative.
Responding to international criticism regarding strikes on commercial traffic, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov previously asserted that commercial vessels were being used to transport weapons, ammunition, and fuel for the Armed Forces of Ukraine, declaring that Russian forces would continue destroying such shipping.
Peskov claimed that Russian attacks on transport arteries were retaliatory measures following Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian economic and refining assets.
Ukrainian authorities and international maritime bodies have categorically rejected the Kremlin’s accusations, emphasizing that the targeted ships are standard merchant vessels engaged in agricultural and bulk cargo transit under international maritime law.

items.title: Калинская снялась с матча в Пекине из-за травмы
items.body_text:
Российская теннисистка Анна Калинская (22-я ракетка мира) снялась с матча второго круга турнира WTA 1000 в Пекине против китаянки Циньвэнь Чжэн (54-я ракетка мира) при счете 7:6 (7:4), 4:6, 0:3 в пользу соперницы. Об этом сообщает Sports.ru.
27-летняя россиянка выиграла первый сет на тай-брейке, но затем уступила второй. В третьей партии после проигранного гейма на своей подаче Калинская вызвала медиков, которые измерили ей давление. При счете 0:3 теннисистка приняла решение прекратить борьбу.
Встреча продолжалась два часа 24 минуты. Чжэн 13 раз подала навылет, Калинская — три раза. Россиянка реализовала один брейк-пойнт из семи, китаянка — четыре из шести.
Чжэн Циньвэнь получила wild card на турнир. В третьем круге 23-летняя китаянка сыграет с победительницей матча Мария Боузкова (Чехия) — Кимберли Биррелл (Австралия). Калинская являлась 15-й сеяной на турнире с призовым фондом 9,4 миллиона долларов.
