items.summary: The cabinet has promised to rewrite part of its new tax plan for savings and investments, just two days after...
items.body_text:
Cabinet backtracks on box 3 tax plans for small savings
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet has promised to rewrite part of its new tax plan for savings and investments, just two days after announcing it, so that fewer people with modest savings are impacted.
Finance minister Eelco Heinen, of the right-wing liberal VVD, made the commitment in parliament on Thursday after MPs from both opposition and coalition parties attacked the plan.
“I have discussed this with the prime minister and with the coalition,” the Financieel Dagblad reported him as saying. “We are prepared to make changes. There will be a proposal to spare small savers.”
Under the plan presented on Tuesday, people would pay 36% tax on returns above €1,000 a year from 2028, down from €1,800 in the earlier version of the reform. Heinen also said he still believed the plan would exempt couples with up to €100,000 in savings.
No funding yet
The minister said he did not yet know how the cabinet would make up the shortfall. Small savers were the main source of funding for the box 3 overhaul, which reports say could cost up to €20 billion.
“We don’t have many levers to pull,” Heinen said. “And every choice you make is enormously complicated.”
The cabinet will send the bill to the Council of State, the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, without an alternative source of funding. Heinen said he would come up with proposals by October 12, when MPs debate the cabinet’s annual package of tax changes.
He also said he would look again at a temporary measure for next year, which would cut the tax-free allowance from €59,357 to €30,846 per person and raise the tax rate. You can find out more about how the changes would affect you in our box 3 explainer.

items.title: Remains of 115 Polish WWII soldiers exhumed in Ukraine
items.summary: The soldiers died defending Lviv, then known as Lwów, when Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union invaded Poland.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two.
The work continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries.
ℹ Komunikat o zakończeniu prac ekshumacyjnych na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie
⚠️ Zakończyły się prace ekshumacyjne na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie, znajdującej się obecnie w granicach administracyjnych Lwowa. Działania… pic.twitter.com/w9rSHuLeua
— Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) September 28, 2026
During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht.
They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September.
On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year.
Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives.
Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains.
“For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council.
“Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”.
Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”.
The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced.
The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN.
The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries.
The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026
Last year, Ukraine also granted permission for the exhumation of Polish soldiers in Lviv. Researchers subsequently found the remains of 31 people, as well as possible remains of dozens more that were difficult to identify due to them having been reburied and the manner of their death in artillery fire.
They were also reburied in Mostyska, at a ceremony attended by prominent officials from both Poland and Ukraine.

items.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs – 21% of its workforce – this year
items.summary: The EU's largest producer of coking coal producer reported a 1 billion zloty loss in the first half of 2026.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish state-owned mining firm Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa (JSW), which is the EU’s largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland’s biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year.
The plans come as JSW seeks to turn around its finances after years of large losses, as well as a broader shift in Poland away from reliance on coal.
Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa do końca 2026 r. zwolni ponad 4,2 tys. osób. – Musimy kierować się interesem spółki – mówił na konferencji prasowej prezes JSW. Więcej: https://t.co/7Sxrhuuaja pic.twitter.com/evJoQal0c3
— Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) October 1, 2026
On Wednesday, JSW’s management board announced that it expected the size of its workforce to decline by 4,248 by the end of this year, bringing it below 16,000, down from 20,135 at the end of March.
“We anticipate that approximately 2,200 people will leave in the third quarter, and about 1,400 in the fourth quarter,” adding to those who have already left, said the firm’s CEO, Bogusław Oleksy, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
Last year, Poland introduced a new law making it easier for coal companies to close mines and reduce their workforce. It provides for large severance payments and other measures intended to soften the blow for those who lose their jobs.
News service Strefa Inwestorów says that, on this basis, more than 3,000 JSW employees have the option to take so-called mining or mineral-processing leave while just under 1,200 can opt for one-off severance payments.
President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill that makes it easier to close down coal mines and provides severance pay of 170,000 zloty to miners.
The measures are seen as a key part of Poland’s transition towards cleaner forms of energy https://t.co/vH6MU4nBsv
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025
The workforce reduction is part of JSW’s recovery plan for 2026-2035, announced this week. Other key objectives include cutting costs and investment without decreasing production while increasing the share of coking coal in output.
When asked how the workforce reduction would affect production, Oleksy said the company would optimise its operations to make more efficient use of employees and equipment. He noted that most of the losses would be administrative positions rather than staff directly involved in production.
In February this year, the company reached an agreement with unions to reduce labour costs in order to help stabilise the company’s financial position. JSW employees almost unanimously supported the agreement, reported broadcaster TVN.
The initial results of the cost-cutting measures are beginning to show. In the first half of 2026, the cost of extraction per tonne fell to 609 zloty (€139) from 778 zloty a year earlier. JSW’s long-term goal is to bring the cost down to around 560 zloty per tonne.
The company is still posting heavy losses, though those have also fallen this year. JSW posted a net loss of just over 1.0 billion zloty in the first half of 2026, around half the 2.1 billion zloty figure from the same period a year earlier.
For the full year 2025, the company recorded a loss of 6.3 billion zloty, which was down from a record figure of 7.3 billion zloty in 2024.

items.title: Polish president backs down and approves government’s windfall tax on fuel companies
items.summary: The government immediately moved to reintroduce subsidies on fuel prices for consumers.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
President Karol Nawrocki has reversed course and signed into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits that he had previously blocked. The government had been pushing the president to approve the measures amid soaring fuel prices.
In announcing his decision on Thursday, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, insisted that he now expected the government to move to lower fuel prices for consumers. A few hours later, the government confirmed that it would do so, and on Friday morning it announced cuts in VAT and excise duty on fuels.
Nie pozwolę rządowi dłużej odsuwać od siebie odpowiedzialności za tę trudną sytuację. Podpisałem ustawę dotyczącą nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych i zakończę proces ustawiania Polaków w roli politycznych zakładników. To rząd ponosi pełną odpowiedzialność za ceny paliw -… pic.twitter.com/7AX8v4a9Q0
— Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) October 1, 2026
The windfall tax will levy a one-off charge of 60% of excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. It is expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€914 million).
When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”.
The tax was intended to offset some of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by cutting VAT and excise duty and introducing a maximum daily price. Those measures were initially in place from March to June.
However, in July, Nawrocki announced that he would not sign the windfall tax into law. He instead sent it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment. That process can take years, effectively killing off the bill.
The president argued that the proposed measures “raised serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that the tax would be retroactive, applying to revenue earned from the beginning of March.
Since then, he and the government have been locked in a dispute over the issue, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk arguing that measures to reduce fuel prices, which were briefly reintroduced in the last two weeks of August, can only be restored if Nawrocki signs the windfall tax.
Nawrocki’s office, however, has argued that fuel companies would pass the costs of the tax onto consumers, therefore actually increasing prices.
President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years
The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026
In September, the government’s majority in parliament passed the windfall tax bill a second time. And Nawrocki has now backed down, announcing in a recorded speech on Thursday evening that he would sign the bill into law. However, he has still asked the TK to assess its constitutionality.
Nawrocki declared that he was seeking to call the government’s bluff. He claimed that they were actually hoping the windfall tax would fail so that the treasury could continue obtaining normal tax revenue from high fuel prices, as well as dividends from state oil giant Orlen.

items.title: Biljana Plavsic, Bosnian Serb War Criminal Who Withdrew Her Remorse
items.summary: Plavsic, who died this week, was the only high-ranking woman political leader prosecuted for mass atrocities by the Yugoslav war crimes tribunal. She expressed sorrow for these acts in court – but then changed her mind.
items.body_text:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp
Biljana Plavsic, who died this week aged 96, came from a well-educated, urban, affluent family in Tuzla, where she was born in 1930. Her father, Svetislav, was a prominent biologist, director of the natural science department at the Sarajevo Museum and custodian of its botanical collection. Her grandfather, Dionisije, was a successful merchant. Her mother was a housewife.
As a child in Sarajevo, Yugoslavia, Plavsic was only 11 when Nazi Germany invaded in 1941. Her teenage years were marked by harrowing events. Some of her relatives were killed or deported to concentration camps by the Ustasha, the Croatian fascist movement, or expelled to neighbouring Serbia. Plavsic witnessed some of these events firsthand.
This left a strong imprint on her identity. When I interviewed her for my book, Madam War Criminal: Biljana Plavsic, Serbia’s Iron Lady, she told me her determination to enter politics was to prevent the “extinction of the Serb people”. Serbs were killed en masse in World War II in concentration camps together with Jews, Roma and others. Plavsic said she feared such massacres would happen again, when the Bosnian war started in the 1990s.
Before the war, Plavsic was a dean of the University of Sarajevo’s science faculty, a Fulbright Scholar who had spent two years in New York conducting botany research, and an author of more than 100 scientific papers. She entered politics in 1990 as a member of the Serbian Democratic Party.
Saw ethnic cleansing as ‘natural phenomenon’
Biljana Plavsic kisses a Bosnian Serb Army flag at an army training camp in Manjaca, October 1998. Photo: EPA/DRAGO VEJNOVIC
When Bosnia declared independence from Yugoslavia in April 1992, a move opposed by the party, Plavsic joined other party members in proclaiming a separate entity, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia. During the Bosnian war, she served as its vice-president under Radovan Karadzic, later to be convicted of crimes including genocide and now serving a life sentence.
She defended the wartime purge of Bosnia’s non-Serbs, chiefly Croats and Bosniaks, as “a natural phenomenon”, justifying the policies of ethnic cleansing, mostly carried out by Serb paramilitaries with theories of ethnic and racial superiority.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, ICTY, convicted her in 2003 of crimes against humanity, “the permanent removal of ethnic population by force”, and sentenced her to 11 years in prison. She was the only woman among 161 people indicted by the ICTY, and the highest-ranking woman ever prosecuted for mass atrocities before any international criminal tribunal.
Over many hours of conversation for my book, she told me her version of the war: what led her to take part in it, why some events happened, according to her, and how. As I wrote elsewhere, humanising someone convicted of crimes against humanity sits uncomfortably with many, as it risks diminishing the gravity of their crimes and their culpability.
These concerns should not be downplayed. Still, understanding how women such as Plavsic, a professor and dean of the university, could be convicted of the most serious crimes matters, if we want to learn how to prevent them in the future.
Although I knew deep down that it was naïve, I had hoped that, by the end of our years-long conversations, she would express some regret. But there was none. Indeed, Plavsic told me she didn’t want to sit through a trial to “listen to all fake witnesses and their lies”.
Plavsic was released early in 2009. When deciding on her request for early release, the court took into account that Plavsic expressed remorse for her crimes and demonstrated overall good behaviour in prison, such as “participation in the institution’s walks” and “baking and cooking”.

items.title: Week in Review: Elections and Struggles
items.summary: Women get a raw deal at elections in Bosnia, a spy chief’s arrest raises security questions in Albania and protesters challenge war crimes verdicts in Kosovo - plus much more in our selection of this week’s Balkan Insight Premium stories.
items.body_text:
Week in Review: Elections and Struggles
Entrenched habits
As Bosnia and Herzegovina heads to the polls, promises of political renewal are colliding with entrenched habits that cut across party lines. The governing Trojka [Trio] has struggled to deliver the clean break from clientelism and politicised institutions it promised, potentially opening a path back to power for the unreformed main Bosniak party, the Party of Democratic Action, SDA – less through renewed enthusiasm for the party than from voter disappointment and apathy.
Women’s participation in politics is another key issue. Although women account for more than 40 per cent of candidates as a result of legal obligations, they head just 15.5 per cent of the electoral lists, with parties often placing them low down, where their chances of winning are slim.
Read more: Failings of Bosnia’s ‘Trojka’ Offer Unreformed SDA a Path Back (September 28, 2026)
Bosnian Parties’ Election Gender Quotas Mask Failure to Empower Women (October 1, 2026)
Fight that wasn’t
When mass protests put Serbia’s government under pressure following the Novi Sad railway station disaster, President Aleksandar Vucic promised a “fierce fight against corruption” backed by arrests. More than 18 months later, only a handful of such cases has reached trial, raising questions about what the campaign achieved.
As Serbia heads towards elections, critics argue that the crackdown served more as political theatre than as a sustained attempt to tackle systemic graft, while experts warn that arrests alone are a poor measure of progress.
Read more: In Serbia, ‘Fictitious’ Corruption Campaign Becomes Tool of Distraction (September 30, 2026)
Justice questioned
The conviction of four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, including former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci, has triggered protests and renewed criticism of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers. Clint Williamson, the US prosecutor whose investigation helped pave the way for the court, told BIRN that Kosovo’s authorities failed to prepare the public for any outcome other than acquittal.
Williamson stressed that the verdict concerns the individual responsibility of the four former KLA leaders, not the legitimacy of the KLA, or Kosovo’s liberation struggle. Beyond Kosovo, Williamson sees the Specialist Chambers as a potential model for international justice – at a time when geopolitical divisions make establishing new international tribunals increasingly difficult.
Read more: US Prosecutor Questions Kosovo’s Failure to Mitigate Thaci Verdict Expectations (September 30, 2026)
Opposition in fragments
Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas’s resignation from the Republican People’s Party, CHP, has worsened the fragmentation in an opposition party already divided by an internal leadership struggle and mounting legal pressure on municipalities it runs. By remaining independent rather than joining the breakaway New Party, Yavas has left open questions about the political future of one of the opposition’s most prominent figures.
Some analysts believe he may retreat from politics altogether, while others argue that distancing himself from increasingly bitter party feuds could strengthen his eventual appeal, as an outsider. But for an opposition struggling ahead of future elections, his departure represents another blow – at a time when President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s rivals all seem increasingly divided.
Read more: Mayor’s Resignation Deals Fresh Blow to Turkey’s Fragmented Opposition (September 29, 2026)
Precious opportunity
Moldova is counting on billions of euros in EU grants and concessional loans to help transform its economy and institutions as it moves towards membership, but Finance Minister Victoria Belous warns in an interview with BIRN that securing the money is only half the challenge. She says administrative delays and limited implementation capacity are already slowing investment, while EU disbursements depend on the country delivering agreed reforms.

items.title: Tributes Paid on Sarajevo’s Streets as Edin Dzeko Plays Final Bosnia Match
items.summary: The capital is thronged with people wearing replica shirts in tribute to national football team captain Edin Dzeko, who plays his final international match for Bosnia and Herzegovina against Sweden on Friday.
items.body_text:
The streets of Bosnia's capital, Sarajevo, are flooded in the colours of the national football jersey, with Number 11 dominant among them. On a building on the main boulevard hangs a huge shirt with the name Dzeko and the words: "Thank you, Diamond!"
Tributes are being paid because national team captain Edin Dzeko is making his final appearance for Bosnia and Herzegovina in a match against Sweden on Friday evening, bringing to an end a 19-year international career in which he became Bosnia’s most-capped player and all-time leading goalscorer.
Dzeko, born in 1986, who has captained the national team for much of his career, has won 151 caps and scored 73 goals for Bosnia and Herzegovina. His international goal tally also places him seventh among the all-time leading men’s scorers for UEFA national teams.
The forward made his senior debut on June 2, 2007, against Turkey and scored on his first appearance. Seven years later, he played a central role in Bosnia’s qualification for the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, Bosnia’s first appearance at a major international tournament. He scored 10 goals during qualifying and added another against Iran at the tournament.
People in Sarajevo wearing replicas of Dzeko’s number 11 jersey. Photo: BIRN.
More than a decade later, Dzeko was part of the team that secured Bosnia and Herzegovina’s second World Cup qualification, earning a place at the 2026 tournament. He reached his 150th international appearance during the group stage.
His 73 international goals include 26 in World Cup qualifying, 14 in European Championship qualifying, nine in the UEFA Nations League and two at World Cup finals.
Dzeko acknowledged that the occasion would be difficult for him personally but stressed that the match remained a competitive fixture rather than a farewell exhibition.
“It will be a difficult match for me personally but in the end everything is about the national team. We know it will be a difficult game. Sweden have been returning to their best in recent months, and you can see the progress under the new coach. They know what they are doing and that is why they have six points from two matches. It will be a difficult game for us, but for them as well,” Dzeko said.
Dzeko jerseys on sale in the streets of Sarajevo. Photo: BIRN.
He also admitted that he was unsure how he would feel when he walked onto the pitch for the final time in a Bosnia and Herzegovina shirt.
“I feel a little confused, I don’t know what to feel. I definitely want to enjoy it and try to get a good result, which is the most important thing for me and always has been. We will give our maximum, although the match will be a little emotional,” he said.
Children in Bosnian national team T-shirts. Photo: BIRN.
Dzeko’s final international match will be played on Friday, when Bosnia host Sweden at Zenica’s Bilino Polje in the UEFA Nations League.
Head coach Sergej Barbarez is expected to lead the team in paying tribute to the veteran forward, while supporters’ group BHFanaticos has organised a coordinated 11th-minute ovation in recognition of Dzeko’s number 11 shirt.
After the match, Dzeko’s 152nd for his country, he is set to return his full attention to his club career with Schalke 04 in the German Bundesliga.
The Association of Sarajevo Cevapi is marking the beloved Number 11’s national team farewell by offering an extra helping of the country’s signature grilled meat dish – servings of 11 cevapi are being given to customers in restaurants in Sarajevo on Friday instead of the usual ten.

items.body_text:
The Hungarian State Folk Ensemble continues its 75th anniversary season with "In Praise of Wine."Continue reading
The 4th Budapest Contemporary Exhibition and Fair (BCT) welcomes visitors until Sunday to Bálna, the distinctive Danube-side cultural and event venue, where thousands of artworks by some 70 exhibitors will be on display.
This year’s event will feature a range of accompanying programs, including guided tours, children’s programs, and art education events organized for students. Chief organizer Ádám Tausz emphasized: “For this fourth edition of the art event, works created since the 1970s will be selected based on a strict set of criteria.”
For the first time this year, the Budapest Contemporary exhibition and fair will place greater emphasis on creative fields closely related to the visual arts, and a contemporary jewelry exhibition will also be on display.
In the design section, visitors can tour the apartment of an “imaginary collector,” while the fashion section will be represented by Kata Szegedi with an unconventional booth, added Tausz.
Art collector Katalin Spengler, curator of the jewelry exhibition “Testközelben” featured in the jewelry section of the Budapest Contemporary exhibition and fair, explained that the exhibition will showcase the works of eight designers, and the public will also be able to view a selection spanning the past twenty years of contemporary Hungarian jewelry.
We selected artists who are, for the most part, well-known figures on the international jewelry scene, including Veronika Fábián and Flóra Vági,”
noted Spengler.
Judit Osvárt, editor-in-chief of the interior design and lifestyle magazine Elle Decor and a design expert, highlighted that in the design section, the “Collector’s Home” booth—spanning more than 400 square meters—showcases the coexistence of design and art in an interior that evokes a real living space. Contemporary and vintage furniture, home accessories, pieces by young Hungarian designers, and unique lamps will also be on display at the venue, she added.
In addition to the selection of visual art, a unique photography collection will also be on display at Bálna: Csaba Kertész’s collection features original, contemporary photographs of influential figures in the Hungarian and international music scenes. The Horn Collection is also on display, bringing together the painterly worlds of artists from two different generations through art collector Péter Horn’s selection.
The Képező Gallery emphasizes the connection between art and social engagement, and at the Moholy-Nagy University of Art and Design’s booth—which is returning to the contemporary art exhibition and fair—students majoring in Media Design at the university will showcase their own works.
In the fashion section, at the Kata Szegedi brand’s booth, visitors can view works by visual artist Márton Nemes, photographer Ádám Jelen, and ceramicist Anett Sáfrán.
The complete list of exhibitors and the detailed program for the fine arts exhibition and fair can be found on the website.
Via MTI; Featured photo: MTI/Balogh Zoltán

items.title: German Company to Acquire Pharmaceutical Plant in Miskolc
items.summary: Sanofi’s plant in the northeastern Hungarian city of Miskolc will be transferred to the German company Cheplapharm, along with two other production facilities and 20 types of medication. Around 400 employees work at the Csanyikvölgy site, and the transaction is expected to close in the third quarter of 2027. Boon.hu asked Sanofi about the future […] The post German Company to Acquire Pharmaceutical Plant in Miskolc appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
The deal saves the Diósgyőr factory from closure.Continue reading
Sanofi’s plant in the northeastern Hungarian city of Miskolc will be transferred to the German company Cheplapharm, along with two other production facilities and 20 types of medication.
Around 400 employees work at the Csanyikvölgy site, and the transaction is expected to close in the third quarter of 2027. Boon.hu asked Sanofi about the future of the employees in Miskolc and the details of the takeover.
From the employees’ perspective, one of the most important questions was whether they would all transfer to the new owner and what would happen to their wages and benefits. The company said that
all permanent employees would continue their work with the new employer under legal succession rules, with their length of service at Sanofi fully recognized, and would receive a three-year employment guarantee.
The new owner plans to make a long-term investment in the Csanyikvölgy district, meaning that individual positions and functions will also be adjusted to the company’s future capacity plans. Salaries and other benefits stipulated in the collective agreement will automatically transfer to the new employer, and these will also be covered by the three-year employment guarantee. Not all details concerning the management and organizational structure of the Miskolc plant have been finalized, but according to Sanofi, neither layoffs nor restructuring are planned as a result of the change in ownership.
As part of the partnership, there will be no layoffs or restructuring at the affected production sites, including those in France and Singapore.
Sanofi and Cheplapharm will work out the details of the organizational structures over the coming months, taking the three-year employment guarantee into account. Sanofi was also asked whether it would maintain a direct presence or any Sanofi-related activities at the Miskolc site following the sale. They said
Sanofi will acquire a 26.4% stake in the new company but will not be involved in its operational management.
The plant in the Csanyikvölgy district of Miskolc has been operating in Miskolc since 1986. The site is one of the key centers for the production of anticoagulant injections and prefilled syringes.
This is not the only significant change affecting Miskolc’s factories this year. The long-established company Nestlé’s plant in Diósgyőr is being taken over by the Vimpex Group.
Via Boon.hu, Featured image: Facebook/Szijjártó Péter

items.title: Moscow Expels Hungarian Diplomats and Warns of Economic Consequences
items.summary: Diplomatic tensions between the pro-EU TISZA government and Moscow have reached a new high. In a direct response to Hungary’s controversial expulsion of ten Russian diplomats a few weeks ago, the Russian government has in turn imposed personnel-related measures, expelling several Hungarian diplomats from the country. As Hungary Today previously reported, the TISZA government decided […] The post Moscow Expels Hungarian Diplomats and Warns of Economic Consequences appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
A new sanction would impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on U.S. exports to countries that are among the top buyers of Russian oil or gas.Continue reading
Diplomatic tensions between the pro-EU TISZA government and Moscow have reached a new high. In a direct response to Hungary’s controversial expulsion of ten Russian diplomats a few weeks ago, the Russian government has in turn imposed personnel-related measures, expelling several Hungarian diplomats from the country.
As Hungary Today previously reported, the TISZA government decided on September 8 to expel ten Russian diplomats. The decision was announced by Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán to the silent applause of the European pro-Ukraine lobby. She justified the Hungarian government’s action by saying that those affected had carried out activities on Hungarian territory that were prohibited under the provisions of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations; in other words, she accused them of carrying out intelligence activities. No evidence was presented in support of these allegations.
The Russian ambassador in Budapest was then asked to arrange for the affected staff members to leave the country.
The specific allegations against the diplomats and the deadline for their departure were not made public. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said at the time on social media that he was determined to protect the country’s sovereignty.
❗️ The statement by Anita Orbán regarding Budapest’s demand that 10 Russian diplomats should leave the Hungarian territory indicates that the new Hungarian authorities have got captured by ideologically driven anti-Russian phobias…
🔗 https://t.co/EST1FCcxUV https://t.co/L7L8F0Oeg1
— Russian Embassy, HU (@RusEmbHungary) September 8, 2026
The announced countermeasure did not take long to materialize. As the Russian news agency Interfax reported, Russia is expelling Hungarian embassy and consular staff.
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, Hungary’s chargé d’affaires in Moscow, Gábor Gergics, was officially summoned on October 1. The Russian side strongly protested the Hungarian measures of September 8, 2026, which it described as “unjustified” and “extremely unfriendly.” The Hungarian diplomat was informed that
a group of staff members from the Hungarian Embassy in Moscow and the Consulates General in St. Petersburg and Kazan would have to leave Russia within two weeks.
Hungary’s Foreign Ministry responded immediately. Budapest said it took note of the decision and regarded it as a response to its own action, but saw no reason to abandon its security considerations.
An escalation is not in Hungary’s interest, and the diplomatic missions in Russia will remain fully operational,
the ministry said.
Beyond diplomatic personnel, the relationship between the two countries now also faces potential economic repercussions. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov commented on Russian outlet URA on whether the dispute could spill over into trade relations, saying,
Unfortunately, I would not completely rule that out.”
Moscow has so far kept the increasingly strained political relationship separate from economic cooperation. The two countries maintain particularly close ties in the energy sector, as Hungary continues to purchase Russian energy products. According to the Kremlin spokesperson, the current Hungarian leadership’s approach toward Russia differs significantly from that of the previous government under Viktor Orbán; in economic matters, however, Budapest has so far maintained a measured approach.
Although Moscow has not yet announced any specific trade or energy sanctions, Peskov’s warning is being viewed as a clear signal to Hungary. Continuing economic relations may be in both sides’ interest, but in the long term they are unlikely to remain entirely insulated from political tensions.
Via interfax.ru, ura.news; Featured image: Pixabay

items.body_text:
Petr Pavel to Miss Local Elections After Trip Planning Error
Prague Morning
Czech President Petr Pavel will not vote in next week’s local elections in Černouček, the village in the Litoměřice region where he lives, because he will be abroad on a private trip.
The Presidential Office confirmed on Friday that Pavel had left the Czech Republic and would not be able to participate in the municipal elections. The Castle said the president regrets the planning mistake.
Pavel is expected to return to his official schedule on October 19, when he will receive newly appointed ambassadors. During his absence, he will remain in contact with the Presidential Office in case a situation requiring his attention arises.
A post by Czech rally driver Martin Prokop has linked Pavel to the Rallye du Maroc. Prokop shared a photograph with the president and wrote that Pavel had visited the event.
The rally is taking place in Morocco from September 28 to October 3.
According to Czech media reports, Pavel’s private trip is a motorcycle holiday. The Presidential Office itself has not confirmed the location of the trip.
The timing of the trip is notable because Pavel himself formally set the dates for this year’s elections in June.
Under recently amended electoral rules, local and regional elections are held on the Friday and Saturday of the first full week of October.

items.body_text:
VIDEO: Hollywood Actress Zendaya Takes Over Prague for New Sportswear Campaign
Prague Morning
Zendaya recently came to Prague to film a promotional campaign for Swiss sportswear and footwear brand On, with several recognizable locations across the city serving as the backdrop.
The actress filmed at the Strahov ventilation towers, the building used by Prague’s Technical Road Administration for tunnel management, and the roof of the National Museum’s New Building.
The two-minute campaign video follows Zendaya as she runs through Prague while being pursued by a group of women. The opening scenes were filmed around the Strahov ventilation towers before the action moves to the brutalist TSK tunnel administration building.
A fight takes place outside the building and continues underneath it, before Zendaya escapes and heads toward the National Museum’s New Building.
The final part of the video was filmed inside the museum building, including its staircase and corridors, and on the roof. The campaign ends with Zendaya jumping from the rooftop.
The video was directed by Pantera, an Argentine directing trio. On selected Prague for the launch of its new collection, using the city as the setting for both still photography and the campaign film.
Zendaya is the latest major international star to film in Prague, which has become an increasingly popular location for international productions.
Several recent projects have used Prague neighborhoods and buildings as filming locations. The horror film Resident Evil was shot at locations including Karlín and Holešovice late last year.
Holešovice has also attracted international television productions.
Apple TV selected a tax office building in Prague 7 as a filming location for Birdwatcher, with production taking place there for two weeks. Wyatt Russell, the son of actors Goldie Hawn and Kurt Russell, is among the series’ lead actors.

items.body_text:
Prague Passengers Can Now Request Czech or English Speaking Bolt Drivers
Prague Morning
Bolt has introduced two new ride categories in Prague that allow passengers to request drivers who speak either Czech or English.
The new options are available at the same price as a standard Bolt ride.
They are open to drivers of any nationality who can communicate in the relevant language at a level suitable for everyday conversation.
Czech-speaking passengers who are less comfortable communicating in English can request a Czech-speaking driver, while foreign residents, tourists and business travellers can choose a driver who speaks English.
Bolt already provides automatic translation for communication between passengers and drivers within its app. Booking information, addresses and messages can therefore be translated automatically. The new categories are designed to cover situations in which communication takes place outside the app, particularly during the journey itself.
The company said the new options are already available in Prague, where it has enough partner drivers who meet the language requirements.
Drivers can choose whether to participate in the new categories. They may offer rides in Czech, English, both languages or continue driving exclusively in the standard category.
Participation is voluntary.
Passengers will see the two new options directly in the Bolt app. The Czech-speaking category is identified by an icon featuring the Czech flag, while the English-speaking option uses an English flag icon.

items.body_text:
Inmate Alleges Sexual Abuse in Prison, Penitentiary Service Denies
Convicted inmate Giorgi Davitadze told the appeals court that he was sexually assaulted at the hands of prison guards in a de-escalation cell and later attempted suicide. Georgia’s Special Penitentiary Service “categorically” denies the allegations and published footage to support the claim, while the Public Defender said it found “no evidence” of ill-treatment in video recordings.
Davitadze, 36, the son of Avtandil Davitadze, a former Georgian Dream member of the Tbilisi City Council, made the allegations during an October 2 hearing at the Tbilisi Court of Appeals. Davitadze is serving a sentence in connection with the wounding of Shalva Peradze, an employee of the Interior Ministry.
An audio recording of the hearing was published by opposition-leaning TV Pirveli. In the recording, Davitadze can be heard telling the court that he was sexually assaulted by employees of Penitentiary Establishment No. 6.
“They took me down to the de-escalation [room] and raped me — with a finger, with a hand. I am saying this here, in the presence of my family,” Davitadze is heard saying in the recording, noting that the video footage shows the guard making “movement near the buttocks.”
He notes that up to 10 prison guards took part in the abuse and did it under the cameras, yet “so that it cannot be seen” in the footage, “but they still cannot conceal it completely.”
Davitadze is also heard saying that the cameras do not contain the voice where the guards allegedly use humiliating phrases against him, and that the abuse intensified after he requested forensic examinations. He also criticized the Public Defender’s Office’s response to his allegations, claiming that its representative had reviewed footage related to his case but failed to adequately respond to his complaints.
“I attempted suicide because imagine having to look again every day at the same guards who raped you,” Davitadze said.
Penitentiary Service Denies Allegations, Publishes Footage
Following Davitadze’s allegations in court, Georgia’s Special Penitentiary Service released video footage from December 21, 2025, when the alleged abuse took place, showing scenes in the de-escalation cell, while again rejecting his allegation of sexual assault as “a complete lie.”
The footage, which contains no audio, shows several prison employees accompanying the inmate inside the room, with the inmate appearing agitated, with his face blurred and his hands making aggressive gestures. Guards are then seen restraining Davitadze and moving him onto a bed before conducting what the Penitentiary Service described as a mandatory inspection, including with what appears to be a detection device.
The footage shows episodes where guards position themselves so that they end up covering part of the inmate’s body, making it impossible to see from the footage the exact nature of procedures they carry out on him. At least one of the guards restraining and inspecting the inmate is seen wearing what appears to be rubber gloves.
The Service said Davitadze had refused to undergo an inspection required when a prisoner is placed in a de-escalation cell and had begun verbally insulting prison employees.
“The footage also shows that only after this, in order to perform their assigned duties, employees of the establishment forcibly conducted an inspection of the convicted prisoner, which was carried out using an electronic detector on his body,” the Service said.
The agency said it had previously refrained from publishing the footage because an investigation into the case was underway.
The video footage came after the Service earlier on October 2 “categorically” denied Davitadze’s allegations, calling them “a complete lie” and “a continuation of the Davitadze family’s campaign to discredit the penitentiary system.”

items.body_text:
Sokhumi, Tskhinvali, Moscow Digest – September 25-October 1, 2026
Below is the weekly digest of key developments and discourses in and around the occupied regions of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia, as well as those concerning Tbilisi–Moscow relations.
Sokhumi
- Abkhazia’s de facto Foreign Minister Oleg Bartsits Holds Talks with Sergey Lavrov
Abkhazia’s de facto Foreign Minister Oleg Bartsits and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held talks in Moscow on economic, humanitarian and security “cooperation”.
Lavrov described Russia-Abkhazia relations as strategic and allied, and highlighted Abkhazia’s support for Russia amid the war in Ukraine. He also noted a 16% increase in bilateral trade in 2025 and a 40% rise in Russian excursion trips to Abkhazia in 2026.
Tourism and infrastructure were key topics. Lavrov said Moscow would support Abkhazia’s plans to increase annual tourist arrivals to five million by 2030. Bartsits highlighted the reopening of Sukhumi airport, saying around 200,000 people had used the airport since its reopening, as well as ongoing railway and maritime cooperation.
The two sides also discussed investment, preferential lending, and cooperation in healthcare, education and culture. Following the bilateral talks, a “trilateral” meeting between Lavrov, Bartsits, and South Ossetia’s de facto Foreign Minister Akhsar Dzhioev was held to discuss regional security.
- Russia and Occupied Abkhazia Agree to Mutual Recognition of ‘Customs Inspection Results‘
Sokhumi and Moscow have agreed to mutually recognize “customs inspection” results, a measure expected to facilitate the movement of goods across the so-called Psou border crossing.
The relevant “protocol” was signed on 25 September by Russia’s Federal Customs Service and the de facto Customs Committee of Abkhazia, following more than four years of negotiations.
According to the document, the two sides will exchange “customs inspection” data electronically. In cases where goods or vehicles have already been inspected by one side, the other side may use the results instead of conducting a duplicate inspection.
The de facto Customs Committee said the new mechanism is intended to reduce processing times and ease congestion at the border, particularly during the tourist and citrus seasons when passenger and cargo flows increase.
Abkhaz de facto officials described “mutual recognition of customs controls” as an established international practice and said the new system would improve the efficiency and capacity of the “border crossing.”
- Russian Tourist Killed in Gagra
A 26-year-old Russian citizen, Amina Bikbova, was killed while on holiday in Gagra in late September. The de facto Interior Ministry detained 25-year-old local resident Edgar Abukhba, who confessed to the killing.
According to the de facto authorities, Bikbova met Abukhba in Gagra on 23 September and later accompanied him to a rented apartment. He initially denied involvement but subsequently confessed to strangling her and showed investigators where he had left her body.
The case has caused widespread outrage because Abukhba had previously been convicted of the rape and violent assault of a Russian tourist in 2019. As he was a minor at the time, his sentence was reduced from nine years, and he was released in February 2024.
De facto Ombudsman Anas Kishmaria attributed the incident to what she described as systemic shortcomings in the penitentiary system, including inadequate rehabilitation and post-release supervision. She called for reforms to penitentiary legislation and greater prevention and awareness efforts concerning sexual violence.
The Gagra district administration covered the cost of transporting Bikbova’s body to Russia and provided assistance to her relatives.
Abukhba has been placed in pre-trial detention for two months. The investigation continues. Read more here.

items.body_text:
Friedrich Naumann Foundation Also Exits Georgia Amid Grant Restrictions
The Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom (FNF) is another major German foundation, after the Konrad Adenauer Foundation (KAS), to announce an exit from Georgia amid funding restrictions introduced by the ruling Georgian Dream party as part of its crackdown on media and civil society.
FNF said in its October 2 statement that it ceased operations in Georgia and closed its Tbilisi office, saying restrictions under Georgia’s Law on Grants had made it impossible to continue its work, citing, among others, the rejection by Georgian authorities of its applications to continue funding the projects under new grants laws.
“The Georgian government’s actions make it impossible for the FNF to continue working in the country,” the statement said.
The decision follows a series of funding restrictions introduced in Georgia since 2024, including amendments to the Law on Grants in 2025 that introduced mandatory government approval for foreign donors to disburse local grants, and March 2026 amendments to the same law that further expanded the restrictions to foreign organizations willing to provide funds to their local branches.
The Foundation, closely affiliated with Germany’s liberal Free Democratic Party (FDP), has operated in the country since 2002.
It said that the “unavoidable” decision was made after it had applied this year under Georgia’s Law on Grants to continue funding projects and working with partner organizations, but “the Georgian authorities demanded that every single program component be subordinated to the priorities of the Georgian government and that appropriate approvals be obtained for all activities.” The FNF said that such conditions “fundamentally undermine the necessary freedom of action required of a liberal foundation.”
It noted that it then had sought to “exhaust all possibilities” to continue its work in Georgia and “support those forces committed to a democratic future for the country,” however, “this application was rejected on July 28, 2026.”
“Therefore, we no longer see any possibilities for work that aligns with our values and principles.”
The FNF said that it has been active in Georgia since 2002, working with “many partner organizations” and “liberal leaders” to promote “a free society, a European future for Georgia, and a close dialogue between societies.”
The Foundation said Georgia had previously been “a symbol of hope and democratic progress,” while noting that it “will continue to stand alongside all Georgians who are committed to a free and democratic order in their country.”
“We will give them a voice from outside the country and support them in working toward a free and democratic future for their nation,” the statement said.
The FNF thanked its staff and partners, saying that in recent years “many of them have had to take on increasing personal risks when they have worked for a democratic liberal order in their country.”
“We therefore view Georgia’s political developments with great concern.”
The announcement came a day after the Konrad Adenauer Foundation (KAS) said that it had closed its Tbilisi office on September 30 after more than two decades of work in Georgia, similarly citing Georgia’s grant restrictions
Georgia’s Tightening Funding Environment
As part of its crackdown on civil society and media, the ruling Georgian Dream party has gradually restricted access to foreign funding through a series of laws since 2024, including the Georgian version of the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) and a repeatedly amended Law on Grants. Under the current versions, both laws carry criminal penalties, including several years in prison, for certain violations related to foreign funding.
That includes failure to seek government consent for certain foreign grants under the Law on Grants, punishable by up to six years in prison, and failure to register as a foreign agent under FARA, punishable by up to five years in prison.

items.title: German political foundations close Tbilisi offices after grant applications rejected
items.summary: Both organisations’ applications to continue financing projects and working with local partners were rejected on 28 July 2026.
items.body_text:
Two German political foundations have closed their offices in Georgia after their applications to continue funding projects under the country’s new Law on Grants were rejected. The closures come amidst a broader tightening of restrictions on foreign funding in Georgia.
The Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung (KAS) and the Friedrich-Naumann-Stiftung für die Freiheit (FNF) both said they could no longer continue their work under the conditions set by the Georgian government.
The two foundations closed their Tbilisi offices on 30 September. KAS described the closure as involuntary, while FNF called the decision unavoidable.
Both organisations’ applications to continue financing projects and working with local partners were rejected on 28 July.
KAS attributed the closure to the political and legal framework created by the Georgian government, arguing that it had become impossible for the foundation to carry out its core work in the country.
The foundation said the Georgian government administration had rejected its applications under the new Law on Grants. Efforts by the German government to find a way for KAS to continue working in Georgia had also failed.
KAS added that approval of its projects appeared possible only if they no longer reflected the foundation’s political character and mission.
‘A mere presence in Georgia without the possibility of fulfilling our actual mission is not a viable alternative’, the foundation wrote.
In turn, the FNF said Georgian authorities had required it to bring each part of its programmes into line with the priorities of the Georgian government and obtain approval for individual activities.
The foundation argued that these conditions left it without the independence it needed to carry out its work.
‘We therefore see no possibilities for work that corresponds to our values and principles’, FNF stated.
The foundation also stated that many of its partners had faced increasing personal risks in recent years because of their work for a democratic and liberal political system.
‘We therefore view Georgia’s political development with great concern’, FNF wrote.
Germany’s newly appointed Ambassador to Georgia, Barbara Voss, made the remarks on Friday during a Day of German Unity event in Tbilisi, where she spoke about the closure of German political foundations and the broader state of German–Georgian relations.
‘All four of our political foundations, which have supported Georgia and its people for decades on its path to European integration, were forced to temporarily suspend their work due to a decision by the Georgian government […] These developments also strain Georgia–EU relations’, Voss said.
She added that preserving German–Georgian relations would be among her priorities during her tenure.
‘In the coming years, I will personally dedicate my efforts as ambassador to preserving as much as possible of what has been built […] between Georgia and Germany’, she said.
Voss also pointed to the situation facing Georgia’s universities, highlighting one institution, Ilia State University, which she described as having become ‘Georgia’s internationally most renowned university’ over the past 20 years.
She said the university, which had received ‘immense financial resources, particularly from Germany’, and cooperated closely with Germany on research, was now facing ‘a threat to its very existence’.
Voss added that she would raise the issue in her dialogue with the Georgian government.
Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili rejected the foundations’ characterisation of the restrictions, highlighting that the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung is a political organisation affiliated with Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
‘The Christian Democratic Union is a member of the EPP and therefore a partner party of the United National Movement’, Papuashvili told journalists.

items.title: Prisoner alleges guards raped him, Penitentiary Service denies claim
items.summary: Georgia’s Penitentiary Service released footage which they claim shows officers searching and restraining Giorgi Davitadze.
items.body_text:
Giorgi Davitadze has claimed that around 10 guards raped and humiliated him in a prison de-escalation room in December 2025. The penitentiary service has called the allegation ‘a complete lie’.
Davitadze, the son of former Tbilisi City Council member Avtandil Davitadze, is serving a 17-year prison sentence after being convicted of stabbing Interior Ministry employee Shalva Peradze. His family links the alleged abuse in prison to the case involving Peradze.
On Friday, the Special Penitentiary Service released footage purported to show guards searching and restraining Davitadze in a de-escalation room at Rustavi’s Prison No 6. They deny his allegation that he was raped by prison staff.
The footage, which is from 21 December 2025 has no sound and the face of the prisoner is blurred. It shows up to 10 penitentiary employees searching the prisoner, including with an electronic detector. Several guards hold his hands behind his back, while at one point they force him onto a bed and search him as he lies on his back.
The guards leave the room about two minutes after bringing him inside.
Davitadze, 36, had previously raised allegations of sexual violence during a Court of Appeals hearing.
‘They took me to the de-escalation room and raped me — with a finger, with a hand. […] Ten men, the guards, raped me. Everything is visible on the camera’, Davitadze told the court.
He also claimed he attempted suicide after the alleged abuse and said he would go on hunger strike unless the employees he identified were held responsible.
In response to his allegations, Davitadze’s family and supporters held a protest on 21 September, demanding that those responsible for the alleged abuse be held accountable.
Davitadze’s mother, Irma Davitadze, told journalists that the footage released by the penitentiary service was only part of the recordings. She claimed she had seen five files totalling around 20 minutes, and that parts of the footage had been cut.
The family says investigators have seized the relevant recordings and questioned penitentiary staff, but that no criminal prosecution has been launched against any of them.
Opposition party Patriot Alliance leader Irma Inashvili, who released footage of prisoners being tortured in 2012, has commented on Davitadze’s allegations, calling for the head of Prison No 6 to be held responsible.
Penitentiary Service and Public Defender cite lack of evidence
The Penitentiary Service has said all prisoners transferred to the de-escalation room undergo a search. The Service claimed Davitadze had refused the search and verbally insulted staff. Guards then forcibly searched him as part of their duties, the service stated.
The agency described Davitadze’s allegation of sexual violence as ‘a complete lie’, and maintains that no violence took place.
The service said it previously withheld the footage because the investigation was ongoing and it did not want the release to be interpreted as an attempt to influence the investigation.
It cited ‘high public interest’, the sensitivity of the case, and what it described as an attempt by Davitadze’s family to discredit the agency as reasons for the release.
The service also stated that continuous footage of Davitadze’s movements inside the penitentiary had been archived since 3 March 2026 and that it was ready to provide the recordings to interested parties in accordance with the law.
On Friday, Public Defender Levan Ioseliani said that his office had examined the case in detail, including archived video recordings.
The Public Defender’s Office found no evidence of physical mistreatment or violence in the material it reviewed, Ioseliani told journalists.
Davitadze had also alleged verbal abuse, and Ioseliani said the Public Defender’s Office had referred that allegation to the Prosecutor’s Office, which had opened an investigation. The Service has previously categorically denied allegations of any violence against Davitadze.

items.title: From nightclub to library: Vantaa gets a new library at Jumbo
items.summary: Housed in the Jumbo shopping centre, the library will cost the city nearly €600,000 a year in rent.
items.body_text:
A new library is opening this month in a former nightclub space in Vantaa.
The new Jumbo Library is the tenth library to open in a shopping centre in the Helsinki metropolitan area.
Some 15 years ago, the same premises were home to a nightclub run by Finnish nightlife entrepreneur Sedu Koskinen. Now, the space is being turned into a library.
"We've paid a lot of attention to acoustics, including the ceiling materials and carpets. We've used a lot of textiles, and the lighting is also quite calm," says Marjo Päivärinta, service supervisor at the Jumbo Library.
According to Päivärinta, a quieter environment has been something library users have wanted for some time.
The library is moving from its previous location at the International School of Vantaa (ISV) in Kartanonkoski, where it shared space with the school. The surroundings could get fairly noisy and busy.
The library has been designed to feel calm and quiet, with carefully chosen furniture and colours. The nightclub, naturally, had rather different priorities.
The new location also gives the library considerably more space.
At the school, the library had less than 800 square metres at its disposal. At Jumbo, it will have around 1,400.
Cost criticism
The new library's location was met with some controversy, however. Some have claimed that schools are a better setting for libraries than shopping centres.
The cost of the move has also come under scrutiny several times. The City of Vantaa will pay just over 580,000 euros a year in rent for the premises at Jumbo, under a 15-year lease.
"In the current economic situation, that feels like quite a lot of money," said Sirkku Ingervo (Left).
The City of Vantaa has justified the move by pointing to the area's growth.
The library at the school has been the only library facility in the entire Aviapolis area, and over the years it has become too small.
At the same time, the number of pupils at ISV has grown considerably in recent years. With the library moving out, the school will be able to use the space for other purposes.

items.title: Government, defence minister survive confidence vote called over Middle East policy
items.summary: Finland's biggest opposition party, the SDP, had called for a vote of no confidence in the entire government.
items.body_text:
Finnish PM Petteri Orpo's (NCP) government as well as Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) each survived confidence votes on Friday.
Häkkänen won Parliament's confidence in a 114-61 vote, while the government won by a margin of 93 to 62.
Finland's biggest opposition party, the SDP, had called for a vote of no confidence in the entire government. According to the SDP, the government's split views on Middle East policy are making Finland's position unclear.
Meanwhile, the opposition Greens' MP Atte Harjanne tabled a no confidence motion against the defence minister, with Left Alliance chair Minja Koskela seconding the proposal earlier this week.
The parties criticised Häkkänen's recent visit to Israel, where he met with Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz. Häkkänen said the visit was related to Finland's order for the David's Sling air defence system from Israel.
At the end of August, Finland and Israel quietly renewed a memorandum of understanding on defence materiel development and procurement cooperation. The memorandum was first signed in 2013.
On Thursday Häkkänen cancelled plans to attend a two-day defence minister's meeting of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) in Reykjavík, citing the pending confidence vote.
According to the defence ministry, JEF's ten member countries aim to build military capabilities, prevent crises, and respond together when needed. The group mainly operates in Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea region.
Since taking office in June 2023, PM Orpo's government has survived several major confidence votes in Parliament

items.title: Inside Sweden: How well does the Swedish Migration Agency understand the law?
items.summary: Richard Orange reflects on the Swedish Migration Agency's handling of migration law, before running through the week's main stories.
items.body_text:
It's an almost impossible task. The Migration Agency's 6,000 employees make decisions on well over 100,000 cases every year. Each of those cases involve people with unique circumstances generating new legal issues. At the same time, migration law in Sweden has been changing at a dizzying pace, as national governments tighten the rules for work permits, citizenship, family reunion and asylum, and EU directives come into force.
The UK Withdrawal Agreement was a particular challenge, as it required the agency to apply EU rules for residency for almost the first time. Even today, EU citizens do not need to have any contact with the Migration Agency to get a personal number, but instead register directly with the Swedish Tax Agency.
So you would expect mistakes to be made. But despite the unusually high number of British citizens Sweden has rejected for post-Brexit residency, the agency has repeatedly insisted that it has been applying the law correctly.
To get a better understanding of how the agency has been applying the law, we managed to get an interview earlier this month with its legal chief, Susanna Fonsell.
It wasn't her first language and our questioning could have been clearer, but when we shared the transcript with three prominent experts in EU law, they agreed nonetheless that she appeared to misunderstand key aspects of EU law as applied to the UK Withdrawal Agreement, including the proportionality rule, residency, income and employment requirements. You can read our interview here.
Migration news
Strict new rules for family reunion came into force on Wednesday, which also brought in the government's solution to the deportations of teenagers and young adults.
Our reporter Mandy Pipher carried out a long interview with Ann-Kari Olsson, Section Head at the Swedish Migration Agency, to find out who is affected – and how. We published it in full as a Q&A.
As soon as the parliament opened the Green Party launched a special 'independent motion' calling for a much more thoroughgoing solution to the teen deportation issue. The Migration Agency on Wednesday also announced that it was resuming the processing of teen deportation cases, which it put on hold in March when the government announced its plans.
On citizenship, Sweden's Migration Court of Appeal said it was on the look-out of a suitable case to grant leave to appeal so that the new stricter citizenship law can be tested at the highest level.
Meanwhile the Swedish Council of Higher Education said the planned language tests for citizenship would now not be held until 2029, three years later than the government originally hoped.
Forming Sweden's next government
This week's news was dominated by drama over the process of building Sweden's next government. Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson abandoned her role as sonderingsperson, the person responsible for building a coalition, on Monday after the Left Party voted for Moderate MP Andreas Norlén to return as Speaker, rejecting the Social Democrat candidate. We wrote a quick analysis of what she was trying to do.
In the end on Friday, Norlén reappointed Andersson sonderingsperson, and the Centre Party invited the Left Party, Green Party and Social Democrats to a meeting with "external actors" to discuss what policies a new joint government could have.
You can hear us discuss the political machinations in this week's Sweden in Focus podcast.
What else have we been writing about?
Finally, we want to know what it is about home that you miss doing now you're living in Sweden. Tell us in the survey here.

items.title: Reader question: Is it possible to transfer a foreign pension to Sweden?
items.summary: A lot of people who move to Sweden do so mid-career. A UK reader asked us if it was possible to transfer an overseas occupation pension to Sweden. You can but it's not always worth it.
items.body_text:
"Hello, I have just hit 50 and have started to think about my pension," the reader writes. "I worked pretty much constantly after I graduated, including a few years for the UK National Health Service. Is it possible to transfer that into my Swedish fund?"
Monica Zettervall, a pensions expert at the Swedish Pension Agency, said that while the transfer of an overseas state pension happens almost automatically, it was less common for people to transfer an overseas occupational pension into their Swedish tjänstepension.
READ ALSO: What are The Local's reader questions?
State pension
The transfer of the basic state pension from other countries where you have lived and worked happens almost automatically. When you retire, the agency asks you about any entitlements to a state pension you might have from overseas.
"When you apply for your Swedish pension, it asks you on the form if you have lived overseas, and if so, when you were working. You also have to give your social security number," Zettervall said. "Then we contact their authorities."
The Swedish Pension Agency will then pay out any state pension you might have accrued overseas together with your Swedish state pension.
Overseas occupational pension
Transferring an overseas foreign pension to Sweden is more difficult.
The bank Nordea and the pension company Futur Pension are the only two providers in Sweden who accept transferred foreign pensions, and, as far as the UK is concerned at least, they are also the only two companies accepted as "Qualified Recognised Overseas Pensions Schemes" (QROPS).
Nordea will handle both the transfer of an overseas pension and act as a pensions manager, whereas Futur Pension will hold the funds, but works with clients through two financial advisory firms, Max Matthiessen and Söderberg and Partners.
"The process depends on different factors - for example country, insurance company and former employer," said Anne Höglund, Head of Insurance Specialists at Nordea. "As long as we are informed that the pension is transferable the process itself is straightforward. Different countries and companies has different requirements for transferring and Sweden has its own laws and rules that will apply for the pension when it arrives in Sweden."
On its website, Nordea says that it is able to move over pensions from EU agencies, the UK, Ireland, Luxembourg, The Netherlands, Jersey, Malta, Belgium and Norway - so long as you have lived there less than 3 years.
Max Matthiessen will handle pensions from all of the above, but also transfers pensions from France, Guernsey, and Isle of Man.
What is the point of transferring an overseas pension?
Ahmed Ben Moussa, who runs the foreign pensions division at Max Matthiessen, told The Local that there were several advantages in consolidating your pension in one country.
"Max Matthiessen’s perception is that the advantages of transferring a workplace pension from other countries is to make it easier when you retire by collecting your pension funds in the same country as where you live," he said.
"And not just easier. “You might have other options in the country, for example, you might be able to access a wider range of investments and get the potential for more flexibility over how you access your funds when you retire, and you might be offered more flexibility over who you can pass your pension on to when you die.”
Some clients were also worried about the risk of double taxation, he added.
"Our perception is that some clients are worried about double taxation and have therefore transferred to the county where they live. However, we always inform our clients that we are not tax advisors and that we cannot give them any tax advice. We always refer our clients to tax advisors if they have any tax questions, we can only assist them with transferring the funds to Sweden.”
One advantage for people living in Sweden is that all of your pension is visible on the Min Pension website, giving you much greater visibility over how much

items.title: Q&A: Who is affected by Sweden's new law on family immigration?
items.summary: The previous Swedish government's law tightening rules for family reunification comes into force on October 1st, 2026. The Local spoke to Ann-Kari Olsson, Section Head at the Swedish Migration Agency, to find out who is affected – and how.
items.body_text:
The new law, called "Stricter requirements for family immigration" (Skärpta villkor för anhöriginvandring in Swedish), puts stringent new requirements on those wanting to bring non-Swedish relatives to live with them in Sweden.
We go over the basics in this explainer article. In brief, the biggest changes are: a new two-year waiting period before certain categories of permit holders can bring relatives to Sweden; an increase, by 30 percent, in the maintenance amount required when applying for relatives to live together in Sweden; and the application of the maintenance requirement to many more cases, including permit extensions/renewals.
To find out more details, you can read our full interview with Ann-Kari Olsson of the Swedish Migration Agency below. Or you can jump straight to one of these key questions:
Who is exempt from the two-year residence waiting requirement?
What counts towards the maintenance requirement?
Are there any exemptions to the maintenance requirement?
Will the family of researchers and doctoral students be affected by the new maintenance requirement?
What changes in this law for the relatives of Swedish and Nordic citizens?
What changes in this law for the relatives of permanent residents?
What changes in this law for the relatives of third-country nationals?
What changes in this law for the relatives of those with EU long-term resident status?
Q&A with Ann-Kari Olsson of the Swedish Migration Agency
The Local: Which groups are affected by this new law?
Ann-Kari Olsson: It applies to everyone—that is, anyone applying for a residence permit based on family ties. So, everyone is covered in one way or another. Of course, it depends somewhat on the grounds for the application, and also on the residence status held by the person with whom the applicant has the family tie.
So what are the major changes and to to whom do they apply?
Ann-Kari Olsson: [They apply to] anyone living in Sweden. After all, it affects everyone in one way or another. But this new legislation—it is designed to feature, you could say, situation-specific rules. In other words, different rules apply to different individuals depending on what the applicant is applying for: which connection to the person already in Sweden (the anknytningsperson) the person applying has (e g. spouse, child), and the specific residence permit or status held by the person already in Sweden. It is quite complex. Furthermore, the aim of this legislative amendment has been to align Swedish law with the EU minimum standards.
As for the major changes, they concern who can serve as the reference person (anknytningsperson) and the level of financial support required. That is, the requirements for reference persons.
The income requirement has been raised, applies in several new situations, and will be enforced for both new applications and extension applications.
There is also a new requirement regarding the duration of stay in Sweden—specifically, a requirement to have resided in the country for two years. Furthermore, the burden of proof regarding biological kinship is being tightened.
This may lead to us offering DNA testing in more cases. It might be a situation where a family relationship exists but is difficult to prove; we may suspect the relationship is genuine but require evidence. In such instances, we can offer DNA testing to verify it. That option existed previously, but its scope has been expanded.
How has it been expanded?
Ann-Kari Olsson: The requirement clarifies that a DNA analysis must be offered if a biological relationship cannot be demonstrated. And that applies in certain cases. Under current rules, DNA analysis is to be offered if the other evidence regarding the relationship is insufficient. The amendment entails a tightening of the rules compared to the current situation—meaning we can require it in more cases where the relationship needs to be clarified.
It essentially places greater emphasis on this, and we can use it in more cases to verify t
