items.title: Brazil’s Election Won’t Fix What’s Broken
items.summary: Reckoning with the country’s real crisis.
items.body_text:
The Brazilian presidential election, which kicks off with a first round of voting on October 4, gives citizens a choice between radically different visions of politics. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, the standard-bearer of the Latin American left, seeks a fourth presidential term against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Jair Bolsonaro, the hard-right former president who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn the results of the previous presidential election. The race is also a contest over how Brazil should conduct its foreign affairs: Lula emphasizes strategic autonomy, including through growing ties with China and other partners, while Flávio Bolsonaro favors close alignment with the Trump administration in the United States.
What unites the two candidates is the assumption that Brazil still has the freedom to choose its foreign policy strategy. Brazil’s vast resources, distance from active conflict, and influx of foreign direct investment should position it well to manage current global upheaval and great-power competition, and to effectively bargain for what it wants. But despite these valuable geopolitical assets, Brazil is losing global influence, and its autonomy to act is at risk. Major powers, including both China and the United States, are increasingly able to dictate their terms of engagement with Brazil. The country is also becoming isolated in South America, where it had until recently led the creation of regional institutions such as the trading bloc Mercosur. Its relationship with Argentina, for instance—which had helped underpin four decades of regional stability—has deteriorated to the point that neither country has an ambassador in the other’s capital.
Brazil is largely responsible for its waning sway. Much of the country’s influence depends on whether foreign partners believe that the deals it strikes today will be implemented tomorrow. That credibility, in turn, rests on the state’s capacity to commit—that is, its ability to mobilize the resources needed to fulfill its promises, coordinate public institutions effectively, and ensure that the bargains it makes survive democratic political turnover. A raft of domestic problems, including mounting fiscal constraints, a political system at war with itself, and widespread corruption, has made it harder for the state to deliver. A major scandal has now engulfed the Supreme Court, an institution meant to enforce rules impartially and which is therefore essential to the durability of Brazilian commitments. The Trump administration’s open meddling in Brazil’s domestic politics has compounded the country’s vulnerabilities by making any deal controversial and partisan and raising the likelihood that future administrations in both Brasília and Washington might try to reverse it.
Whoever wins the upcoming presidential election will inherit these sources of weakness. So far, the candidates have not offered any clear plan to address them. Neither a tilt toward Washington nor an embrace of multilateral diplomacy will solve the deeper problem that is eroding Brazil’s foreign policy autonomy and keeping it from turning its assets into real strength.
RUNNING WILD
Brazil has not always struggled to project credibility to the world. In the 1990s, the country’s economic stabilization plan brought down runaway inflation, its leaders consolidated and strengthened its democracy, and it signed agreements with Argentina on economic integration and nuclear safeguards that improved regional security. All these commitments persisted through multiple leadership transitions. In the eyes of powerful players such as Europe and the United States, Brazil was an appealing place for investment and a growing force in multilateral diplomacy.

items.title: Why Iran Escalates
items.summary: Tehran’s strategy to drive America out of the Middle East.
items.body_text:
These, it might seem, are good days for the Islamic Republic of Iran. After years of being diplomatically isolated, economically strangled, and militarily assaulted, the Iranian regime came face-to-face with its nightmare scenario—a full-blown war with Israel and Washington—and survived. The United States began bombing Iran on February 28 with the goal of destroying the country’s nuclear program, its missile program, and even its government, only to fail spectacularly at each objective. In fact, Tehran may now be stronger than it was when the war began. It successfully seized the Strait of Hormuz and shuttered it, sending energy prices skyward. Its armed forces have proved capable of continuing to damage American military bases despite coming under heavy bombardment. U.S. support for the war, always weak, has fallen, and international anger at Washington has spiked. Little wonder, then, that many analysts think Tehran will stay the course over the coming year.
Iranian officials are no doubt proud of how their country has fared against Israel and the United States. They have publicly bragged about their success and even declared victory. But in private conversations, the regime’s elites remain quite nervous. They know that the United States has many tools and tactics it can use to increase the pressure on Iran, and they are concerned that the factors that seem to be holding Washington back—dwindling stockpiles of ammunition, domestic public opinion, and international opposition—could go away, grow manageable, or otherwise become unimportant to American officials.
For the United States, this might seem like good news. If Tehran still fears Washington, perhaps the U.S. government can pressure Iran’s leaders into making concessions. But this misreads the mood in Iran’s capital. The country’s elites have been hardened by the war, which killed their friends and family members. They see February 28, 2026, the same way Israelis see the October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas—as the moment their enemy proved willing to slaughter them, and thus as proof it must be permanently defeated. They never had much faith in American negotiators; now, they have virtually none.
Iran, then, is adopting a strategy toward the United States defined by escalation and continuous offense. That means it will neither stay the course nor compromise with Washington. Instead, it will start doing even more to hurt the economies of the United States’ regional partners and to decimate global energy markets, as well as expand its attacks on U.S. military infrastructure. It could try to assassinate American and Israeli officials. It may even launch ground offensives against its neighbors, including by trying to seize U.S. bases located in Gulf Arab countries.
This approach might fail to make the United States relent. But even if neither side can overpower the other right now and both accept a settlement, peace is unlikely to last. Tehran believes that Washington will regroup and, eventually, start fighting again. The regime is committed to responding forcefully to any American provocation, and perhaps even attacking without one. It does not think it can live with a U.S. presence in the Middle East, so it is willing to go full tilt to get the United States out. Iran’s enduring goal, in other words, will be to make staying in the region so painful that Washington has no choice but to withdraw most of its troops, accept Tehran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz, and acknowledge the Islamic Republic as an enduring power.
FEAR AND LOATHING
When the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, was at a meeting in Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s compound. items.title: The Well-Funded Fight to Keep Latinos Voting Republican
items.summary: Amid deportations and Trump’s lagging popularity, one Koch-backed group has recruited Michigan Latinos to reach more than a hundred thousand voters for Mike Rogers.
items.body_text:
One Saturday morning in late August, Ricardo Alfaro, an immigrant from El Salvador, approached a low-slung white house in Holland, Michigan. The place looked as if it had been the site of a party: a fire pit in the driveway still smelled of smoke, and cans of Modelo were strewn across the concrete. A resident named Veronica Cruz appeared at the door holding a baby and a stick of string cheese. Alfaro said that he was there to stump for Mike Rogers, a former Republican congressman now running for Senate in Michigan, against Abdul El-Sayed. “He’s focussed on the American Dream—I think that’s something that we share, as Latinos,” Alfaro told Cruz, in Spanish. As Alfaro gave his spiel about how Rogers would slash regulations, reduce government interference, and reform the American immigration system, Cruz studied a door hanger that he’d given her as the baby bit into the cheese stick. “So,” she said, “there’s more elections? This November?”
Alfaro, who’s twenty-seven and the youth director at an evangelical church, has decided to devote his time to turning Latinos into Republican voters. “Maybe you see things on the news, or on social media, but you’re not getting the facts or reliable information—that’s what we want to share with you,” he told Cruz. He introduced himself as a volunteer, but he is the Michigan strategic director for the Libre Initiative, a center-right group that’s affiliated with Charles Koch’s political-action committee Americans for Prosperity. In the past fifteen years, Libre has captured a significant share of the market for Latino voter-turnout operations on the right, with a presence in thirteen states, including all the electoral battlegrounds. Although Libre originated in Texas, a state with more than twelve million Latino residents, the organization chose not to funnel its money into the Senate contest there this fall. Daniel Garza, Libre’s founder and president, said that campaigning statewide for Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general and the Republican candidate for Senate, would have been too expensive, and that the group could have more of an effect on other races. But, “if Paxton loses by a point, two, three points, I won’t be sleeping at night for at least a year,” he told me.
Garza believes that his group can have the greatest influence in Michigan, and Libre has allocated seven figures toward campaigning for Rogers, who lost, in 2024, by fewer than twenty thousand votes. Michigan’s Latino community is small—about six per cent of the state’s population—but there are pockets where it’s highly concentrated. Holland, for instance, a city settled by Dutch Calvinist separatists in 1847, is about a quarter Hispanic. Vionelkis Coen, an immigrant from Cuba and Libre’s grassroots-engagement director in Michigan, pointed out that there was a statue downtown of the city’s founder with his hand on the Bible—a sign, to her, that Holland was culturally “a conservative city.” “I tell people we’re, like, in a bubble,” she said. Since January, Libre has contacted more than a hundred and twenty-five thousand voters in Michigan between phone-banking and door-knocking.
Libre also inhabits a kind of bubble in the electoral ecosystem. It is one of the largest efforts on the right dedicated to motivating Latinos to vote for conservative and libertarian ideals, but its policy goals, such as enacting comprehensive immigration reform and reducing the size of the government, are at odds with President Donald Trump’s efforts to build and execute the largest deportation operation in U.S. history, in addition to other aspects of his agenda, such as his tariff program and the war with Iran. In Grand Rapids, Alfaro introduced me to Miguel Mota, a barbershop owner who voted for Trump but has grown frustrated with him over immigration policy—he’s heard that some of his own clients have been detained. items.title: Why Doesn’t Anyone Want to Fix One of America’s Scariest Roads?
items.summary: The Million Dollar Highway, prone to rockfall and avalanches, is the site of horrific crashes and courageous rescues.
items.body_text:
In the valley where I live, along a quiet stretch of the Uncompahgre River, in southwestern Colorado, there is only one paved road, and, like most people around here, I don’t drive it south without a good reason. In that direction, the road—U.S. Highway 550—passes through the small mountain town of Ouray, and then it climbs more than two thousand feet in the span of six miles. This section of the two-lane road has been carved directly into the red-quartzite cliffs of the Uncompahgre Gorge, and almost none of it has a shoulder; in some places, the highway is only twenty-three feet wide. The speed limit is twenty-five miles an hour, and one way to identify locals is that they often drive faster than that. This is because they worry about what can happen above the road. Rockfalls are common, and so are avalanches. There are more than sixty named slide routes along this part of the highway, and residents refer to them in personal terms, like bad neighbors who are always home: Riley Boy, Mother Cline, Slippery Jim. Highway 550 is the most avalanche-prone road that’s open year-round in the United States.
Visitors are more likely to be concerned with what lies below. Many sections of the road have a sheer drop of more than four hundred feet, and there are no guardrails, because of the need to push snow off after avalanches. When the route was constructed, in the eighteen-eighties, it was considered one of the greatest achievements in road engineering in the American West. Its purpose was to serve the silver and gold mines of the San Juan Mountains, but almost immediately the road also began to attract tourists. At some point in the early twentieth century, for reasons that are now obscure, the section above Ouray became known as the Million Dollar Highway.
In 2013, USA Today featured the Million Dollar Highway; the Death Road, in Bolivia; the Highway of Death, in Iraq; and nine other infamous routes in an article titled “World’s Most Dangerous Roads.” Less than a year later, the paper’s “10 Best Bucket-List Road Trips” also included the Million Dollar Highway. Strictly speaking, there’s nothing contradictory about the same road appearing on both lists, although it helps explain why the Ouray County coroner used the phrase “attractive nuisance” when we talked about the road recently. People can behave erratically on the Million Dollar Highway. There has been at least one instance in which a driver got into a heated argument with her passengers, pulled over, kicked them out, and then, in full view of everybody, accelerated straight off the edge, to her death. One man travelled all the way from the Netherlands just to propel himself off the road. The G.P.S. data on the Dutchman’s phone showed that he had driven repeatedly up and down the highway before choosing one of the most dramatic drop-offs.
Occasionally, a vehicle seems to vanish. Last year, early on the morning of August 5th, a tourist from Oregon named Adam Hynes was approaching one of the most treacherous sections of the gorge when he looked ahead and saw a silver Honda Civic moving in reverse. Hynes found it strange that somebody would be driving backward in such a spot, but then his view was obscured as he went around a sharp bend. By the time Hynes came out of the turn, the Honda was gone.
Hynes dropped a pin on his phone. There was no signal, so he continued down the highway until he was able to call 911. Then he circled back and parked at a pullout not far from the pin. The gorge was so precipitous that Hynes couldn’t see the bottom, but he had a DJI Mavic 3 drone. He set the machine aloft, and its camera captured the Honda, which had fallen three hundred and twenty feet—about the height of a thirty-story building. The silver vehicle lay upside down in the Uncompahgre River, crumpled like an aluminum can.

items.title: At the Department of Justice, Many Lawyers Are Wondering If It’s Time to Quit
items.summary: The quandary faced by government lawyers who think that the Trump Administration is subverting justice.
items.body_text:
On March 7, 2025, Celia Cohen, a prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York, was finishing up a meeting at 26 Federal Plaza, in lower Manhattan, when she learned that a federal marshal had arrived on the premises and wanted to see her. She was soon led to a conference room where the marshal served her with a letter from Todd Blanche, then the Deputy Attorney General, informing her that she and Andrew Rohrbach, another prosecutor at the S.D.N.Y., were being investigated and placed on administrative leave. After Cohen collected her personal belongings, the marshal escorted her out of the building.
Cohen, who has a reserved bearing, was deeply embarrassed. By the time she was back home, in Westchester County, her shock had settled into despair. Prosecutors at the S.D.N.Y., the nation’s most prestigious federal trial court, typically stay for five to seven years before moving on to jobs at private law firms, where they can earn vastly higher salaries. Cohen had no such plans. Since her early twenties, when she’d spent a year working as a paralegal at the Department of Justice, she’d dreamed of becoming a prosecutor. A few years after she graduated from law school, mentors at the Manhattan law firm where she was working encouraged her to apply to become an Assistant U.S. Attorney at the S.D.N.Y. When Preet Bharara, who was then running the office, called to offer her a job, she exclaimed, “This is the best day of my life!”
Cohen joined the S.D.N.Y. on the Monday after the 2016 Presidential election. She started out at the General Crimes Unit before moving to Violent Organizations and Crime, and then to Public Corruption. Although the hours were long and the salary was relatively modest, she loved the job and planned to spend the rest of her career in the office.

items.title: Christa Pike’s botched execution exposes the deep contradictions of a ‘painless’ state-imposed death
items.summary: Lethal injections are not typically administered by doctors, given executions are incompatible with their oath to protect lives.
items.body_text:
A US woman sentenced to death is now receiving life-saving medical treatment, after surviving a botched execution in Nashville that involved two doses of the drug pentobarbital.
Christa Pike, now 50, was convicted for the 1995 murder of a classmate, committed alongside her boyfriend when she was aged 18. She was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years, but was sent to a medical facility when the drug failed to kill her.
Late on Thursday, US time, Pike’s lawyer said the failed execution “was not just inefficient, it was cruel and it was torturous”.
Witnesses described Pike breathing, snoring and opening her eyes as the drug was being administered. One said Pike lifted her head up to ask if it was “normal” to feel a burning sensation.
Unsurprisingly, critics of the death penalty have condemned the incident. But here’s why it should trouble even those who support this type of punishment.
The ethics of capital punishment
Advocates of the death penalty typically make one of two arguments.
The deterrence argument says the death penalty has good consequences overall, as it discourages people from committing crimes that are punishable by death.
The retributivist argument says criminals who have committed certain offences deserve to die, either because this punishment is proportionate to their crime, or because any lesser punishment would fail to show proper respect for the victim.
These arguments are contested. Some doubt deterrence works; others question whether killing is an appropriate form of retribution; and both secular and religious commentators argue all humans have a right to life that cannot be forfeited, no matter what they have done.
Opponents of capital punishment have seen many political successes – a dwindling number of countries still carry out executions. Pike, however, was sentenced in Tennessee, which retains the death penalty.
If we are against the death penalty, it is easy to criticise the decision to sentence Pike to death in the first place. But the case should also trouble those who believe the death penalty can be an appropriate punishment.
What it means to kill a prisoner
It is easy to articulate what is bad about physical pain. We consciously experience pain, and the experience is a negative one. Put simply, pain hurts.
The same is not true of death. While dying can involve pain, we do not suffer from death itself, because when it comes we are no longer around to experience it.
Some philosophers argue that it’s this feature – the deprivation of experience – that distinguishes what is bad about death from what is bad about pain. Death is a punishment not because we suffer from it, but because it deprives us of all the good things about living.
In Pike’s case, however, what she experienced was not the deprivation of death, but rather the physical suffering associated with the administration of the drugs, and whatever medical complications may follow. These may include brain injury.
If she survives this botched execution she may face returning to death row, with the prospect of a rescheduled execution ahead of her.
To accept death as an appropriate punishment for some crimes does not automatically mean we should also accept the infliction of physical suffering.
Even states that permit capital punishment typically reject punishments such as whipping or physical mutilation. They also reject execution methods that involve significant suffering beyond the death itself, such as burning prisoners at the stake.
Whatever our view on whether death can be an appropriate punishment, the suffering involved with botched executions should give us pause.
Where to from here?
For defenders of the death penalty, it is important to show that executions can be carried out without involving additional suffering. In the case of lethal injections, this is easier said than done.

items.title: Dozens of men failed to stop an alleged gang rape at Cornell – here’s the misperception that keeps bystanders from intervening and how to short-circuit it
items.summary: People may accept bad behavior – even sexual assault – when they overestimate how acceptable their peers think it is. But there are ways to undermine this thinking and make intervention more likely.
items.body_text:
As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.
A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”
I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.
I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim or contact campus or local police departments.
This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?
Misperceiving that you’re the only one
Data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not.
Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.
The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were.
Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence – even when this belief is wrong – inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression.
What’s behind these mistaken beliefs
Men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed – in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men.
Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves.
This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.
Resetting a social norm
Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s getting people to see what it actually already is.

items.title: Social media hasn’t killed personal style, it’s killed how we communicate it
items.summary: Put down the coffee, walk away from the zebra crossing, think beyond chic and get more creative.
items.body_text:
This summer, social media was filled with posts declaring that almost anything was “kinda chic”. Repeating outfits was kinda chic. Being overdressed was kinda chic. Doing something unfashionable could, apparently, also be kinda chic.
But can you remember the content of many individual “kinda chic” posts now? Probably not. What is much easier to remember is the format itself: the language, the rhythm, the way an ordinary behaviour or object was reframed as evidence of taste.
That distinction tells us something important about fashion online. We often worry that social media is making everyone dress the same, but perhaps the greater similarity lies in how we communicate being fashionable.
Social media does not only circulate products and trends, it circulates recognisable ways of presenting them. A city street or a zebra crossing becomes the setting for an outfit photograph. Coffee appears alongside carefully placed handbags. Hotels, holidays and fashion events become backdrops. Accessories are photographed in close-up, bodies adopt familiar poses and captions perform effortlessness even when the accompanying image is highly composed.
The individual content changes but the mode of communication often does not.
Fashion has always depended on shared meanings. Clothes can distinguish us precisely because other people understand something about what they signify. Cowboy boots, a Chanel jacket or a football shirt come with cultural associations long before an individual wears them.
No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
Read more from Quarter Life:
Indie sleaze: a brief fashion history, from messy rebellion to mainstream revival
A brief history of embroidery – and how to get started yourself
What social media has changed is the speed and scale at which those meanings, and the conventions used to communicate them, can circulate.
When difference starts to use the same language
In a study of 390 Instagram posts from three established luxury fashion influencers between 2022 and 2024, I examined how fashion meaning was constructed through combinations of pose, location, styling, captions, editing and cultural references.
What I found was not simply repetition of particular brands or garments, but recurring ways of making fashion understandable.
Some posts communicated aspiration through polished styling, exclusive settings or access to fashion events. Others used everyday routines, informal language and familiar places to create relatability. Cultural knowledge, industry connections, humour and lifestyle storytelling introduced other ways of signalling authority and taste.
These practices frequently overlapped. An expensive outfit could be photographed on an ordinary street. An exclusive event might be accompanied by an informal caption. Highly controlled imagery could be placed alongside coffee, travel or mundane moments of everyday life.
The clothes differed, but the communicative patterns were often recognisable.
This matters because influencers do more than encourage people to buy products. They translate fashion into forms that work on platforms.
Fashion magazines and runway shows have historically used particular visual conventions to communicate taste, status and desirability. Instagram and TikTok operate through another set of conventions, shaped by speed, intimacy, entertainment, searchability and visibility.
Influencers move between these languages. They retain recognisable signs of taste and distinction while reshaping them into forms suited to social media. This offers another way to understand why personal style can begin to feel increasingly similar online.

items.title: El Niño: Mozambique ranked as one of the 'most vulnerable' African countries
items.summary: The powerful weather system is projected to bring severe heatwaves, below-normal rainfall, and heightened drought risks across Southern Africa.
items.body_text:
Mozambique
As the world faces a record-breaking super El Niño, the United Nations has warned that Mozambique is ranked as one of the 'most vulnerable' countries in Africa.
The powerful weather system is projected to bring severe heatwaves, below-normal rainfall, and heightened drought risks across Southern Africa.
"Mozambique is among the countries most vulnerable to climate change on the planet, despite having contributed very little to it, said Elisa Morgera, UN Special Rapporteur on climate change.
Speaking at the end of an 11-day working visit to the country, she said in the “coming months, in the context of the 2026 super El Nino, prolonged droughts, cyclones, and floods are predicted."
This latest climate warning comes as Mozambique faces acute economic strain following catastrophic flooding earlier this year.
Morgera called on multinational companies operating in the country to avoid environmental damage.
"It is necessary to define very clear obligations for private companies that they have a responsibility to respect human rights and avoid foreseeable environmental and climate damage; this is particularly true for fossil fuel companies,” she said.
Three and a half million people are already experiencing acute food insecurity in Mozambique. The two other most vulnerable countries in Africa have been named as Malawi and Madagascar.

items.title: DR Congo: Trial of post-Ebola exposure drug underway
items.summary: Some 250 people, who have all been exposed to the rare Bundibugyo virus, are taking part in the trial could stop them from contracting Ebola.
items.body_text:
Democratic Republic Of Congo
At a medical centre in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s eastern Ituri Province, more than 250 people are taking part in the trial of a drug that could stop them from contracting Ebola.
They have all been exposed to the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus for which there is currently no licensed vaccine.
Experts see the trial as a critical step in the fight against what is the country’s deadliest outbreak of the disease.
“What motivated me to take part was the death of my uncle. When he died, the results were positive [for Ebola]. Since I was a contact case with him, this motivated me to come here,” said one trial participant.
Another said that she had seen families where, when a case is found, almost the entire house is contaminated.
“But compared to that, when I joined this EBO-PEP trial, I found that no one from the family found themselves sick with this disease. That is to say, these tests are working really positively in our bodies," she said.
The experimental antiviral pill being tested is a post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP, which is administered immediately after suspected contact with the virus. Investigating physician at EBO-PEP drug trial, Jacques Zawadi, said the overall feeling of participants was one of satisfaction.
"To identify a medication, to treat a disease that does not have medication, this gives hope. Most of the participants are happy to be with us and to be able to benefit from this treatment, although it is still a trial," he said.
The trial began in July and is one of several studies launched to try to fight the disease. Il aims to recruit nearly 1,000 adults or children over the age of 12 who have come in contact with a confirmed case within the last five days but have no symptoms.
Participants are monitored in-person every day for 21 days, with a final phone call or visit after 42 days.
At least 8,300 confirmed cases, including 4,000 deaths, have been recorded since this Ebola outbreak was declared in mid-May.
Congo started vaccinating health workers with the Ervebo vaccine which was effective during previous Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common virus.
Authorities have said Ervebo could offer some protection against Bundibugyo virus, but whether the vaccine can actually prevent the illness is still being studied.

items.title: Mixed reaction in Guinea-Bissau after ousted president barred from returning
items.summary: Military leaders cited 'security conditions' and the need to preserve public order for barring Umaro Sissoco Embalo's return.
items.body_text:
Guinea-Bissau
There has been mixed reaction from residents in Guinea-Bissau’s capital, Bissau, to the military junta’s decision to bar the ousted president’s return from exile.
Earlier this week, former president Umaro Sissoco Embalo vowed he come back to the country on Sunday and contest the presidential election due to take place in December.
Military leaders cited “security conditions” and the need to preserve public order for blocking his return.
"You can’t stay on the sidelines, you’re a citizen, you’re part of this land. It’s the people who decide. They’re the ones who choose their leaders,” said Bissau resident, Maimuna Seide.
Another person living in the capital, Lamine Djassi, said Embalo had not been prevented from coming back. “Those who are supposed to ensure his safety have said they are not in a position to do so,” he said.
But he added that given that the elections are approaching, he felt measures could be put in place to guarantee the ousted president's safety.
“I simply want to make it clear that I am not in favour of him being banned from coming," said Djassi.
Embalo has been living in exile in Morocco since military officers took power in November last year, following a disputed election in which both he and the opposition candidate claimed victory.
A new constitution approved in a referendum in August has expanded presidential powers and changed electoral rules.
Among other provisions, it requires presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for the preceding five years.
It was unclear how that provision might have affected Embalo's candidacy.
The junta reiterated Thursday that restrictions on demonstrations, gatherings, and meetings for political purposes - which were implemented after it came to power -- remained in place.
Guinea-Bissau, which is wedged between Senegal and Guinea, has experienced five coups and numerous attempted putsches since independence from Portugal in 1974.
Many observers suspected Embalo of orchestrating the 26 November coup to halt an election process he appeared to be losing.
The military takeover took place one day before provisional results were to be announced.

items.body_text:
Capacity Substitution: How Tunisia’s Problems Became Someone Else’s Priorities
In the summer of 2023, a young man from Gafsa tried to cross the Mediterranean on a small boat. He did not make it. His story is one of thousands — and it is increasingly understood by Tunisian institutions through the language of border management. It is also a story about who defines what a problem is.
In June 2023, the European Commission announced a package for Tunisia: up to €900 million in proposed macro-financial assistance, €150 million in budget support, and €100 million for border management, search and rescue, anti-smuggling, and returns. In July, the EU and Tunisia signed a Memorandum of Understanding formalising the partnership. By September, a further €105 million was allocated to migration-related programmes. By December, the €150 million budget-support programme was operational.
The sequence is documented. What it produces institutionally is less visible. This article examines a mechanism I call capacity substitution. Capacity building strengthens a state’s ability to solve its own problems. Capacity substitution makes a state more efficient at solving problems defined by someone else. The distinction is simple. Its consequences are not.
Consider Tunisia’s migration apparatus. The EU–Tunisia Memorandum links European support to border management, anti-smuggling operations, search and rescue, and returns. These are legitimate European objectives. They are also objectives that European institutions can define, fund, monitor, and measure. European support has equipped units, funded training, and strengthened interception capacity.
What it has not done — and was not designed to do — is strengthen Tunisia’s capacity to address the economic conditions that generate migration. Youth unemployment stood at 35.4 percent in 2026. Graduate unemployment was 26.6 percent. Regional inequality remains entrenched.
The argument is not that European funding caused these figures. It is that external funding concentrates institutional development on a specific set of functions. Those functions become better equipped, better staffed, and more internationally connected. The functions that would address the structural conditions producing migration are not developed through an equivalent institutional investment. This is what capacity substitution describes.
A young unemployed person in Gafsa is unlikely to attempt to cross the Mediterranean simply because Tunisia lacks another surveillance system. The deeper driver is the narrowing of his economic and social horizon. If institutional capacity is concentrated on managing his departure, while the capacities that would address the conditions producing it are not developed through an equivalent investment, then the state becomes more effective at managing the symptom. It remains structurally less equipped to govern the cause. It does not require coercion. It does not require a conspiracy. It only requires that the external priority be better resourced than the domestic one.
Migration is not the only domain where this mechanism operates. European energy cooperation with Tunisia is another. EU funding for renewable energy, electricity interconnection, and green hydrogen is increasingly organised around projects that also serve European energy security: cross-Mediterranean interconnection such as the ELMED project, export capacity, and the decarbonisation of European supply chains.
Domestic energy challenges subsidy reform, grid reliability, and energy poverty are not absent from the relationship. But they are not the organising priority around which much of the external financing is structured. The result is a similar pattern: institutional capacity is strengthened in functions that serve externally defined priorities, while capacities addressing domestic structural conditions do not necessarily receive an equivalent institutional investment.
What migration and energy share is not a conspiracy. It is a logic. Ex

items.body_text:
What Washington Agreed to Last Month
Somaliland’s president spent two weeks in Washington this month offering almost everything he has. Access to the port at Berbera. Access to the territory’s minerals. Military access, which he called a matter for negotiation and declined to rule out. He only asked for one thing in return. Recognition. He went home without it. The same month, the United States secured expanded security rights in Greenland and agreed in writing that sovereignty stays with Denmark.
What Somaliland Offered
Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Irro, arrived on September 5 for his first visit to the United States since winning Somaliland’s presidency in November 2024. On the 14th, he gave the keynote address at the Hudson Institute, at an event titled Somaliland as a Strategic Partner in the Horn of Africa.
His pitch was the seaport. Irro described Berbera as a modern deep water facility that United States Africa Command had already assessed and in which the Emirati operator DP World has invested $442 million. More than twelve percent of global maritime trade passes through the Bab el-Mandeb strait every day. He argued that Somaliland has protected its coastline from militants and pirates for three decades without any recognition at all.
Two days later he went further. In an interview with Semafor he said Somaliland was not giving anything away for free. He offered American investors the port and the minerals. On military access he said it was a matter for negotiation, and he would not rule out a future base agreement. Ten days later he added more. In an interview with the Council on Foreign Relations he suggested renaming Berbera International Airport after President Trump, having earlier floated a Trump Tower in Hargeisa.
What They Got
Nothing, so far. Irro himself said there is no American promise on recognition. A source told Politico there is no change in American policy towards Somaliland.
On September 16, China warned Irro that crossing its line on Taiwan would bring serious consequences, and publicly affirmed that Somaliland remains part of Somalia. That handed Mogadishu an endorsement from a permanent member of the Security Council in the middle of a rival’s tour.
The Hudson appearance also drew criticism at home. Clips circulated of Irro hesitating on questions about minerals and regional security. The event’s moderator, Joshua Meservey of the Hudson Institute, said afterwards that Irro had made the right argument, while also observing that Somaliland has not consistently made the case for the reason recognition is necessary.
What Happened For Greenland
On the evening of September 18, President Trump announced an agreement with Denmark and Greenland giving the United States permanent control over security in Greenland. He described it as an agreement with no end, at no cost. The three governments signed it in New York on September 22, and the White House released the text the same day.
Copenhagen and Nuuk described something narrower. Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said the agreement recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of Greenlanders to self-determination. A State Department official told CBS News it gives permanent access and overflight rights, allows more bases and bars non-NATO members from building their own.
None of this is new ground. American forces have been in Greenland since 1941, and a 1951 defence agreement gave the United States the right to operate bases there, with Danish sovereignty expressly preserved. Reading the text signed this month, ABC News reported that it does not appear to add materially to that access. What Washington secured was a broader scope and a bar on rival powers. The access itself it already had.

items.body_text:
African Newsrooms Can No Longer Delay Creating the Conditions for Women to Stay
When one Black South African journalist decided to leave the profession after only four years, she did not walk away because she had stopped believing in journalism: ‘I mourned because I knew I could have done so much in that space.’
Her experience is documented in a 2025 Reuters Institute fellowship paper by South African journalist Bongekile Macupe. After difficult experiences in the newsroom, including during her pregnancy, the journalist eventually decided to leave. Yet her words suggest that what disappeared with her departure was not her passion for journalism, but the possibility of what she might have contributed had the conditions allowed her to stay.
That sense of loss is part of what the Kigali Declaration on the Elimination of Gender Violence in and through Media in Africa by 2034 is trying to prevent.
Led by African Women in Media (AWiM), the Declaration calls for action across the media ecosystem; from media organisations and professional associations to journalists, journalism educators, funders, digital platforms and regulators, to address gender violence both within media institutions and through the content they produce.
Its ambition builds on a problem that has been documented for years: for many women journalists across Africa, entering a newsroom is only the first step. Staying, progressing and practising journalism without discrimination, harassment or violence can prove to be another challenge altogether.
Entering journalism is not enough
In 2020, AWiM and Fojo Media Institute published Barriers to Women Journalists in Sub-Saharan Africa based on questionnaire responses from 125 women journalists across 17 African countries, alongside interviews and focus groups. Significantly, the research did not look only at women’s ability to enter journalism. It examined barriers to entering, progressing and staying in the profession.
The women who participated had entered journalism with strong ambitions. Passion, societal good and the desire to tell overlooked stories emerged prominently among their motivations.
One Kenyan journalist explained: ‘I loved the career and still do because I wanted to inform and highlight some issues affecting people in remote communities.’
Another participant described journalism as a way of telling ‘untold stories’ capable of influencing policy and improving people’s lives. Yet the professional environments encountered by women did not always nurture those ambitions.
The AWiM study identified job stagnation and salary disparities, gendered allocation of assignments, sexual harassment, bullying, sexism and racial discrimination, family responsibilities and unequal access to leadership among the barriers affecting women’s careers.
The research also documented how gendered expectations around family life could affect retention. Women spoke about the difficulty of reconciling journalism with childcare and family responsibilities, particularly when combined with poor pay and limited opportunities for progression.
The contrast is striking: women described entering journalism because they wanted to tell stories, serve communities and create change, while the structures of the profession could eventually make remaining within it difficult.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether women can become journalists. It is whether the conditions exist for them to remain journalists.
When leaving becomes an option
Macupe’s 2025 Reuters Institute paper brings that question into sharper focus. She interviewed ten Black African women with newsroom experience ranging from one year to more than 30 years in South Africa. One of the observations that troubled her most was generational: younger journalists described experiences echoing those of women who had entered the profession decades earlier.
The women spoke about unequal access to opportunities and resources, exclusion from networks of influence and repeated challenge

items.title: Africa’s next consumer battle will be fought beyond the megacities, McKinsey says
items.summary: Gen Z and hyperlocalisation, or granularity, will be the two forces to watch from African shoppers in 2027.
items.body_text:
Africa’s next consumer growth frontier may lie beyond its biggest cities, as companies look to peri-urban areas and smaller urban centres for the next pools of demand. That is one of the conclusions Damian Hattingh, partner and leader of McKinsey’s Consumer practice in Africa, draws from the consultancy’s latest State of Consumer Africa report.
“Many Tier 1 urban markets are already highly competitive, even if consumers are not yet perfectly served everywhere,” Hattingh tells The Africa Report. “One area to watch closely is the next layer of growth beyond the largest city centres: peri-urban areas and Tier 2 and Tier 3 geographies.”
The shift matters because national averages increasingly disguise where money is being made. Urban per-capita consumption across the markets McKinsey studied is already around 1.8 times national averages. Urban consumers are also substantially more willing than suburban or rural shoppers to pay more for quality, healthy products and convenience.
“The question is, increasingly, not just which market, but which consumers, in which locations, through which channels,” Hattingh says.
That presents a more complicated growth proposition for companies accustomed to making decisions country by country. A large population and rising consumption can look attractive from headquarters, while logistics costs, fragmented distribution and intense local competition erode margins on the ground.
Value, not simply cheapness
The report describes the emergence of a more “pragmatic” African shopper, but Hattingh explains that the behaviour is not simply a temporary product of inflation.
Consumers are trading down in some categories, while continuing to spend more where quality, safety or reliability matters. Some 37% of those surveyed said they were willing to pay extra for high-quality food, even as 46% planned to search more actively for promotions and 73% said they stocked up during sales.
“Consumers are not simply trading down across the board,” Hattingh says. “They are deciding more deliberately where it is worth spending more.”
If incomes recover in 2027, some behaviours forced by the cost-of-living squeeze may soften. But Hattingh expects the underlying focus on value to endure. That puts pressure on companies to strip costs from products without stripping out the attributes consumers care about – what McKinsey calls “design to value”.
The same pressure is helping spread the logic of sachetisation well beyond packaged goods. Consumers accustomed to buying detergent or cooking oil in small quantities are increasingly being offered fractional investments, short-duration credit, flexible insurance payments and cheaper media packages.
But Hattingh cautions against assuming that smaller transactions automatically create better businesses. “An accessible entry product can bring a consumer into the franchise and create an opportunity, over time, to serve more of their needs,” he says. “But that depends on retention, responsible product design and an efficient cost to serve.”
Digitising informality
Another potentially important shift is taking place inside Africa’s informal retail economy. Rather than eliminating informal trade, digital payments and merchant technologies may professionalise it.
In Nigeria, account-to-account payments rose from 25% to 44% of online transaction value between 2019 and 2025, according to the report. Banks, fintechs and telcos are increasingly trying to connect those payment rails to physical commerce.

items.title: Ethiopia’s Tigray conflict hits Addis Ababa as regional alliances fracture
items.summary: As militarised commercial drones hit the capital, expelled ambassadors and Red Sea posturing threaten to drag East Africa into a wider war.
items.body_text:
Drone strikes likely caused explosions at the army headquarters in Addis Ababa this week, a diplomatic source said Friday, as the conflict with rebels triggered a breakdown in Ethiopia’s relations with Eritrea and Egypt.
Fighting erupted last week in northern Ethiopia as the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) launched attacks against federal forces, raising fears of a return to the devastating 2020-2022 civil war.
The government accuses Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, and the two countries broke diplomatic relations on Thursday.
Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara, while Eritrea responded that it would “sever all diplomatic ties”.
Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat without explanation, prompting a reciprocal move by Cairo. The two were already at odds over Addis Ababa’s new Nile mega-dam, with Egypt strengthening ties with Eritrea in recent months.
Meanwhile, Eritrea has long feared landlocked Ethiopia plans to invade and seize access to its coastline. Jervin Naidoo, a Senior Political Analyst with Oxford Economics, called it the most serious deterioration possible short of direct military conflict.
The TPLF’s leader, Debretsion Gebremichael, said in a video published late Thursday that “the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea”.
The African Union, based in Ethiopia, said it was “following with concern the heightened tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt”, urging “maximum restraint”.
“Ethiopia’s expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat further highlights the rising regional temperature,” he added. “With direct communication channels closed between Ethiopia and Eritrea, and mistrust rife among neighbouring states, the risk of miscalculation and escalation is increasing.”
Tigray frontlines
On the frontlines in northern Ethiopia, there were signs that the Tigrayan rebels were being pushed back on Thursday.
A humanitarian source told AFP the TPLF had been dislodged from the town of Erebti in Afar, which it seized earlier this week, and was now fighting near the mountainous border between Afar and Tigray.
A pro-government militia said on X it had retaken Erebti, as well as Maychew town in southern Tigray.
Verification is difficult as media are prevented from travelling to affected areas and there are significant communications disruptions.
Drone strikes
For the first time, the conflict appeared to reach the capital overnight Wednesday-Thursday when an explosion was reported at the Ministry of Defence, which houses the headquarters of the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF).
Drone strikes were the “most likely” cause, a diplomatic source based in the city told AFP, “though we haven’t been able to obtain imagery or independent confirmation”.
The devices used were likely FPV (First-Person View) drones — “essentially militarised commercial drones fitted with an explosive charge”, the source said, adding that an army base in the capital was hit around the same time.
Though the military has a far more substantial fleet of drones, rebel forces have deployed them against airbases and airports elsewhere in the country — including three attacks last Sunday in Oromia and Amhara states, according to conflict monitor ACLED.
The Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank, said on Friday rebel forces had “launched a drone strike campaign across Ethiopia”, including Addis Ababa, to demonstrate “its ability to expand the conflict across the country”.
The government and army have refused to comment on the strikes in the capital, which were also reported to AFP by residents and workers near the army headquarters in the Tor Hayloch area of Addis Ababa.

items.title: Taiwan’s New F-16s: Why They Still Matter
items.summary: The Republic of China Air Force waited 20 years for these aircraft. What are they for?
items.body_text:
The arrival of the first pair of the 66 F-16C/D Block 70 aircraft on order to the Republic of China Air Force (ROCAF) has been a long time coming – and not just because of production delays. First sought as 66 F-16C/Ds under U.S. President George W. Bush, the request was blocked by his administration and remained unapproved under President Barack Obama, before the sale was signed off in 2019 during the first term of President Donald Trump. Yet their arrival comes after years of debate over whether Taiwan’s vulnerable air bases could sustain fighter operations in wartime, raising questions over what role the aircraft can realistically play.
Taiwan’s F-16 story begins in the 1970s. During that decade, it was quickly becoming clear that the island’s fleet of F-100 and F-104 combat aircraft was heading toward obsolescence. While agreement had been reached between Washington and Taipei for the co-production of the upgraded F-5E/F for the ROCAF, many U.S. officials themselves regarded additional F-5Es as inadequate as a long-term solution. Complicating any follow-on agreements, however, was the steady reconciliation between the U.S. and mainland China.
In 1978, Taipei’s request for F-16s was dismissed out of hand, leaving the F-4 and additional F-5E/Fs as the main options. A decision that year settled on the latter. High-performance fighters again topped Taiwan’s arms requests the following year, but Washington maintained its refusal to supply the F-4, F-16, or F-18.
In December 1978, Washington announced that diplomatic recognition would shift to Beijing on January 1, 1979, and formally gave the one-year notice required to terminate the U.S.-ROC Mutual Defense Treaty, which became defunct on January 1, 1980. This appeared to close the door on a major new fighter sale, despite the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act specifying that it was U.S. policy “to provide Taiwan with arms of a defensive character,” although what sales that required would be determined by the President and Congress.
Washington repeatedly calibrated Taiwan’s fighter access to its assessment of China’s capabilities and to the wider U.S.-China relationship. Ronald Reagan’s 1980 election campaign featured positive rhetoric toward Taiwan. However, after considering Taiwan’s requests for the F-5G (which would become the F-20) and the F-16/79 (a deliberately lower-performance export version of the F-16), the decision was once again made to reject the request and focus on the F-5E/F, as well as giving authorization for the transfer of used F-104 fighters from West Germany. Washington judged the F-5E/F qualitatively adequate against China’s then-current fighters.
Reagan institutionalized the arms sales problem in 1982, when the Third Communiqué between Washington and Beijing featured a pledge that arms sales to Taiwan would not exceed recent levels, with Washington stating that it intended to gradually reduce them over time, conditional on Beijing’s continued peaceful approach to the Taiwan issue. At the same time, the Six Assurances issued to Taipei sought to confirm that the U.S. had not agreed to set a date for ending arms sales, but the communiqué nonetheless remained part of the U.S.-China policy framework. At this point, Taiwan began the journey down alternative aircraft procurement paths, including what eventually became the F-CK-1 Indigenous Defense Fighter, produced with extensive assistance from U.S. industry.
However, the end of the Cold War once again changed the dynamic, and in September 1992, during his re-election campaign, George W. Bush signed off on the purchase by Taiwan of 150 F-16A/B aircraft. The decision was in part justified by China’s purchase of Russian Su-27 aircraft. Domestic politics also favored the decision: General Dynamics built the F-16 in Fort Worth, and Bush announced the sale there during an election campaign in which Texas aerospace employment was politically salient.

items.title: India’s Foreign Minister Jaishankar Openly Calls Out the US
items.summary: Previously, India sorted out its differences with friendly nations quietly. Last week, it aired its grievance with Washington publicly.
items.body_text:
On September 28, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi had a telephone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump to review progress in bilateral cooperation. In a post on X, Modi described the conversation as “productive.” “We reviewed our bilateral cooperation in trade, defence, energy, critical technologies and other areas. We agreed to maintain close engagement to take our Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership forward,” he said.
While Modi’s post about his conversation with Trump was not negative, it was far less effusive than in the past, even bland. As Yashraj Sharma observed in an article in Al Jazeera, it was a “cold and formal depiction far removed from his description of the US president as a ‘good friend’ in previous years.”
The Trump-Modi phone call came at a time when already fraying bilateral relations hit yet another difficult phase.
Ten days earlier, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA) of 2026, which gives the U.S. president the authority to impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas. India, which is among the largest buyers of Russian energy, could potentially be impacted.
India-U.S. cooperation has deepened and widened over the past two decades. Despite “complexities,” ties were expected to grow under Trump; the outlook was upbeat.
However, Trump 2.0 has not been good for the partnership. Within weeks of the inauguration of Trump’s second presidential term, ties began unravelling not only over tariffs and immigration but also Washington’s cozying up to Pakistan on a raft of issues, including terrorism, an issue that Delhi is highly sensitive about.
India was among the countries that were hit the hardest by Trump’s “reciprocal tariffs” announced last year. Adding insult to injury, India was then slapped with another 25 percent “punitive tariffs” for buying Russian oil.
Should the U.S. press ahead with imposing SRIA on India, it would hit India’s oil imports and, consequently, its energy security.
Over the past 19 months, although Indians took note of Trump’s abrasive remarks and insensitive tweets, they took it in their stride. The diplomatic establishment seemed to have adopted a patient wait-and-watch policy. India, after all, needed the U.S and benefited from economic and security cooperation with Washington. The current uncertainty was seen as temporary.
However, that mood in Delhi is changing. Its patience with Trump seems to be wearing thin. Officials and analysts are calling on the government to be more realistic in its assessment of the current India-U.S. relationship.
In an article in The Week, Navtej Sarna, a former Indian ambassador to the U.S., wrote: “We need to accept, without caveats, that the relationship has cratered significantly. In America’s eyes, India is not the strategic partner that we believed we were.”
A change is evident not just in Delhi’s mood but also, in its approach.
“India has reached the end of its tether with Trump,” a former official in India’s MEA told The Diplomat. “In the past we abhorred megaphone diplomacy, preferring to sort out nettlesome issues with friends quietly and only via diplomatic channels. That was India’s approach towards Russia’s intervention in Afghanistan in 1979, and its invasion in Ukraine in 2022, for example. But that is clearly changing,” he said. “India today is not averse to calling out, even friends, on difficult matters if core concerns are being undermined.”
This change was on full display last week during India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar’s visit to the U.S.
At an event at the Asia Society in New York, Jaishankar did not hold back in drawing attention to Washington’s lack of “understanding or appreciation or empathy” for Delhi on issues of concern and sensitivity to the latter. items.title: Concerns About ‘WWII Allies’ at US-China Summit
items.summary: How China is weaponizing WWII history
items.body_text:
At the U.S.-China summit in September 2026, both leaders spoke of the fact that the United States and China had been allies in World War II and had fought together. Of course, the United States and China (the Republic of China) were indeed Allied nations in WWII and fought together against Japan and others, and if the summit remarks were intended simply to reaffirm that historical fact and invoke shared memory, then they should give rise to no particular concern.
It is also worth recalling that in 2015, the 70th anniversary of the end of the war, U.S.-China relations were relatively stable, and China was emphasizing that it had fought alongside the United States and other major Western powers as key members of the Allied coalition, and had jointly created the postwar order. At that time, China was using the phrase “New Model of Major-Country Relations” in its relations with the United States. If the invocation of wartime partnership at the recent summit was intended to evoke memories of that 2015 period and signal an intention to restore the “New Model of Major-Country Relations,” that too would be comprehensible as a matter of Chinese policy.
However, more than ten years have now passed since 2015, and China’s narrative on history today is different from what it once was. So the fact that wartime partnership was raised by both sides at this summit is, in fact, a cause for concern. To explain, it is necessary to look at how China has recently been employing its historical narrative — with particular attention to its relationship with Russia.
The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 and China’s response to it, together with Russia’s war in Ukraine beginning in 2022, generated widespread international criticism of both countries. That criticism brought China and Russia closer together, and the two countries more openly positioned themselves in opposition to Western nations. In 2024, the 75th anniversary of the establishment of Sino-Russian diplomatic relations and a year in which the pandemic was still fresh in mind and the war in Ukraine was very much ongoing, Russian President Vladimir Putin made an official visit to China in May and issued a joint statement. It included the following passage:
“China and Russia will continue to firmly defend the results of the victory of the Second World War and the postwar world order enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations, and oppose the negation, distortion, and falsification of the history of World War II. They plan to solemnly celebrate the 80th anniversary of the victory of the Chinese People’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Soviet Union’s Patriotic War in 2025 and jointly promote a correct view of the history of World War II.”
This statement signaled that China and Russia intended to jointly insist on what they view as the “correct history” of WWII to the world, while refusing to accept any historical perspective that differs from their own.
In March 2025, at a press conference on the occasion of China’s National People’s Congress, State Councilor Wang Yi stated that, marking the 80th anniversary of victory in WWII, China and Russia were reaffirming that they had fought together in Asia and Europe at the cost of blood, and went on to say that, building on this past, the two countries would jointly promote a correct understanding of WWII history, defend the fruits of that victory, uphold the international system with the United Nations at its core, and advance the international order in a more just and reasonable direction. China and Russia have thus pledged not only to reaffirm their wartime partnership but to jointly seek to shape the present international order on that basis. For China and Russia, historical narrative is inseparable from the shaping of the current international order.

items.title: Flydubai attack feeds Netanyahu’s ‘protector’ line as polls near
items.summary: The apparent attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight carrying 170 mostly Israeli passengers was another reminder to Israelis of the constant threat of terror and war. Only the bravery of the chief pilot and passengers prevented a major disaster. A few hours earlier, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video warning of attempts to harm […] The post Flydubai attack feeds Netanyahu’s ‘protector’ line as polls near appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
The apparent attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight carrying 170 mostly Israeli passengers was another reminder to Israelis of the constant threat of terror and war. Only the bravery of the chief pilot and passengers prevented a major disaster.
A few hours earlier, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video warning of attempts to harm Israelis in the lead-up to the country’s general election on October 27.
Initially, his opponents criticized this as a stunt to divert public discourse towards security concerns, and away from his part in the devastating failures that enabled the October 7 Hamas attacks.
But after the suspected terror incident on the Flydubai plane, Netanyahu can claim he was right. With the elections approaching, the longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history is hoping he can still restore his image as “the protector of Israel.”
Netanyahu was quick to incorporate the plane attack into his campaign by posting on his social media accounts a video and images of him embracing and praising one of the passengers (a Netanyahu supporter) who stormed the cockpit, his shirt still stained with blood.
Growing criticism over October 7 failures
Despite public outcry, Netanyahu refuses to accept blame for the October 7 attack. He has blocked the creation of a judicial commission of inquiry to investigate what led to the attack, while failing in his attempts to set up a different investigative committee more favourable to him.
Netanyahu has repeatedly argued that security officials failed to warn him of the impending assault, saying “if they had woken him up” earlier on October 7, “things would have been very different.”
Recent reports, however, paint a different picture. Numerous media outlets have reported that Israel’s security agencies, as well as Netanyahu himself, received explicit warnings days before the 2023 attack.
These came from high-ranking Arab officials (Egypt’s intelligence minister) and leaders (the United Arab Emirates’ Mohammad bin Zaid). A new book also claims Netanyahu received a direct warning from Hamas’ leader, Yahya Sinwar, the mastermind of the attack.
The prime minister and his top security officials, however, understood these warnings of an “earthquake” (to use Sinwar’s own term) erupting in Gaza as a demand for economic concessions for Palestinians.
Israeli decision-makers were captive to what is called a conceptzia in Israel – a detailed and entrenched set of assumptions about the enemy’s capabilities and intentions. (The term was coined to describe Israel’s intelligence failures before the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.)
In 2023, Netanyahu’s conceptzia, supported by many security officials who misread or were fooled by Sinwar, was that Qatari money going to Hamas would “buy quiet”, in the words of his critics.
Netanyahu approved the transfer of millions of dollars from Qatar to Gaza from 2018 onward. Yet, instead of assisting needy Gazans, Israeli intelligence believes much of these funds ended up feeding the growth of Hamas’ military abilities and underground terror infrastructure.
Can the opposition capitalize?
In the election, Netanyahu is facing strong opposition from the “ABBA” (Anyone But Bibi Again, in reference to Netanyahu’s nickname) bloc. His main rival is the Yashar! Party (which translates as “direct” or “straightforward”), headed by a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, whose son was killed in the Gaza war.
Polls consistently suggest Yashar! will be the biggest party after the elections. Yet, forming a coalition may prove difficult because Eisenkot’s bloc is made up of a mishmash of right, left and center-aligned parties, with little common ground except their goal of ousting Netanyahu. A similar coalition, under Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, fell apart quickly in 2022.
Furthermore, many Zionist parties demand the next government be “Zionist-only”, refusing to participate in a coalition that includes the Arab Islamic party Ra’am.

items.title: Big Oil fears the evidence of its deliberate climate lies
items.summary: No one knows how the US Supreme Court will rule in Suncor v. Boulder, the case that will kick off the court’s fall term next week and will likely decide whether the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, will be able to put oil giants ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy on trial for deceiving the public for decades about the climate harms of fossil […] The post Big Oil fears the evidence of its deliberate climate lies appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
No one knows how the US Supreme Court will rule in Suncor v. Boulder, the case that will kick off the court’s fall term next week and will likely decide whether the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, will be able to put oil giants ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy on trial for deceiving the public for decades about the climate harms of fossil fuels.
But one thing that can be said with certainty is that Big Oil and the fossil fuel industry are absolutely terrified of facing cases like Boulder’s at trial, where state and local governments will be able to present evidence of Big Oil’s decades-long climate deception to a jury.
Big Oil’s own lawyers have admitted that the companies face “massive monetary liability” from the dozens of climate deception cases against them, and that stopping communities from having their day in court is a “big priority… for the entire industry.”
That’s because the evidence of Big Oil’s climate lies is overwhelming—and the discovery process in climate deception lawsuits could produce even more damaging proof that companies like Exxon have knowingly fueled climate chaos for decades while concealing the harm, undermining the science, and obstructing every effort to address the problem.
As the Supreme Court prepares to hear Exxon’s pleas to escape trial in just one of the dozens of climate deception lawsuits, the Center for Climate Integrity has released a newly updated collection of 101 internal industry documents and other pieces of evidence that the fossil fuel industry is desperate to stop a jury of Americans from seeing.
“Climate Fraud 101: Big Oil’s Climate Deception Explained in 101 Documents, 1957-2026″ shows how fossil fuel companies helped shape the emerging field of climate science beginning in the 1950s. By the late 1970s and early 80s, Exxon scientists were warning of “catastrophic” climate impacts if the world did not shift away from fossil fuels.
Over the course of the 1980s, the oil giant and others came to understand that climate change posed two profound existential risks: one to “civilization” itself, and the second to their business model, because the only way to “avoid the problem” was by “sharply curtailing the use of fossil fuels.”
Big Oil then chose their own interests over humanity’s and launched the most consequential corporate deception campaign in history to “emphasize the uncertainty” in climate science before measurable impacts became detectable and undeniable.
By the 1990s, the oil and gas majors responded to increased public awareness of climate change by publicly contradicting what their own scientists had been telling them for decades, casting doubt on well-established climate science and obstructing efforts to mitigate the impacts of global warming.
Then, once the problem became undeniable, Big Oil and the fossil fuel industry shifted to lie about the solutions—undermining the urgently needed transition to renewables while claiming they could make dirty fossil fuels more climate friendly through false solutions like natural gas and carbon capture and storage (CCS).
Throughout these decades, the impacts of the climate crisis became worse and worse for communities across the globe, with wildfires, floods, droughts, extreme heat, and other climate damages becoming more deadly and destructive as a result of the industry’s obstruction.
On October 5, Exxon and Suncor will beg the Supreme Court to shield them from having to face the evidence of their wrongdoing in a Colorado court. But the fossil fuel industry’s quest to escape accountability is much larger. They’re desperately lobbying Congress and state legislatures to give them outright immunity from climate lawsuits and place them above the law entirely.
