items.title: Cambodia’s Japan security aid is a hedge, not a pivot from China
items.summary: In February 2026, weeks after Cambodia’s National Assembly approved a draft law to ratify the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), a convention Phnom Penh signed in 1983 but never ratified, Japan unveiled plans to extend Official Security Assistance (OSA) to Cambodia. The announcement did not come out of nowhere and […] The post Cambodia’s Japan security aid is a hedge, not a pivot from China appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
In February 2026, weeks after Cambodia’s National Assembly approved a draft law to ratify the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), a convention Phnom Penh signed in 1983 but never ratified, Japan unveiled plans to extend Official Security Assistance (OSA) to Cambodia. The announcement did not come out of nowhere and followed a year of quiet groundwork.
Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet met then-Prime Minister Ishiba Shigeru in Tokyo in May 2025, after Japanese minesweepers made the first foreign port call at Ream Naval Base since its reconstruction. Cambodia’s army commander and Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force chief of staff exchanged visits and agreed potentially to establish an army-led signal school.
Cambodia finally became the 13th OSA recipient on July 19, receiving 500 million yen (US$3.2 million) for a communications school and patrol boats for the Royal Cambodian Navy. Most of the commentary since has asked whether the equipment matches Cambodia’s actual threats. The more revealing question is why Phnom Penh wanted the package at all.
Since 2023, OSA has supported countries Japan considers like-minded amid what Tokyo calls a deteriorating Indo-Pacific security environment, a concern central to the 2022 National Security Strategy. In practice, the program has targeted China.
Cambodia’s security issues lie elsewhere. Unresolved border demarcation with Vietnam, Thailand and Laos keeps territorial security at the center of Phnom Penh’s strategic calculations. Recent border clashes with Thailand have reinforced this focus.
Cambodia’s Defense Policy 2022 extends this land-first orientation to the sea, tasking maritime forces with piracy, trafficking, transnational crime and illegal fishing rather than naval deterrence.
Illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing off Sihanoukville, Kampot and Koh Kong has depleted stocks that coastal households depend on, and Cambodia still scores 2.39 out of 5.00 on the IUU fishing index.
UNCLOS ratification then added a legal duty to monitor waters Cambodia lacks the capacity to watch. A state with these priorities has little reason to build its security policy around the maritime contest that shapes most of OSA.
Nor does a patrol boat do much about any of this. A hull can only intercept what someone else has already found, and Cambodia has very little that finds anything: no coastal radar chain, no vessel monitoring that can separate a licensed trawler from an unlicensed one.
The communications school helps units talk to one another, not to see things. Phnom Penh accepted the package anyway, and that is the part worth reading closely.
What Cambodia acquired was standing and a wider range of strategic options. The Ream port call carried the signal. For years, the controversial base was the central exhibit in the argument that Cambodia had effectively handed military control of its coastline to China. The government’s answer was to open it to Japanese vessels first.
UNCLOS ratification worked the same way. The convention gives Cambodia legal standing over the maritime zones it claims, and joining it placed Phnom Penh inside a framework Japan has promoted across the region. Neither decision was costless, and the government made both knowing how each capital would read them.
Neither move was a step away from China, either. Chinese finance still builds the roads, the canal and the ports. Golden Dragon remains by a wide margin Cambodia’s largest joint military exercise.
Nothing in the Japanese package substitutes for any of that, and Phnom Penh has never asked it to. At the same time, China remains Cambodia’s largest source of foreign investment and its largest bilateral creditor, and no combination of partners now on offer could replace it within a decade. Cambodia is not switching patrons so much as strategically adding names to a list that had recently grown too short.

items.title: War and diplomatic crisis in the Horn of Africa: Why Ethiopia is at odds with its neighbors
items.summary: Renewed fighting in Ethiopia has fueled a diplomatic crisis with Eritrea and Egypt amid accusations of foreign support for armed groups Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
War and diplomatic crisis in the Horn of Africa: Why Ethiopia is at odds with its neighbors
Renewed fighting between Ethiopia’s federal government and regional armed groups has escalated into a diplomatic rupture with former wartime ally Eritrea. What was an internal conflict has become a wider regional confrontation over ports, water, and alleged foreign interference. The violence threatens a fragile 2022 peace deal that ended Ethiopia’s two-year Tigray war, raising fears of a return to full-scale conflict.
What triggered the diplomatic rupture?
Ethiopia announced on Thursday the closure of its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered ten Eritrean diplomats stationed in Addis Ababa to leave Ethiopia within 48 hours. Its Foreign Ministry accused them of threatening national security and blamed Eritrea for “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia.”
Eritrea reciprocated the measure and severed “all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries that this entails.” It rejected the allegations and accused Addis Ababa of planning to take Eritrean ports and of training and arming Eritrean opposition groups to pursue regime change. Addis Ababa said it remained committed to peaceful coexistence and resolving disputes through dialogue.
The breakdown in relations came days after Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of financing armed groups seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Asmara denies the accusations.
What are they fighting over?
The conflict grew out of a struggle over federal power and regional autonomy. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the political party governing Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, dominated national politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. Tigrayan leaders accused his government of seeking to centralize power at the region’s expense. Their confrontation erupted into war in November 2020.
Eritrean troops and Amhara forces fought alongside the federal army. Hundreds of thousands died before an African Union-mediated agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 halted the large-scale fighting. But disputes over territory claimed by both Amhara and Tigray, the return of displaced people, and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces remained unresolved. Addis Ababa accuses the TPLF of failing to disarm; Tigrayan leaders accuse the government of failing to honor the settlement.
The TPLF further strained the settlement in May by restoring Tigray’s prewar regional council, displacing the interim administration established under the agreement. Amhara militia fighters known as Fano, meanwhile, had turned against Addis Ababa in 2023 after the government moved to dismantle regional security forces.
Separate disputes have widened the confrontation. Landlocked Ethiopia wants sovereign access to the Red Sea, particularly through Eritrea’s Assab port, which it calls vital to its economy and security. Asmara fears an attempt to take its coastline by force. Egypt and Sudan also dispute Ethiopia’s operation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, fearing threats to their water supplies and demanding a binding agreement governing its filling and operation.
Why has fighting resumed in Ethiopia?
On September 20, seven armed groups, including the TPLF and its former battlefield enemies, announced an alliance pledging to oust Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration. The coalition, known as the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, accused the ruling Prosperity Party of imposing “dictatorial” rule and pushing the East African country toward disintegration.
Clashes erupted two days later. TPLF forces took control of airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, prompting state-owned Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to all three cities. Flights were also suspended to the Amhara town of Lalibela, home to UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches, as fighting spread.

items.title: Thousands flee Ebola-hit displacement camp in DR Congo – UN
items.summary: Thousands have fled an Ebola-hit camp in eastern DR Congo as insecurity and a fire disrupt efforts to contain the outbreak, the UN has said Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Thousands flee Ebola-hit displacement camp in DR Congo – UN
Thousands of people have fled an Ebola-hit displacement camp in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo), leaving it largely abandoned after clashes erupted during a security operation, the UN said on Thursday.
The Kigonze camp in Ituri Province had housed around 19,000 people. Residents began fleeing after security forces entered the site to search for weapons and suspected members of armed groups, with gunfire reported during the operation.
”The enormous challenge of halting the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo just became even harder,” the UN said.
An Ebola transit center at Kigonze was also destroyed by fire this week, further disrupting containment efforts. The facility, operated by International Medical Corps and supported by more than 50 staff, was used to isolate and assess suspected cases before patients were transferred for treatment.
Fighting has also hampered the Ebola response elsewhere in eastern DR Congo. More than 3,000 people have fled the Rhoe displacement camp in Ituri’s Djugu territory since clashes intensified on September 27, according to the UN humanitarian agency OCHA. At least four people were reportedly killed and seven injured.
The outbreak, declared a public health emergency in May, has spread to seven of the country’s 26 provinces, with Ituri remaining the epicenter.
As of September 29, Congolese authorities had recorded 8,224 confirmed cases and 3,982 deaths, putting the case fatality rate at 48.4%.
On Thursday, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned against interpreting a recent decline in reported cases as evidence that the outbreak is easing, saying insecurity has disrupted surveillance in affected areas. Of the 63 health zones affected, 45 were still reporting active transmission.
”Falling in this curve doesn't mean that the outbreak is totally under control,” Africa CDC’s Dr. Wessam Mankoula said. “We cannot say at this stage the outbreak is under control.”
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola and has surpassed the toll of DR Congo’s 2018-2020 epidemic. There is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the strain, although candidate vaccines and treatments are being studied, according to the World Health Organization.

items.title: Algeria moves to expand death penalty
items.summary: Algerian lawmakers have backed expanding the death penalty to forest arson and serious crimes against children Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Algeria moves to expand death penalty
Algeria’s lower house of parliament has approved expanding the death penalty to cover forest and field arson and crimes against children. The North African country retains capital punishment, but no executions have been carried out since 1993.
The People’s National Assembly moved to make the amendments to the Penal Code on Thursday. The legislation must still pass the Council of the Nation, parliament’s upper house, before taking effect.
“The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes,” Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa said following the vote.
The legislation introduces capital punishment for “anyone who deliberately sets fire to forests, bushes, or fields, whether planted, unplanted, trees, or parts of forests” and timber stored within forest areas. The amendments would raise the maximum punishment for such offenses from 20 years in prison to death. Algerian law already allowed the death penalty for arson if the fire resulted in a person’s death.
The changes follow a wave of deadly wildfires that swept parts of Algeria in late summer. At least 12 people were killed, while on August 27 alone, Civil Protection recorded 193 fires across several provinces. Three days later, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune instructed the justice minister to amend the Penal Code to expand the application of capital punishment for arson.
The amendments also apply capital punishment to certain forms of intentional destruction of public or private property carried out on behalf of foreign parties in cases involving treason, espionage, or organized crime, according to Algeria Press Service (APS).
The revised code expands the use of the death penalty for crimes against children, prescribing capital punishment for anyone who abducts, tortures or sexually assaults a child or amputates one of a child’s limbs. Those convicted of the offenses would also be barred from invoking mitigating circumstances.
The tougher penalties for crimes against children were added to the proposed amendments in early September, amid public outrage over the killing of a five-year-old boy in Blida Province. The authorities have also linked the measure to an increase in such crimes in recent years, without providing nationwide figures.
The NADA Network for the Defense of Children’s Rights has estimated that around 1,000 children in Algeria are victims of abductions or attempted abductions each year, according to figures cited in a 2026 academic study.
In Algeria, capital punishment is already provided for offenses including murder and certain terrorism and state-security crimes. In 2025, its scope was expanded to cover several drug-related offenses. Algerian courts have continued to hand down death sentences, but no executions have been carried out for more than 30 years.
The death penalty remains on the books in a number of African countries, although most have either abolished it or stopped carrying out executions.
Amnesty International criticized the bill and urged Algeria’s upper house to reject it. The group called the move a “dangerous step backwards” and warned that it comes alongside government statements indicating that executions could resume after more than three decades.

Pope Leo XIV receives the President of Montenegro
Vatican News
Pope Leo XIV received the President of Montenegro, Mr. Jakov MilatoviÄ, in audience on Saturday morning in the Vatican.
The President subsequently met with Vatican Secretary of State, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, accompanied by Vatican Secretary for Relations with States and International Organizations, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher.
According to a communiqué issued by the Holy See Press Office, during cordial talks at the Secretariat of State, the good relations existing between the Holy See and Montenegro were noted, and matters of common interest were discussed.
The conversation also focused on a number of international and regional issues, with particular attention to the integration of Montenegro and other Western Balkan countries into the European Union, as well as the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine.
During his presidency, President MilatoviÄ has also been received in audience by the late Pope Francis, on 7 March 2024.

By Deborah Castellano Lubov
âThis one Faith in Christ is the principle of unity among the faithful,â Pope Leo XIV said, recalling that the Lord prayed for His disciples to be united.
The Pope made these remarks on Saturday in the Vatican when he addressed the community of the Pontifical Teutonic College of Santa Maria in Campo Santo on the 150th anniversary of its foundation.
He encouraged its members to make Christâs prayer for unity their own and to ensure that the College remains a place where such unity âcan be concretely lived and made visible.â
Such unity, Pope Leo reaffirmed, âconstitutes an essential element for the credibility of our witness.â
Rich history
The Holy Father began by expressing his joy at meeting the community and recalling the long history of the Campo Santo as a privileged point of reference for pilgrims travelling to Rome from the territories of the Holy Roman Empire, dating back to the eighth century.
In the nineteenth century, Pope Leo recalled, the site assumed particular importance for priests from those countries, at a time when the ministry of the clergy was severely impeded, if not rendered altogether impossible, as a result of the ecclesiastical policies of the Kulturkampf in the German Empire.
Through the hospitality extended by the Archconfraternity of the Campo Santo Teutonico, the Pope explained, the site became âa place of refuge and studyâ for priests from the German-speaking regions.
The Campo Santo subsequently developed, Pope Leo continued, âinto an important centre for Christian archaeology, Church history, and research into Christian origins.â
The Pope told those gathered that they could look back with gratitude upon âthe rich fruits of this history.â
An important role today
The Holy Father went on to highlight the Collegeâs importance for the Church today.
âEven today, the College for priests seeks to be a secure place of formation,â Pope Leo said, so that the clerics who live there may deepen their âintellectual and spiritual journey.â
The Pope explained that this formation should enable them to respond to the questions of people in their homelands âin the face of the great challenges of our timeâ and to âgive an account of the hope that is in usâ (cf. 1 Pt 3:15).
Pope Leo also highlighted a distinctive characteristic of the College: its unique proximity to the tomb of Saint Peter the Apostle.
From the very beginnings of the institution, the Pope said, this closeness has gone hand in hand with âa faithful adherence to the Roman Pontiff.â
Pope Leo noted that this is reflected in the title âPontifical Collegeâ, which Pope Benedict XVI conferred upon the institution in 2010.
Preserving closeness and unity with the Successor of Peter
âSuch an honour,â Pope Leo said, âalso entails a commitment: to preserve this closeness and unity with the Successor of Peter and with the Faith of the Apostles which he proclaims.â
The Pope then returned to the importance of Christian unity, urging the members of the College to make Jesusâ prayer their own.
âMake this heartfelt supplication of Jesus your own,â Pope Leo said, urging them to âask for this gift,â so that the community of the College may be a place where unity âcan be concretely lived and made visible.â

items.body_text:
Pope appoints Cardinal Gambetti as new Archbishop of Chieti-Vasto
By Vatican News
Pope Leo XIV on Saturday appointed Cardinal Mauro Gambetti, 60, a Conventual Franciscan, as the new Archbishop of Chieti-Vasto, transferring him from his positions as Vicar General of His Holiness for Vatican City, Archpriest of St. Peterâs Papal Basilica in the Vatican, and President of the Fabric of Saint Peter.
He succeeds Archbishop Bruno Forte, 77, who submitted his resignation from the pastoral governance of the archdiocese due to the age limit.
Created a Cardinal by Pope Francis in November 2020, Gambetti was called on February 20, 2021, to take up his positions at the Vatican. Previously, from 2013 to 2020, he served as Custos of the Sacred Convent of St. Francis in Assisi.
Born on October 27, 1965, in Castel San Pietro Terme in Bologna, after obtaining a degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Bologna, Mauro Gambetti began his journey with the Order of Friars Minor Conventual in September 1992, making his final profession of vows in September 1998.
After obtaining a Bachelorâs degree in Theology from the Theological Institute of Assisi in Perugia, he earned a Licentiate in Theological Anthropology from the Central Italy Theological Faculty in Florence.
He was ordained a priest on January 8, 2000, in Longiano at the Convent of the Most Holy Crucifix. There, he served as director of youth and vocational ministry for Emilia-Romagna and, from 2005 to 2009, also served as guardian friar, responsible for and animator of the religious community.
In the spring of 2009, his fellow friars of the Bolognese Province of St. Anthony of Padua elected him Provincial Minister. Then, on February 22, 2013, the Orderâs Minister General called him to serve as General Custos of the General Custody of the Sacred Convent of St. Francis in Assisi for the four-year term from 2013 to 2017.
In 2017, he was reconfirmed as Custos of the Sacred Convent for the 2017â2021 term, a position he held until October 30, 2020, when he was assigned the titular see of Tisiduo with the personal title of Archbishop. He received episcopal consecration on November 22, 2020, at the Basilica of St. Francis in Assisi.
At the consistory of November 28, 2020, Pope Francis created and proclaimed him a Cardinal, assigning him the Deaconry of the Most Holy Name of Mary at the Trajan Forum.
Following his appointment, on February 29, 2021, as Vicar General of His Holiness for Vatican City, Archpriest of St. Peterâs Papal Basilica in the Vatican, and President of the Fabric of Saint Peter, Francis also appointed him in June 2023 as a judge of the Court of Cassation of the Vatican City State.
Cardinal Gambetti is a member of the Dicastery for Institutes of Consecrated Life and Societies of Apostolic Life.
